papers.abstract: Modern video moment retrieval systems often propose windows that overlap the target event, yet still select the wrong one. We study this scorer bottleneck on QVHighlights with a fixed QD-DETR-derived temporal expert: the parent-aware temporal expert reaches 64.71 R1@0.5, while diagnostic oracles over the same candidate family reach 75.68 R1@0.5 within the parent-reranked pool and 94.97 R1@0.5 over the full 100-candidate evidence pool. We introduce OVET-Consensus, a rank-preserving counterfactual event verification layer that keeps the temporal expert's ranked list as the default and permits only high-confidence rank-1 overrides from a policy calibrated on held-out training videos. The verifier uses parent-aware interval evidence, structured Qwen3-VL event judgments, VideoLLaMA3 pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence, but never lets those signals freely reorder the top-K list. On QVHighlights validation, OVET-Consensus improves the parent-aware temporal expert from 64.71 to 65.35 R1@0.5 with a positive paired-bootstrap interval, while mAP is largely unchanged, from 42.67 to 42.74; it makes 20 overrides, with 15 helpful corrections and 3 harmful corrections. The results point to a practical constraint on verifier design: semantic compatibility is useful evidence, but temporal grounding still requires deciding where the event starts, changes, and ends inside a visually compatible scene.
bullets: Targets the scorer bottleneck: systems often retrieve windows overlapping the event but select the wrong one.
Combines parent-aware interval evidence, structured vision-language judgments, pairwise temporal signals, and dense temporal evidence.
Preserves the temporal expert’s ranking by default; only high-confidence rank-1 counterfactual overrides are permitted.
On QVHighlights validation, R1@0.5 rises from 64.71 to 65.35, while mAP remains nearly unchanged (42.67 to 42.74).
Among 20 overrides, 15 were helpful and 3 harmful, highlighting the need for precise temporal boundary grounding.

papers.abstract: State-of-the-art world models have been used to produce sequences of gameplay that accord with provided user-input actions. However, high quality, consistent gameplay generation often comes at the cost of inference speed, making real-time interactive play and ideation challenging. The substantial quantities of data used to train state-of-the-art models have also made custom training of these models appear impractical, limiting many of their potential uses in creative fields. In this work we demonstrate a major step towards efficient world models: achieving both fast high-quality inference, and improved data efficiency. This is done by replacing the next-token prediction paradigm with a two-stage discrete diffusion-based approach, introducing a lightweight refinement transformer which carries out iterative masked predictions. Building on an autoregressive world model capable of generating highly consistent and complex sequences over minutes (Kanervisto et al., 2025), we achieve substantial model speed-up (79x) with a modest quality trade-off. Additionally, we demonstrate that this model can be trained to reproduce high-quality, consistent gameplay using a dataset containing approximately one day (28 hours) of gameplay data. Our results demonstrate progress towards removing barriers to the use of world models in settings where real-time inference and data efficiency are essential.
authors: Raluca Stevenson, David Bignell, Jennifer C. White, Tabish Rashid, Emanuele Aiello, Mariya Hendriksen, Junha Hyung, Sadegh Aliakbarian, Abdelhak Lemkhenter, Marko Tot, Katja Hofmann, Sarah Parisot
bullets: Targets the slow inference and heavy data requirements that limit interactive and creative uses of world models.
Replaces next-token prediction with two-stage discrete diffusion and iterative masked prediction via a lightweight refinement transformer.
Builds on an autoregressive model designed for consistent, complex gameplay over minutes.
Demonstrates high-quality, consistent gameplay training using approximately one day of gameplay data.
Scope: the speed–quality trade-off and data-efficiency claims are demonstrated for gameplay generation.

papers.abstract: Reward models for instruction-guided video editing can favor temporal consistency at the expense of motion. We study this failure, termed \emph{motion collapse}, using controlled motion-suppression variants of real edits. On VE-Bench, the evaluated composite reward prefers a motion-suppressed candidate in $97\%$ of cases. Learned video rewards and a VLM judge also struggle with mild suppression, while latent optimization and reward-guided fine-tuning exploit this weakness to increase reward as motion declines. A linear probe of our base reward backbone performs near chance on mild suppression, motivating an explicit inter-frame dynamics input. We propose a motion-aware reward model that combines an RGB frame-difference stream with preference training against motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives. A distillation anchor preserves alignment with human quality judgments. On the VE-Bench motion ladder, our model reduces the rate of selecting motion-suppressed candidates to $0\%$ while achieving a Spearman correlation of $0.57$ with human quality ratings. It also detects unseen suppression variants and preserves motion during reward-guided fine-tuning on two editing pipelines. These results support explicitly modeling motion in rewards for video editing.
authors: Li Li, Xiangbo Gao, Bo Ni, Samyadeep Basu, Viet Dac Lai, Jing Shi, Seunghyun Yoon, Gang Wu, Yu Wang, Thien Huu Nguyen, Tyler Derr, Franck Dernoncourt, Zhengzhong Tu, Yue Zhao
bullets: The study identifies “motion collapse,” where reward models prefer motion-suppressed edits; the baseline does so in 97% of VE-Bench cases.
Learned video rewards, a VLM judge, latent optimization, and reward-guided fine-tuning all show vulnerability to motion suppression.
The proposed model adds an RGB frame-difference stream and trains on motion-suppressed and fabricated-motion negatives, with a human-quality distillation anchor.

It selects motion-suppressed candidates in 0% of motion-ladder cases, reaches 0.57 Spearman correlation with human ratings, detects unseen suppression variants, and preserves motion during fine-tuning.
Scope: the method is evaluated on VE-Bench and two editing pipelines.

papers.title: Motion-Aware Reward Modeling for Instruction-Guided Video Editing
papers.tldr: A motion-aware reward model prevents video-editing rewards from favoring temporally consistent but unnaturally static edits.

papers.abstract: Omnimodal large language models (Omni-LLMs) integrate audio, video, and text for multimodal reasoning, yet remain vulnerable to cross-modal hallucinations, where one modality improperly influences predictions about another. Existing training-free decoding methods mitigate these errors through modality perturbation or relevance-based weighting. However, due to interference from irrelevant modality cues during fusion and difficulty detecting shared errors, these methods may suppress correct unimodal predictions and allow erroneous consensus to persist. To address these limitations, we propose Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding (PACD), a training-free framework for mitigating cross-modal hallucinations. PACD comprises two complementary paths based on whether the branches reach consensus. For non-consensus cases, Relevance-Guided Candidate Arbitration identifies task-relevant unimodal evidence and selectively arbitrates between predictions using alternative candidates. For consensus cases, Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery leverages the outranking principle to evaluate the consistency and strength of layer-wise modality evidence for alternative answers, selectively resolving erroneous consensus under confidence constraints. Extensive experiments on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across two tasks demonstrate the superiority of PACD. Compared to existing methods, PACD achieves up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding across CMM, AVHBench, and SVHalluc for cross-modal hallucination mitigation, and an average relative improvement of 7.7% over best baseline across OmniVideoBench and FutureOmni for general audio-visual reasoning.
authors: Chang Sun, Yijun Tian, Zhenwei Tang, Yuchen Deng, Yifan Simon Liu, Chenxu Wang, Wei Wang
bullets: Targets hallucinations caused when irrelevant or misleading audio, video, or text cues distort another modality’s prediction.

Uses Provenance-Based Consensus Recovery when branches agree, checking layer-wise evidence consistency and strength to detect false consensus.
Evaluated on four Omni-LLMs and five benchmarks across hallucination mitigation and audio-visual reasoning tasks.
Reports up to 27.6% relative improvement over standard decoding and 7.7% average improvement over the best baseline, as stated in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Training-free decoding to mitigate cross-modal hallucinations in Omni-LLMs; directly relevant to multimodal LLM reasoning and video-language understanding.
papers.title: PACD: Provenance-Aware Consensus Decoding for Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations in Omnimodal Large Language Models
papers.tldr: PACD is a training-free decoding framework that reduces cross-modal hallucinations in omnimodal LLMs by using modality evidence provenance to arbitrate disagreement and correct erroneous consensus.

papers.abstract: Large sign-language corpora benefit from temporal labels at two scales: subtitle spans for subtitle alignment and word spans for sign spotting. Sign spottings already locate words in time at corpus scale, but training subtitle alignment jointly on subtitle and word spans remains underexplored. We present SignAligner, a prompt-conditioned visual-language span generator that maps a sign-language video and a subtitle-sentence or target-word query to a textual start/end frame interval. It is first trained jointly on subtitle spans and word spans from sign spottings, then refined with overlap-based rewards while retaining auxiliary word examples. On the subtitle test set of the British Broadcasting Corporation-Oxford British Sign Language (BOBSL) corpus, the refined model reaches 66.68 F1@0.50 (F1 with a temporal intersection-over-union threshold of one half), the best among compared systems without external sign-video resources. This overlap-reward refinement outperforms cross-entropy continuation from the same jointly trained model. Joint training with word spans improves subtitle alignment in a pair of our generators matched in code, labels and maximum update budget. The advantage remains after both models of the pair are refined with overlap rewards. For word queries, the refined model follows the queried word, not a fixed position in the video: when the word's sign lies away from the video centre, it is far more accurate than predictions that use position alone. Together, these findings support one shared span generator refined with overlap rewards, aligning subtitles and producing word spans for human review.
authors: Jongbhin Woo, Youngjoon Jang, Joon Son Chung
bullets: Targets two granularities: subtitle spans for alignment and word spans for sign spotting.
Uses a prompt-conditioned visual-language generator to predict start/end frames for sentence or word queries.

Achieves 66.68 F1@0.50 on the BOBSL subtitle test set, best among compared systems without external sign-video resources.
Word-query predictions follow the queried sign rather than relying on fixed video position; scope is evaluated on BOBSL and matched comparison systems.

papers.abstract: Video understanding with multiple multimodal language models requires a communication interface that can transfer complementary visual observations. Text-based communication is interpretable, but introduces an intermediate generation stage and can omit information relevant to subsequent reasoning. We study Cross-Modal StateKV Injection, a provider--carrier framework that communicates through key--value (KV) states at visual-token positions. Provider models observe complementary video frames; their visual KV states are aligned and projected into the carrier representation space and integrated through gated residual updates. Injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while retaining the additional computation required by the providers and the communication module. The reported experiments on MLVU and Video-MME compare carrier-only inference, text-based communication, and StateKV with two provider architectures. Results show modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower reported latency than the evaluated text-communication baseline, with some categories remaining unchanged or decreasing. Increasing provider-side frame coverage offers additional gains on selected tasks without extending the carrier cache. These findings motivate further study of visual KV communication under explicitly controlled observation and computation budgets.
bullets: Addresses information loss and extra generation cost in text-based communication between multimodal language models.
Provider models observe complementary video frames and transfer projected, aligned visual KV states to a carrier model via gated residual updates.
The injection preserves the carrier KV-cache sequence length, while adding provider and communication-module computation.
Experiments on MLVU and Video-MME report modest, task-dependent accuracy gains and lower latency than the evaluated text-based baseline.
More provider-side frame coverage helps selected tasks, but some categories are unchanged or worse; computation budgets remain an open consideration.

papers.selection_reason: Cross-modal KV-state communication between MLLMs for video understanding while preserving carrier cache length, touching both video understanding and KV-cache efficiency.
papers.title: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection for Communication in Multi-LLM Systems across Temporal Segments
papers.tldr: Cross-Modal StateKV Injection enables multimodal LLMs to communicate complementary video information through aligned visual KV states, yielding modest task-dependent gains and lower latency than text communication.

papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models rely on a decoder to map denoised latents to pixels, adding complexity and inference cost. We introduce Decoding Without a Decoder (DWD), which lets a finetuned diffusion transformer produce final pixels directly through a linear head. Unlike previous methods, where the denoising output leads to final pixels, DWD separates the two roles: the original denoising head continues to drive sampling, then the new DWD head predicts the pixels at the final step. We extend pretrained latent models with DWD efficiently by finetuning only the last few transformer blocks, training the DWD head with pixel quality losses while anchoring the denoising head to the pretrained model to preserve the sample trajectory. Across latent image and video generators, DWD removes the decoder and reduces inference cost while maintaining or even improving pixel quality. On Wan video generation, it visibly reduces detail distortion and flickering, lowering warping error by 23%. Remarkably, the same separation also improves pixel diffusion models that do not even use a decoder: a final-step DWD head produces substantially better texture detail in text-to-image generation, and improves ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43, a new state of the art among pixel flow models.
authors: Hansheng Chen, Shengqu Cai, Jan Ackermann, Rayhan Zirvi, Gordon Wetzstein, Xinchen Yan, Leonidas Guibas
bullets: Addresses the complexity and inference cost of decoders in latent diffusion models.
Adds a linear DWD pixel-prediction head while retaining the original denoising head for sampling.
Efficiently adapts pretrained models by finetuning only the final transformer blocks and anchoring the denoising behavior.
Works across image and video generators, reducing detail distortion and flickering; Wan’s warping error drops by 23%.
Also improves pixel diffusion models, raising ImageNet FID from 1.55 to 1.43 and enhancing texture detail.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Last-layer tokens support more accurate linear pixel reconstruction. (b, c) Probes of last-layer tokens preserve finer image detail and reduce video ghosting before finetuning.

(a) On the latent FLUX.2 klein models, DWD closely matches the baseline’s content and texture without the decoder (zoom in to view detail). (b) On the pixel AnisoFlow model, DWD preserves the composition while recovering photorealistic texture in bark, foliage, and clouds. The large panels are zoomed crops, with the full image inset.

papers.selection_reason: Removes decoder from latent diffusion transformers with a direct pixel-prediction head, improving video and image diffusion generation and reducing inference cost.

papers.tldr: DWD enables diffusion transformers to predict final pixels directly, eliminating the latent decoder while preserving or improving image and video quality.

papers.abstract: Short-video platforms are now a common way for the public to follow unfolding events. Their rapid, visually persuasive format also makes fake news easier to spread. Unlike text-image posts, short-video news interleaves multiple modalities and changing scenes, making it difficult to identify which frames verify a claim. Existing detectors either pool sampled frames homogeneously or select them by text-frame similarity. Both overlook that aligned frames may repeat a misleading claim, whereas less dominant context may challenge it. We present CEVA (Complementary Evidence Verification Approach), to our knowledge the first short-video fake news detection framework to explicitly organize frames by their evidential roles before multimodal fusion. Its Dual-Branch Complementary Reorganization (DBCR) module separates explicit-alignment frames from candidate complementary-context frames, and cross-modal fusion with bidirectional contrastive regularization operates on the reorganized evidence. On FakeSV and FakeTT, CEVA achieves the best overall results among the compared methods. Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based selection and improves two structurally different detectors. Together, these results establish pre-fusion evidence organization as an effective and transferable component of short-video fake news detection.
authors: Wenshen Yang, Junfeng Hao, Jing Li, Decheng Liu, Yangkunfei, Shuyu Jiang, Haizhou Wang
bullets: Short videos combine changing visual scenes and multiple modalities, making relevant verification frames difficult to identify.
CEVA’s DBCR module separates explicitly aligned frames from potentially complementary context frames.
Bidirectional contrastive regularization is applied during cross-modal fusion of the reorganized evidence.
CEVA achieves the best overall results among compared methods on FakeSV and FakeTT.
Under fixed frame budgets and backbones, DBCR outperforms uniform, random, and similarity-based frame selection across two detector architectures.

papers.title: CEVA: Complementary Evidence Verification via Frame-Level Reorganization for Short-Video Fake News Detection
papers.tldr: CEVA improves short-video fake news detection by reorganizing frames according to whether they support or challenge a claim before multimodal fusion.

papers.abstract: The effectiveness of a video diffusion model's inference budget depends on where computation is spent along the denoising trajectory. Across eight equal-budget inference configurations, VBench total scores span 4.80 points, highlighting the importance of explicit allocation design. Our key insight is that guidance evaluations are not equally valuable across diffusion time: retaining the sampling updates while selectively reusing guidance can preserve generation quality with fewer denoiser evaluations. We introduce BATMoS (Budget Aware Temporal Mixture of Strategies), which routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser. A magnitude-based temporal rule assigns guidance reuse to low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh guidance for the remaining blocks, with a single integer controlling the computation budget. The resulting schedule requires no additional router training or per-budget threshold search. Evaluated on CogVideoX-2B with 4,720 videos per configuration across all sixteen official VBench dimensions, BATMoS achieves the highest total score among the eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full classifier-free guidance using 20\% fewer branch evaluations. BATMoS also composes with feature reuse, reducing computation from 80 to 62 effective branch evaluations with a 0.11-point decrease in total score. These findings make temporal guidance allocation a practical mechanism for extracting more generation quality from a fixed inference budget.
authors: Zhixu Du, Kuo Yang, Jingwei Sun, Hai "Helen" Li, Yiran Chen
bullets: Inference quality varies substantially with how a fixed computation budget is allocated along the denoising trajectory.
BATMoS routes between fresh classifier-free guidance and cached guidance using a single pretrained denoiser.
A magnitude-based temporal rule reuses guidance in low-magnitude blocks and reserves fresh evaluations elsewhere, controlled by one integer budget parameter.
On CogVideoX-2B across all 16 VBench dimensions, it achieves the best score among eight allocation policies and comes within 0.10 points of full guidance with 20% fewer branch evaluations.
Combined with feature reuse, it reduces effective branch evaluations from 80 to 62 with a 0.11-point score decrease.

The vertical axis is logarithmic. The shaded region contains the blocks selected for guidance reuse at 𝐵 = 80. (b) Replacing one five-update block of fresh CFG with guidance reuse saves five branch evaluations. A prefix of the fixed magnitude ranking determines the schedule, with 𝐵 = 100 − 5𝑘 .

Fig. 3: Guidance allocation and feature reuse retain different quantities. (a) Full CFG refreshes the conditional– unconditional difference. A later guidance-reuse update combines that cached difference with a fresh conditional prediction. (b) Internal residual reuse operates inside two-branch CFG runs. Run boundaries refresh the stack, and one-branch guidance-reuse updates execute all blocks. The strip shows full-stack CFG (dark blue), guidance reuse (hatched red), and residual reuse (pale blue). Their update counts are 21, 20, and nine, yielding 62 effective NFE.

papers.abstract: A grounded reasoning chain cites a frame span and a box for every step, so a reader can check where the model looked. Whether the answer depends on the cited region is a different question. We test it by intervention: the regions a model cited in its own chain are blacked out, and the share of correct answers that flip is compared with blacking out boxes of the same size elsewhere on the same frames. The paired difference, the cite gap, needs no annotation. We apply it to 2-3B video-language models trained on exact CLEVRER chains and on pseudo-labelled NExT-QA chains. With the same weights, the cite gap is 0.089 on CLEVRER and 0.003 on NExT-QA. Pooled over models, masking the cited boxes flips 2.2 times as many correct answers as the control on CLEVRER and 1.1 times as many on NExT-QA, also among the answers that depend on the video at all, while the boxes pass a grounding check on both. Masking the cited entity on every frame, instead of the cited box, flips 1.9 times as many answers as its control. The NExT-QA chains were supervised to cite two frames of entities that stay visible on most frames, so this outcome is what the supervision predicts; the point is that the usual check on grounded chains cannot see it. A citation can be verifiable and relevant without the answer depending on it, and a test of grounded reasoning should remove what a chain names, not only where it points.
bullets: The study tests whether answers depend on the regions models cite in their reasoning chains.
It blacks out cited boxes and compares answer flips with same-sized control boxes elsewhere in the frames; the difference is the cite gap.
On CLEVRER, the cite gap was 0.089, with cited-box masking flipping 2.2× as many correct answers as controls.
On NExT-QA, the cite gap was 0.003 and cited-box masking caused only 1.1× as many flips; cited entities remained visible across most frames.
Grounding checks alone miss this distinction: citations can be verifiable and relevant without being causally necessary for the answer.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Pipeline and tests. Chains are generated exactly for CLEVRER and pseudo-labelled for NExT-QA (real frames with the evidence boxes of one chain), and a 2–3B model learns to emit them. Both tests start from the regions the trained model cited: the self-citation test masks the cited boxes or the same boxes moved elsewhere; the entity-track test does the same for the named entity on every frame.

Figure 1. The self-citation test on two items from the same model. Left: the frame with the regions the mixed chain SFT model cited (orange). Middle: those regions blacked out. Right: boxes of the same size at random positions (illustrative placement). On CLEVRER (top) masking the citations flips the answer and masking elsewhere does not; on NExT-QA (bottom) the citations sit on the named entities and the answer survives either mask.

Figure 3. Cite gaps on CLEVRER and NExT-QA (95% question-clustered bootstrap intervals). Left: on CLEVRER the answers of all five tested chain models depend on their cited boxes, somewhat less than on the annotated evidence (hollow). Right: on NExT-QA the cite gap of the models trained on NExT-QA chains, of a second seed and of a chain-free control is at most 0.004; removing the cited entities from every frame (diamonds) gives a gap of 0.05 over all items and 0.10–0.11 on correct options.

Per-opt. is per-option accuracy (always-“no” 0.80), Sel. picks the option judged “yes” and is comparable to the letters prompt, and the blind gap is in per-option accuracy (per-question for the letters row). Flip rates are over the items correct under the plain input; 95% intervals in brackets. ‡ Control: this chain-free model is masked with the mixed chain SFT model’s citations. The pooled row covers the five models trained on NExT-QA chains. Further accuracy columns are in the supplement (Tab. S4).

papers.selection_reason: Counterfactual intervention test for grounded reasoning chains in video-language models, directly relevant to video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: Does the Model Use What It Cites? Counterfactual Tests of Grounded Reasoning Chains in Small Video-Language Models
papers.tldr: A citation can be correctly grounded yet irrelevant to a model’s answer, so grounded reasoning should be tested by removing what the chain names—not just where it points.

papers.abstract: Deepfake detectors often perform well on the dataset they are trained on, but their performance drops when tested on videos from different datasets. In this paper, we study whether a predictive video model can provide a signal that generalizes better across datasets. Instead of relying only on generator-specific artifacts, as many existing detectors do, we use a model trained to predict natural video and measure the difference between what it predicts and what it observes in a video. Using V-JEPA 2.1, we keep the encoder frozen and adapt the predictor using rank-16 LoRA. We define the difference between the predictor output and the frozen encoder target as the prediction residual. We hypothesize that manipulated clips produce, on average, larger prediction residuals than authentic clips, and use this as our consistency-margin prior. We process these residuals using a lightweight Latent Consistency Head (LCH), which separates residual magnitude from direction for training and classification. To test whether the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset generalization, we compare standard and reversed margin objectives while keeping the remaining training setup fixed. We match the two settings on FF++ validation performance before evaluating them on unseen data. The reversed-margin setting exhibits a larger cross dataset generalization gap on average, providing evidence that the direction of the consistency margin affects cross-dataset transfer. Our complete model adds only 8.25M trainable parameters, which is 2.47% of the total 334M parameters. Trained only on FF++, it achieves an AUC of 90.5 on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well across several other cross-dataset benchmarks. Our ablations show that separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using a low-rank projection improve cross-dataset generalization in our experiments.
authors: Pradip Gupta, Shubham Mandloi, Ravi Kumar Satzoda, Sujeeth Bharadwaj, Yassine Benajiba, Dan Roth
bullets: Deepfake detectors often lose accuracy across datasets because they rely on generator-specific artifacts.
The method uses V-JEPA 2.1 with a frozen encoder, a rank-16 LoRA-adapted predictor, and a Latent Consistency Head to analyze prediction residual magnitude and direction.
It tests standard versus reversed consistency-margin objectives; the reversed direction produces a larger cross-dataset generalization gap.
Trained only on FF++, the model reaches 90.5 AUC on Celeb-DFv2 and performs well on other cross-dataset benchmarks.
Ablations support separating residual magnitude from direction, reducing dataset-specific variation, and using low-rank projection; the model adds 8.25M trainable parameters.

papers.abstract: Play is used as an indicator of positive welfare in dairy calves, but openly available video of group-housed calves with individual behaviour annotations is scarce. We describe video from four camera deployments of about one week each in group pens of dairy calves on two farms in the Netherlands: a research and teaching dairy farm (2024 and 2025) and a commercial dairy farm (2024). The recordings comprise 1,173 video files spanning 651 h. For eight observation days, trained observers coded calf behaviour continuously in Noldus The Observer XT with an 18-item ethogram of play and other behaviours, covering 104 h of video, 90 h of which have every calf in the pen coded. The release also contains 1.1 million decoded frames from seven annotated sessions, a per-frame timestamp read by optical character recognition from the camera clock burned into each frame, per-calf segmentation tracks and per-calf frame-level play labels. The data support studies of calf behaviour and welfare and the development and evaluation of automated behaviour recognition.
authors: Haiyu Yang, Heidi Lesscher, Enhong Liu, Miel Hostens
bullets: Covers four week-long camera deployments across research and commercial farms in the Netherlands.
Includes 1,173 video files spanning 651 hours of group-housed calf recordings.
Trained observers annotated eight days using an 18-item ethogram, including play and other behaviours.
Provides 1.1 million decoded frames, camera-clock timestamps, per-calf segmentation tracks, and frame-level play labels.
Supports behavioural welfare research and development or evaluation of automated recognition systems.

papers.abstract: The EgoLink Challenge at ACM Multimedia 2026 benchmarks egocentric multimodal intelligence linking first-person perception, social reasoning, and interactive action. Unlike benchmarks centered on visible objects and activities, EgoLink evaluates whether models can interpret emotional and social cues, resolve visually grounded references, and convert user requests into verified tool-mediated actions. Its two tracks cover social reasoning in egocentric video and interactive agents that complete service tasks through dialogue, tool use, and closed-loop execution. Together, they test whether perception, reasoning, and decision-making remain coupled under both offline question answering and state-changing interaction. We highlight a multi-stage Track 1 data pipeline for multiple-choice question (MCQ) generation, chain-of-thought generation, automatic quality grading, and video-contribution filtering. We summarize the task design, evaluation metrics, rules, leaderboards, and representative solutions. The benchmark combines objective answer scoring with process- and result-based evaluation, enabling analysis of both final correctness and execution quality. The best Track 1 system achieved 0.9263 accuracy, while the best Track 2 system achieved 0.844 joint success and 0.916 micro accuracy. Participant reports reveal a shared principle: strong systems make intermediate evidence explicit through candidate verification, option-robust reasoning, scenario-aware planning, tool canonicalization, and state-aware correction before answering or acting. These findings highlight the importance of process verification and evidence-grounded reasoning for reliable egocentric multimodal intelligence.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
bullets: Addresses missed brief or localized artifacts and the rigidity of fixed multi-agent inspection workflows.
Uses an investigator agent to select artifact types, inspection windows, and stopping points.

Reports 95.2% average accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain, and agentic benchmarks, with localized evidence grounding.

papers.abstract: Video anomaly detection (VAD) is a fundamental and safety-critical task in computer vision. Recent generative approaches detect anomalies from a distributional perspective, but remain limited by local anomaly modes. Meanwhile, video anomaly anticipation (VAA), as a proactive extension beyond post-hoc detection, introduces additional challenges. In particular, the contrastive inference paradigm in VAD, which relies on ground-truth frames, is not applicable to VAA, hindering its development. To address these challenges, we propose a unified score-driven framework, termed Uni-DSM, based on denoising score matching (DSM), which models anomaly patterns through likelihood estimation and score functions over the learned data distribution. Within this unified framework, we adopt a shared noise-conditioned score transformer backbone with scene-dependent embeddings and motion-aware weighting for distribution-level modeling. Instead of introducing separate architectures, Uni-DSM unifies VAD and VAA through different inference and supervision paradigms built upon the same score-based formulation. For VAD, we instantiate an autoregressive denoising score matching (ADSM) mechanism, which progressively accumulates anomalous evidence via autoregressive denoising, enabling enhanced perception of local modes beyond visual cues. For VAA, we extend the same architecture by incorporating a lightweight auxiliary decoder and a novel self-distilled denoising score matching (SDSM) mechanism. By constructing supervision from output discrepancies instead of relying on unavailable future ground truth, our method achieves efficient training suitable or early anomaly anticipation. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both VAD and VAA while maintaining high efficiency, establishing a unified and scalable pipeline from anomaly detection to anticipation.
bullets: Addresses local anomaly-mode limitations in generative VAD and the lack of future ground truth in VAA.
Uses a shared noise-conditioned score transformer with scene-dependent embeddings and motion-aware weighting.
Applies autoregressive DSM for VAD to accumulate anomalous evidence beyond visual cues.
Applies self-distilled DSM with a lightweight decoder for efficient early anomaly anticipation without future labels.
Reports state-of-the-art performance and high efficiency across multiple benchmark datasets, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Generating high-quality and controllable camera motion is essential for AI-assisted cinematography, video synthesis, and 3D scene understanding. We introduce TKCAM, a Text- and Keyframe-conditioned CAMera-motion synthesis framework based on generative masked modeling. We represent camera dynamics using a 12-dimensional kinematic feature comprising position, velocity, and a continuous rotation representation and discretize them into hierarchical motion tokens via a Residual Vector Quantizer (RVQ). A two-stage masked transformer architecture then learns to reconstruct and refine these tokens, utilizing explicit self- and cross-attention modules for multimodal conditioning. A central feature of our framework is sparse visual keyframe conditioning: users can provide free-form text prompts together with RGB observations at selected timestamps, which provide temporally localized visual guidance for generating coherent in-between trajectories. Furthermore, to advance evaluation standards, we curate RealEstate10K-Cap, a large-scale text-camera dataset, and establish a cross-domain benchmark with a Universal CLaTr Evaluator. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TKCAM surpasses recent state-of-the-art baselines on Fréchet distance (FID), text-motion matching scores, and retrieval metrics (R@K), while additional analyses evaluate temporal smoothness and cross-domain generalization. Code and RealEstate10K-Cap dataset are available at https://github.com/linearalgebrayhz/TKCAM.
bullets: Addresses coherent, high-quality camera-motion synthesis for cinematography, video generation, and 3D scene understanding.
Encodes camera dynamics as 12-dimensional kinematic features, discretized into hierarchical tokens with a Residual Vector Quantizer.

Reports improvements over recent baselines in FID, text-motion matching, and retrieval metrics, with analyses of smoothness and generalization.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of our proposed pipeline. Given per-frame camera poses M as trajectory, a text description T and sparse keyframe images V , we first encode the continuous 12-dimensional camera trajectory into latent features and discretize them with a multi-level Residual Vector Quantizer (RVQ), producing a hierarchy of base-layer (green) and residual-layer (orange) motion tokens. During training, a masked base transformer predicts masked base-layer tokens conditioned on the text embedding from a frozen T5 encoder and visual tokens extracted by a frozen CLIP encoder, while a masked residual transformer refines higher-level residual tokens conditioned on the previously predicted tokens and the same multimodal context. Finally, a motion decoder reconstructs smooth and temporally coherent camera trajectories from the predicted hierarchical motion tokens.

papers.abstract: Audio-driven facial animation underpins real-time avatars, telepresence, and embodied virtual agents. And it must run online: each frame emitted from audio observed up to the current time, at interactive rates. Recent progress is dominated by diffusion models, which need many network evaluations per sample and are therefore a poor fit for streaming. We argue the cost is unnecessary in this domain. Audio-conditioned facial motion occupies a comparatively low-dimensional manifold, a regime where a single-pass GAN suffices. The obstacle is not capacity but stochastic structure. We show that a causal, time-invariant generator driven by i.i.d. noise cannot suppress its output spectrum over a band without collapsing its per-step innovation. We proposed FaceGAN, which dissolved the limitation by shaping the noise pathway acausally. Because the driving noise is synthetic, its future can be sampled now, so the audio-to-expression path stays causal, and the model supports fully causal operation. FaceGAN emits expression and head pose in a single forward pass per frame and matches or outperforms state-of-art approaches in generation quality. Being feed-forward with bounded attention windows, it generates indefinitely without drift.
bullets: Targets streaming facial animation for avatars, telepresence, and embodied agents without diffusion’s many per-sample evaluations.
Shows that causal, time-invariant generators driven by i.i.d. noise struggle to suppress output-spectrum bands without losing per-step variation.
Shapes the synthetic noise pathway acausally, while preserving a causal audio-to-expression path and fully online operation.
Generates facial expression and head pose in one forward pass per frame, with bounded attention windows for indefinite generation without drift.
The abstract reports generation quality matching or outperforming state-of-the-art approaches.

papers.abstract: Long video generation should keep the subject and background consistent while supporting rich, natural motion. However, autoregressive models are often distilled with distribution matching distillation (DMD) over short windows, which does not train them to keep this consistency over long ranges. As a result, the subject and background can drift over time. Methods that manage the key-value (KV) cache retain or retrieve history to reduce drift. Yet this history may itself have drifted. We propose Reference Forcing, which uses the initial frames as an appearance reference. We first build a teacher that uses attention masks to force each region of a new frame to attend to the same region in the initial frames. The teacher finds these regions with off-the-shelf segmentation models. We then distill this behavior into a separate attention path of the student, which needs no external models at inference. We further introduce value correction, which corrects drifted values in the KV cache toward the matching values of drift-free initial frames. Experiments show that Reference Forcing achieves state-of-the-art subject and background consistency among long-video methods on different base models, and its advantage grows with video length. Ablations show both components are needed to gain consistency without losing motion. More visualizations and code are available at https://zhaosheng-thu.github.io/reference-force/
authors: Sheng Zhao, Haitian Zheng, Weikai Lin, Junjie Zhao, Yuhao Zhu
bullets: Addresses consistency loss caused by training autoregressive video models on short windows.
Uses segmentation-guided attention masks to make new-frame regions attend to matching regions in the initial frames.
Distills this reference-guided behavior into a separate student attention path that requires no external models at inference.
Applies value correction to move drifted KV-cache values toward corresponding values from the initial frames.
Reports state-of-the-art subject and background consistency across different base models, with larger gains for longer videos; both components preserve motion.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Reference Forcing. (a) Each chunk Xn is generated from the first chunk X0, the recent window, and noisy tokens, with the anchor path of (b) and the value correction of (c). (b) In every layer, the student adds an anchor path (LoRA on the query and keys, and the anchor gate w) to the frozen native attention and learns to match the prediction of a teacher whose anchor path is masked by the subject mask and the background flow. papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding is becoming increasingly important for real-world interactive systems. Such systems must be proactive for natural and useful human interaction: they should respond as soon as sufficient evidence becomes available while avoiding premature, redundant, or incorrect responses. We present BLIP-Live, a framework unifying data, metrics, harness, and training around a shared formulation of proactivity as effective causal response decisions balancing the two competing objectives of responding vs silence. First, we construct BLIP-Live-780K dataset containing human annotations of proactive response content and timing, which defines this desired behavior. We then propose PAUC-F, a metric to effectively measure our desired proactive behavior. PAUC-F combines existing response timeliness metrics with firing precision to reward early useful responses without rewarding excessive firing. With our desired behavior defined and measurable, we finally investigate model-agnostic inference harnesses that draw out proactive streaming capabilities of offline vision language models (VLMs), together with training pipelines that learn to further improve their proactive responsiveness. Across both settings, we find that combinations of sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured response outputs consistently yield strongest proactive performance. Our experiments result in two models, with our BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieving state-of-the-art performance across four proactive streaming benchmarks, with gains up to 44% over baselines and outperforming multiple closed API models. Our code and data will be released publicly.
authors: Kanchana Ranasinghe, Honglu Zhou, Dominick Reilly, Le Xue, Shusheng Yang, Juan Carlos Niebles, Silvio Savarese, Ran Xu
bullets: Introduces BLIP-Live-780K, a human-annotated dataset covering proactive response content and timing.
Proposes PAUC-F, which balances response timeliness with firing precision.
Studies model-agnostic inference and training pipelines for making offline VLMs proactive in streaming video.
Finds that sliding visual windows, online interaction memory, and structured outputs consistently work best.
The BLIP-Live-Qwen model achieves state-of-the-art results on four proactive streaming benchmarks, with reported gains of up to 44% over baselines.

papers.abstract: Understanding long videos requires locating evidence, resolving visual details, and integrating observations into an answer. Even when relevant evidence is present, performing these operations within long, dense visual sequences burdens both perception and reasoning. Video agents enable selective inspection, but returning frames to the planner still accumulates visual information in its reasoning context. Delegating perception reduces this burden, yet sparse sampling can miss decisive details, and per-frame descriptions can preserve context growth. We introduce VideoNexus, a training-free framework that separates detailed video perception from evidence-driven planning and reasoning. The planner controls where to inspect, what to resolve, and how densely to sample. Perception sub-agents process native audio-video in independent contexts and return compact, temporally grounded evidence for iterative search and verification. Using Gemini 3.8 Flash for both planning and perception, VideoNexus achieves 88.6% accuracy on full LVBench, exceeding same-backbone static ingestion and built-in agentic processing by 3.6 and 1.1 points, respectively, at 44% of the latter's measured API cost. A paired LVBench subset ablation shows lower planner input and higher accuracy. With Kimi K3 as the shared backbone, VideoNexus improves over the official Video-GAIA ReAct harness by 8.5 points in our evaluation. These results support compact evidence exchange for combining detailed observation with efficient planning and reasoning.

papers.abstract: Visual artifact tasks test agents' ability to translate task specifications and source materials into outputs that meet practical needs. Evaluation across artifact families helps distinguish broadly applicable authoring capabilities from strengths confined to a particular medium. We introduce VisualArtifactSpec 1.0 (VAS), a benchmark of 211 creation and modification tasks spanning presentations, static graphics, animations and videos, and web interfaces. Each task specifies authoring objectives, source materials, constraints, and deliverables. Existing benchmarks provide limited support for systematically evaluating how authoring choices suit different audiences, purposes, and media across artifact families. VAS evaluates two aspects separately: Task Fulfillment verifies explicit requirements and applicable functionality, while Artifact Performance assesses Content, Organization, Visuals, and Delivery. Task-specific rating anchors instantiate shared criteria for the intended audience, purpose, and medium, with judgments grounded in source materials and artifact inspection records. We evaluate nine model-harness configurations on all 211 tasks. Overall scores range from 42.12 to 70.52, with Artifact Performance accounting for 73.4% of the gap between the highest- and lowest-scoring configurations.

papers.abstract: Streaming video LLMs can continuously observe the world, yet often handle user requests in isolation. We introduce ALIVE, an interactive streaming video model supporting proactive monitoring, streaming task coordination, and feedback-seeking interaction. We construct ALIVE-SFT-288K and ALIVE-RL-3K for two-stage training. Contrastive supervised fine-tuning teaches when and how to respond, while reinforcement learning with Behavior-Aligned Credit Assignment (BACA) combines trajectory-level and local advantages to refine decisions, responses, and silence across multi-turn interactions. We also introduce FSI-Bench to evaluate feedback seeking and subsequent task completion. ALIVE achieves the highest overall scores among the compared models on four public benchmarks and FSI-Bench, demonstrating strong streaming understanding and interactive capabilities.
authors: Jinzhao Li, Yuan Xu, Jinxuan Wu, Yukun Wang, Yijia Lei, Hanyu Ji, Yinuo Chen, Zining Huang, Chi Zhang, Hang Ye, Yiwu Zhong, Honglei Yan, Panwang Pan, Yizhou Wang, Yin Li, Miao Liu
bullets: Targets the limitation of streaming video models that process user requests in isolation.

papers.abstract: Streaming video generation must sustain quality beyond the training horizon while handling self-generated history and growing cache costs. To address these challenges, we present MovieRoll, a base-to-distilled framework that connects streaming fine-tuning, long-rollout distillation, and long-horizon inference. We first establish a robust multi-step base through Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF), which jointly denoises chunks at progressive noise levels with bidirectional attention within each window and causal access to preceding history. To retain historical context efficiently, hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) exploits layer-wise attention patterns, retaining full history in shallow layers and sink--recent history in deeper layers. This reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality. Building on this base, cumulative long tuning with distribution matching distillation (CuLT-DMD) holds parameters fixed throughout each long self-rollout and averages local gradients before updating. Each update therefore combines supervision across temporal positions while retaining only one local computation graph, enabling efficient long-rollout training of a few-step generator. To extend generation beyond the training horizon, KV recomputation bounds context for both models, while guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) reduces guidance toward the clean endpoint to stabilize MovieRoll-Base. Complementing these modeling advances, FBCA attention and PS-VAE decoding support efficient training and streaming output. On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30s after training on videos of up to 15s, and MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among the compared methods across single- and multi-event evaluations up to 60s, combining sustained naturalness with active motion.
authors: Yunyang Ge, Weijie Kong, Ryan Xu, Yue Wu, Qi Tian, Jiangfeng Xiong, Bin Lin, Mingzhe Zheng, Shenghai Yuan, Zheyuan Liu, Jianwei Zhang, Li Yuan
bullets: Targets quality degradation beyond the training horizon, self-generated history, and increasing KV-cache costs.
WinTF builds a multi-step base using window-wise denoising with local bidirectional attention and causal access to prior history.
HieraKV reduces cache memory by up to 78% while improving generation quality by adapting retained history across layers.
CuLT-DMD enables efficient long-rollout distillation by aggregating gradients across temporal positions while keeping one local computation graph.
On HeliosBench, MovieRoll-Base remains competitive at 30 seconds, while MovieRoll-Distilled achieves the highest total scores among compared methods through 60 seconds.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of MovieRoll. Window-wise Teacher Forcing (WinTF) trains MovieRoll-Base through parallel window supervision conditioned on clean history and event prompts. After ODE initialization, Cumulative Long Tuning with Distribution Matching Distillation (CuLT-DMD) trains a few-step generator by averaging local gradients across long self-rollouts. Both models jointly denoise a rolling window, use hierarchical KV-cache compression (HieraKV) to retain history across layers, and rebuild the cache at a history threshold or prompt switch. Classifier-free guidance annealing (AnnealCFG) gradually reduces guidance during base-model denoising.

Figure 3 WinTF learns rolling generation through parallel supervision of windows with progressive noise levels. Phase offsets expose the model to both short prefill windows and full decoding windows. Within each window, later chunks receive higher noise levels. The attention mask combines bidirectional interactions within a noisy window with access to clean preceding history, while isolating noisy windows from one another. This allows multiple windows to be trained in parallel, each conditioned on its own event prompt and preceding clean history.

Figure 5 CuLT-DMD combines supervision across a long rollout in each generator update. The top panel shows local distillation supervision from teacher and critic predictions. LongLive-style training updates the generator from individual windows while carrying detached history forward. CuLT-DMD instead keeps parameters fixed throughout the rollout and averages the local gradients before updating. This incorporates supervision from multiple temporal positions while retaining one local computation graph at a time.

Figure 6 AnnealCFG reduces the late-denoising extrapolation produced by constant guidance throughout 30s generation. Across prefill and early, middle, and late decoding, the left plots show the additional latent-update magnitude induced by guidance. The right plots show its share in the final 20% of denoising steps. Annealing lowers both the late-step peaks and their contribution to the total update. Results aggregate 32 paired prompts, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals shown by bands and whiskers.

Figure 7 KV recomputation refreshes historical context for generation beyond the training horizon. Fullhistory caching expands the context as video length grows, while sliding-window caching retains dependencies on evicted chunks. At the history threshold, recomputation selects sink, intermediate, and recent chunks and causally re-encodes them into a fresh cache. This bounds the retained context and removes cached dependencies on discarded chunks before generation continues.

Figure 8 Flash Block-wise Causal Attention (FBCA) implements block-causal attention with efficient FlashAttention kernels. Each query block gathers its visible prefix, historical states, and current states into an independent attention sequence. KV unfolding and grouping organize these sequences within a per-call packing budget, and variable-length FlashAttention processes them before restoring the original block order. This preserves the required attention pattern while controlling the size of each packed buffer.

Figure 1 MovieRoll generates a minute-long video with continuous subject identity across six events. The sequence shows the same woman performing successive actions in one studio setting, with a new prompt every 10s. Each frame represents one event, and the text below summarizes its prompt.

Figure 4 Layer-dependent attention patterns motivate hierarchical history retention. In the WinTF-trained model, shallow layers distribute attention broadly across historical chunks, while deeper layers place relatively more attention on the sink and most recent chunks. The heatmap and lower entropy and coverage plots show this shift with depth. HieraKV follows these patterns by retaining full historical context in shallow layers and restricting deeper layers to the sink and most recent chunks.

Figure 9 The Parallel Streaming Variational Autoencoder (PS-VAE) supports continuous video decoding through temporal caching and spatial parallelism. The upper panel shows how cached decoder states carry temporal context across arriving latent chunks, allowing each chunk to be decoded as it becomes available. The lower panel distributes high-resolution decoding across GPUs through row partitioning and boundary exchange. Together, these designs support streaming output and reduce per-GPU decoding cost.

Figure 10 Qualitative comparison of 10s single-event video generation. Under the same prompt of a mermaid combing her hair on a seaside rock, MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled retain recognizable subjects and consistent surroundings as poses and waves change. Rows compare methods evaluated under the same prompt, and columns show successive temporal intervals within each 241-frame video.

Figure 11 Qualitative comparison of 30s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled preserve the facial features, clothing, and surroundings of a man eating at a bar as the action continues. Rows compare methods under the same prompt, and columns follow the 721-frame sequence, showing how subject and background consistency evolve during generation.

Figure 17 Memory and latency comparison across full-history and sink--recent attention allocations. The left plot shows slower cache-memory growth when fewer layers retain full history. At 18 cached chunks, the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local layers reduces memory from 48.7 to 10.8 GiB and peak denoising-step latency from 33.8 to 15.8s relative to all-global attention. Measurements use MovieRoll-Base with CFG on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Each timed denoising step includes both conditional and unconditional DiT evaluations. Timing excludes KV recomputation and VAE encoding/decoding.

Figure 16 Ablation of long-horizon extrapolation strategies. All three strategies use the same Stage 1 MovieRollBase checkpoint to extend generation from 10s training clips to 30s videos. Full-history and sliding-window caching produce increasingly washed-out backgrounds, whereas KV recomputation preserves clearer subject and street details through the end of the sequence.

Figure 12 Qualitative comparison of 60s single-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves the diver and underwater environment with relatively stable colors as generation continues. Rows compare methods under the same diver-and-wreck prompt, and columns follow successive 10s intervals of the 1441-frame videos.

Figure 26 Examples of multi-event video generation with sequential prompts. The upper examples show threeevent, 30s videos from MovieRoll-Base, and the lower examples show six-event, 60s videos from MovieRoll-Distilled. Prompts change every 10s, with one frame representing each event. Both models retain recurring characters and settings as new interactions develop, such as a cat reacting to a robotic vacuum and a keeper responding to a seagull.

Figure 13 Qualitative comparison of 30s multi-event video generation. The sequence progresses from sketching a flower to observing a frog and raising a camera, with a prompt change every 10s. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts these action changes while retaining the botanist and rainforest setting. Each row shows one method, and each pair of columns corresponds to one event.

Figure 14 Qualitative comparison of 60s multi-event video generation. The sequence develops from paddling to successive interactions with an otter, including surfacing beside the kayak, handling a rock, and approaching the hull. MovieRoll-Distilled depicts this event progression while maintaining a consistent lake setting. Rows compare methods under the same six sequential prompts, and each column represents one 10s event.

Figure 27 Potential extensions of rolling-window video pretraining. (a) Smaller chunks allow finer noise progression and temporal advances at a fixed frame budget, while loss weighting or regularization could balance learning across noise levels. (b) Total-duration conditioning could guide overall pacing, while duration triggers locate active windows and shot transitions. Together with multi-shot training, these conditions could support coordinated shot sequences under one prompt.

Figure 24 Examples of 60s single-event videos generated by MovieRoll-Distilled. This first set of six examples includes miniature ships, an origami dragon, and underwater performances. MovieRoll-Distilled preserves subject appearance as waves, steam, and gestures evolve. Each two-row group follows one 1441-frame video from left to right and then top to bottom, with frame indices overlaid and its prompt below.

Figure 18 Ablation of HieraKV attention allocations. The comparison varies the allocation of 54 transformer blocks between full-history and sink–recent attention. With the default HieraKV allocation of 6 global and 48 local blocks, the rider and horse remain recognizable throughout the sequence. All-global attention progressively crops the subje ts, while all-local attention shifts toward a close rear view.

Figure 22 User preference comparison for multi-event video generation. MovieRoll-Distilled wins a majority of judgments against every evaluated baseline, with win rates from 62.3% to 81.9%. Each bar reports win, tie, and loss rates from the MovieRoll-Distilled perspective under the same prompt sequences, pooling judgments across 30s three-event and 60s six-event videos with ties included in the denominator.

Table 8 Shared architecture and history-cache configuration of the MovieRoll models. Both variants use an 8.3-billion-parameter backbone with text conditioning, a causal video VAE, and a five-chunk active window. The first six transformer blocks retain full history, while the remaining 48 retain the sink and most recent chunks, preserving broad historical context through a small subset of layers.

Table 2 Comparison of video decoding speed, memory use, and reconstruction quality. Single-GPU PSVAE outperforms the tested tiling methods in runtime and reconstruction PSNR. Spatial parallelism further reduces decoding time and per-GPU memory. With eight GPUs, PS-VAE achieves a 3.97× decoding speedup over its singleGPU version while preserving high numerical agreement. Measurements decode 1441 frames at 480× 864 on NVIDIA H20 GPUs in FP16.

Table 9 Inference settings of MovieRoll-Base and MovieRoll-Distilled. Distillation reduces sampling from 50 steps to 5 while preserving the shared rolling-generation pipeline. MovieRoll-Base uses guidance annealed from 4 to 1, whereas MovieRoll-Distilled operates without CFG. Both use the same chunk and window sizes and rebuild their KV caches at the same history threshold. Denoising passes are counted per output chunk, with the conditional and unconditional CFG branches contributing separately to the reported count.

Table 1 Efficiency comparison of block-causal attention implementations. The comparison evaluates fullhistory attention with three or five windows on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. FBCA achieves the lowest forward and backward runtimes across fixed and varying input shapes, with preparation taking less than 0.1s when shapes vary. In multiple-shape tests, it also reduces peak memory relative to FlexAttention, supporting efficient training across inputs with different spatial resolutions.

Table 10 Training stages and hyperparameters of MovieRoll. The two base-model stages introduce single-event and multi-event streaming generation. ODE initialization then transfers the base model to a few-step student, and CuLT-DMD trains it on self-generated rollouts. The columns summarize the data and optimization settings supporting this progression. The two distillation phases are denoted by P1 and P2, while G and F identify the generator and fake-score critic in the optimization settings for each phase.

Table 6 Single-GPU inference efficiency for 60s video generation. The table compares denoising and endto-end costs across methods at the listed resolutions for 1441-frame videos on one NVIDIA H20 GPU. Switching from FlashAttention-3 to SageAttention increases MovieRoll-Distilled end-to-end throughput from 1.52 to 2.04 FPS. Single-GPU throughput remains below the 24 FPS playback rate required for real-time generation.

Table 5 Quantitative ablations of training and inference designs. WinTF outperforms chunk-wise formulations, while the selected HieraKV allocation, KV recomputation, long-rollout CuLT-DMD, and AnnealCFG schedule achieve the highest total scores within their respective comparisons. Shaded rows identify these choices. Autoregressive formulations are evaluated at 241 and 721 frames, and the remaining comparisons use 721 frames. Higher ratings indicate better quality and less drift.

Table 14 Comparison ofGPT-5.2 andGemini-2.5-Proas video evaluators. Both evaluate the same 30s single-event videos and rank MovieRoll-Distilled first and MovieRoll-Base second. Method rankings agree closely, with Spearman correlation ρ = 0.930. We use Gemini-2.5-Pro because it provides greater score separation between methods, as shown by the statistical measures in the lower section.

Table 11 Rollout settings for the two CuLT-DMD training phases. Phase 1 uses single-event, 241-frame rollouts lasting 10s. Phase 2 extends training to two-event, 721-frame rollouts lasting 30s. Both phases average local gradients across each rollout, allowing one update to incorporate supervision from multiple temporal positions. Bounded score clips keep distillation supervision local as the generated sequence grows.

Table 15 Distribution of user-study judgments across baselines and video durations. The study collects 2616 preference judgments across single-event and multi-event comparisons. Each cell counts individual judgments for MovieRoll-Distilled versus the listed baseline at a given duration. Judgments are pooled across durations to calculate win, tie, and loss rates for each baseline, separately for single-event and multi-event generation. Each judgment contributes one vote, including ties.

Table 13 Conversion of HeliosBench quality and drift metrics to a common rating scale. The listed intervals map raw metric values to ratings from 1 to 10 for weighted aggregation. Higher quality scores and lower drift scores receive higher ratings, so higher converted ratings consistently indicate better performance.

Table 7 Inference scaling across GPU counts and attention backends. Increasing the GPU count improves MovieRoll-Distilled throughput with both backends, and SageAttention is faster at every tested count. On eight NVIDIA H20 GPUs, the best setting generates a 60s video in 152.2s, reaching 9.47 FPS. Real-time generation at 24 FPS remains a limitation even with eight GPUs. Videos contain 1441 frames at 480× 864.

Table 12 HeliosBench metrics, evaluators, and aggregation weights. Five full-video metrics cover aesthetics, dynamics, motion smoothness, semantic alignment, and naturalness. papers.abstract: Few-step autoregressive video diffusion enables efficient long video generation, but inference still incurs substantial computational costs from repeated denoising and KV cache operations. Existing acceleration methods reduce parts of this overhead, while historical KV reading and cache construction remain costly across video chunks. To address these challenges, we propose ScoutCache, a training-free framework that jointly optimizes denoising, historical KV reading, and cache construction. We observe that shallow feature changes provide useful information for estimating clean latent updates, while historical KV dependence varies across Transformer layers and attention heads but remains relatively stable across video chunks. Based on these observations, we develop Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations. We further introduce Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical reading budgets based on attention output perturbations, and Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to reduce cache construction costs by selecting informative spatial tokens while maintaining spatial coverage. Extensive experiments on Self-Forcing and LongLive using VBench and MovieGen demonstrate that ScoutCache achieves up to 2.28$\times$ and 1.86$\times$ speedups, respectively, while consistently improving generation quality without modifying pretrained model parameters.
authors: Hao Tan, Jinghui Qin, Xuming Hu
bullets: Targets the remaining inference bottlenecks in long-video generation: repeated denoising and KV-cache operations across video chunks.
Uses Conditional Denoising Readout (CDR) to estimate intermediate denoising updates from shallow feature changes and known noise variations.
Applies Output Risk Guided Historical KV Reading (ORHR) to allocate historical KV-reading budgets across layers and attention heads.
Uses Content and Coverage Guided Sparse Cache Construction (CCSC) to select informative spatial tokens while preserving coverage.
Achieves up to 2.28× speedup on Self-Forcing and 1.86× on LongLive, with consistently improved quality and no pretrained-parameter changes.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in image and video generation have enabled high-fidelity synthesis at higher resolutions and longer durations, making the quadratic cost of dense self-attention a major bottleneck as visual token sequences grow. Sparse attention seeks to preserve generation quality at lower computational cost by retaining informative query-key interactions and omitting less consequential ones, with end-to-end gains depending on the cost of constructing sparse support and the efficiency with which the system maps the resulting workload to hardware. We survey sparse attention for visual generation through a 4+1+3 analytical framework that links algorithmic design to system implementation. The framework examines how static and dynamic methods use source information and the evidence derived from it to decide which interactions to retain and at what granularity, while accounting for the roles of reuse in reducing repeated computation and correction in compensating for omitted contributions. We relate these algorithmic choices to their implementation on hardware through the framework's three system dimensions of data organization, execution, and dataflow. We summarize common evaluation metrics and discuss open challenges and research directions, providing researchers and practitioners with a reference for the joint design of sparse attention algorithms and systems.
authors: Majun Zhang, Yuan Guo, Decheng Wu, Jiayang Xu, Changhao Pan, Fan Zhuo, Xiaoda Yang, Chenyuhao Wen, Zhou Zhao
bullets: Dense self-attention becomes a major bottleneck as image and video token sequences grow.
The proposed 4+1+3 framework analyzes static and dynamic sparsity, selection granularity, reuse, and correction for omitted interactions.
It links algorithmic choices to three system dimensions: data organization, execution, and dataflow.
The survey reviews evaluation metrics, implementation considerations, open challenges, and future research directions.

papers.abstract: While the ability of video generation models to accurately depict scientific phenomena has received growing attention, determining whether these models genuinely understand the underlying principles remains a critical challenge. Existing benchmarks typically evaluate video samples in isolation, making it difficult to expose models that simply fit superficial visual priors. In scientific experiments, a small change in one condition produces a markedly different outcome even when the rest of the setup remains fixed. Capitalizing on this sensitivity, we introduce SciWorldBench, a benchmark comprising paired scientific experiments. Each pair varies a single condition in an otherwise fixed setup, yielding two mutually exclusive expected outcomes. Each generation prompt specifies the condition but omits the expected outcome. We evaluate ten text-and-image-to-video (TI2V) models using an independent vision-language model (VLM) that assesses each video without access to the condition text or the label identifying the correct outcome. A pair is scored as correct only when both videos depict their respective scientifically correct outcomes. Across all ten models, we find that the two videos in an experimental pair frequently depict the same outcome even though the conditions require different results. This recurring failure suggests that current video world models struggle to apply the underlying scientific principles reliably during generation. We will publicly release the benchmark dataset and open-source the evaluation code.
authors: Xue Yang, Haonan Cai, Xinyu Hang, Zhimeng Huang, Xuanyi Liu, Chuanmin Jia, Siwei Ma
bullets: Introduces paired scientific experiments with mutually exclusive expected outcomes and a single changed condition.
Evaluates ten text-and-image-to-video models using an independent vision-language model blinded to prompts and labels.
Scores a pair as correct only when both videos show the scientifically correct outcomes.
Finds that models often generate the same outcome for both conditions, indicating unreliable scientific reasoning.
The benchmark dataset and evaluation code will be publicly released.

papers.abstract: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.
authors: Xudong Ling, Wenjie Luo, Chaorong Li, Tianxi Huang, Tao He, Guiduo Duan
bullets: Addresses the cost and blurring caused by independently sampled generative ensemble forecasts.
Uses a vision-language model to generate a textual storm-evolution scenario that conditions a Rectified Flow generator.
Shares early sampling steps across ensemble members, then branches with fresh noise for local convective details.
Uses support-consensus decoding instead of pixel averaging to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores.
Across six datasets, achieves the best high-threshold CSI, with reported relative gains of over 10%–84%; an 8-member ensemble costs 5.2× rather than 8× a single forecast.

papers.abstract: Real-time camera-controlled video re-filming aims to synthesize target views from a streaming source video under online user-specified camera trajectories. This task poses two key challenges: maintaining synchronization and content consistency across views, and achieving low-latency rendering with long-horizon stability. Existing approaches are predominantly designed for offline full-sequence processing and rely on bidirectional attention or costly depth-based geometric preprocessing, making them unsuitable for low-latency streaming scenarios. To address these limitations, we develop a teacher-to-student framework that distills a high-fidelity bidirectional re-filming teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student. We introduce Cross-Frame Injection to interleave each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent, thereby establishing direct cross-view correspondence and improving content consistency. To ensure stable long-horizon generation, we further propose Shared Relative RoPE, which bounds temporal indices within the pretrained range, and Cycle Streaming Tuning, which exposes the student to extended cyclic trajectories during streaming training. These designs enable low-latency online video re-filming with precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency over long streaming rollouts.
authors: Youcan Xu, Xinjie Huang, Jiaxin Shi, Hengye Lyu, Zhen Wang, Jun Xiao, Long Chen
bullets: Targets online novel-view video synthesis under user-specified camera trajectories.
Distills a high-fidelity bidirectional teacher into a few-step causal autoregressive student.
Cross-Frame Injection links each incoming source frame with its synchronized target latent for cross-view consistency.
Shared Relative RoPE and Cycle Streaming Tuning support stable long-horizon streaming generation.
The abstract reports precise camera control and sustained spatiotemporal consistency, without specific quantitative results.
