papers.abstract: Multimodal humor detection requires interpreting language, vocal delivery, and visual behavior jointly. Expressive fusion must also regulate how interactions of different orders enter the final judgment. We propose M\"obius Interaction Filtering (MoIF), which learns a modality-subset prediction function and imposes order-selective spectral regularization through its aggregation structure. Private temporal encoders and balanced reciprocal interaction construct supervised unimodal, bimodal, and trimodal predictors. Their uniform aggregate is exactly a M\"obius-domain filter with a geometrically decreasing interaction-order response. This formulation retains higher-order representations while regulating their contribution to prediction. Controlled UR-FUNNY perturbations reveal a pronounced decline in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio across interaction orders. The induced filter improves the final ratio by 1.62-2.79 times relative to the co-trained trimodal predictor while preserving its own clean class-aligned signal under perturbation. Five-seed experiments achieve 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, exceeding thirteen reproduced methods on these detection metrics. CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI evaluations establish applicability to sentiment prediction, and cross-seed analyses show more stable estimates on all three datasets. MoIF connects the organization of multimodal interactions to their statistical reliability through an executable spectral constraint. Code is available at https://github.com/D-ST-Sword/MoIF.
bullets: Targets unreliable high-order interactions in joint language, vocal, and visual reasoning.
Uses private temporal encoders, balanced reciprocal interactions, and unimodal/bimodal/trimodal predictors.
Applies a uniform aggregate as a Möbius-domain filter with geometrically decreasing emphasis on interaction order.
Perturbation studies show a 1.62–2.79× improvement in label-aligned signal-to-noise ratio over a co-trained trimodal predictor.
Reports 70.6% accuracy and weighted F1 on UR-FUNNY, with applicability and more stable estimates on CMU-MOSI and CMU-MOSEI.

papers.tldr: MoIF filters multimodal interactions by order, preserving useful higher-order information while reducing noise in humor and sentiment prediction.

papers.abstract: We introduce CNP-Flow, a flow matching framework for temporal generation that learns conditional source distributions through flow reversal. Whereas standard conditional flow matching (FM) incorporates conditioning through the vector field and draws source samples from a standard Gaussian, CNP-Flow uses a conditional noise predictor (CNP) to produce an isotropic Gaussian source for each temporal condition. The CNP is supervised by source samples obtained through flow reversal, which maps observed targets backward through a pretrained FM model. A three-stage pipeline pretrains the FM model, trains the CNP, and fine-tunes the FM model using the learned source distribution, while preserving the FM backbone architecture. Across video prediction, video interpolation, and 7-DoF Franka robot motion planning, CNP-Flow consistently improves generation quality. It also matches baseline performance with fewer function evaluations. Project page: https://embodiedai-ntu.github.io/cnpflow
bullets: Standard conditional flow matching uses a fixed standard-Gaussian source and encodes conditions only in the vector field.
CNP-Flow trains a conditional noise predictor to generate an isotropic Gaussian source tailored to each temporal condition.
Its three-stage pipeline pretrains flow matching, learns sources from backward-reversed target samples, then fine-tunes the flow model.
The method improves generation quality across video prediction, video interpolation, and 7-DoF Franka motion planning.
It matches baseline performance with fewer function evaluations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the proposed three-stage training pipeline. Stage 1: A pretrained FM is used to obtain flow-reversal-induced source samples, defining a source distribution aligned with the target data. Stage 2: The CNP is trained to model this distribution by predicting a conditional Gaussian prior via NLL and KL objectives. Stage 3: The FM model is fine-tuned using source samples drawn from the learned conditional prior, resulting in more coherent and target-aligned transport trajectories.

papers.abstract: Benchmark scores license claims about the capabilities being evaluated. We audit the inference licensed by an evaluation protocol, rather than the predictive model alone. Using procedural action anticipation as a controlled case study, we study a broader evaluation-validity failure mode: a protocol can remain temporally causal and free of classical target leakage while still supplying a privileged intermediate representation. The failure is not merely optimistic accuracy, but a mismatch between the capability claimed and the construct actually measured. On Breakfast, matched recognizer-history and GT-history regimes score 30.3% and 62.3% (Delta_PH(R_BA) = +32.0, 95% Student-t interval [+24.1, +39.8]). A fixed-checkpoint 2 x 2 intervention isolates a +14.6-point test-time oracle contrast; a matched no-video provenance probe yields a +26.8-point gap; and a boundary-independent query/history control retains a +19.4-point gap. We refer to this discrepancy as a privileged-information gap, defined relative to a specified non-oracle recovery pipeline, and propose a reusable four-condition audit. Across five evaluation settings the gap is heterogeneous; a standard 50 Salads long-term-anticipation re-implementation provides cautious support beyond the audit-specific next-action construction.
bullets: Audits the validity of evaluation protocols, not just predictive models.
In Breakfast, ground-truth history scores 62.3% versus 30.3% for recognizer history, a 32.0-point privileged-information gap.
Controlled interventions show the gap persists without video and under boundary-independent history controls.
Proposes a reusable four-condition audit and finds heterogeneous gaps across five evaluation settings.
Evidence beyond the audit-specific setup is cautiously supported by a 50 Salads re-implementation.

papers.tldr: Evaluation protocols for action anticipation can appear causal yet overstate capability by giving models privileged intermediate information.

papers.abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Sicheng Gao, Junan Hu, Kunyang Li, Dongyang Chen, Yiyang Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Yong Jae Lee, Radu Timofte, Yuzhang Shang
bullets: Addresses difficulties in precise spatial structure, coherent motion, and controllable scene composition in video generation.
Uses code-driven 3D scene construction to produce draft videos with structural and motion signals for downstream generators.
Introduces a training pipeline with supervised fine-tuning, agentic reinforcement learning, and dual execution/video rewards.
Employs an annealing strategy that shifts reliance from execution feedback to video quality during training.
Reports gains of approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0, with data, models, and code released.

papers.abstract: 3D spatial reasoning from video remains challenging for VLMs because videos provide sequential, view-local observations rather than persistent metric scene records. Many questions must be answered in a query-specified perspective rather than the observed camera viewpoint, and prompting with a fixed set of RGB views may miss sparse or occluded visual cues. To address these gaps, we introduce BEV3SR, a training-free and backbone-agnostic framework for RGB-D videos with camera parameters. BEV3SR turns video observations into queryable metric bird's-eye-view (BEV) scene memory and formalizes each query into an evidence-aware spatial task. The Spatial Task Formalizer specifies the query's reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and evidence requirement. The evidence requirement determines the appropriate reasoning pathway. A query treated as requiring geometric evidence is handled by the Geometric Reasoner, which deterministically computes the answer using the metric BEV records in the query-specified reference frame. Otherwise, a query treated as requiring visual evidence is passed to the Visual Evidence Aligner, which uses BEV-indexed object records and their associated supporting views to retrieve object-consistent and scene-context RGB frames for VLM grounding. Within a standard 16-frame budget, BEV3SR consistently improves different VLM backbones across multiple 3D scene QA benchmarks, delivering large gains on spatially intensive questions and significant improvements on open-ended scene QA. These results demonstrate that BEV3SR offers an effective, efficient, and interpretable framework for explicit 3D spatial reasoning from video.
bullets: Addresses view-local, sequential video observations, query-specific viewpoints, and sparse or occluded evidence.
Formalizes each query’s reference frame, spatial constraints, objective, and required evidence.
Computes geometry-based answers deterministically from metric BEV records in the requested reference frame.
Retrieves object-consistent and contextual RGB frames for VLM grounding when visual evidence is needed.
Improves multiple VLM backbones across 3D scene QA benchmarks, especially spatially intensive and open-ended questions, within a 16-frame budget.

papers.abstract: Editing a video stream in real time, without access to future frames, is essential for interactive applications. Existing training-free video editing methods, however, assume full offline access to the entire sequence, while streaming approaches either rely on additional training or are limited to specific editing techniques. We show that this limitation can be removed by analyzing the self-attention dynamics of DMD-distilled autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models. We uncover a key asymmetry: queries and keys remain stable and aligned with their source counterparts across denoising timesteps, while values diverge and encode the evolving content. Inherited from the non-distilled bidirectional teacher, this asymmetry is strongest at high noise, where few-step streaming models operate. The resulting mechanism is simple: a single forward pass suffices to capture source identity in the value features, which can be reused throughout generation. Starting from pure Gaussian noise and injecting only these source values reconstructs the input with fidelity matching or surpassing inversion-based methods, effectively eliminating inversion. Based on this insight, we introduce AR-Edit, a training-free, inversion-free method that caches source values once and selectively injects them during denoising. Across multiple AR backbones, AR-Edit enables real-time streaming editing with superior source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.
authors: Hovhannes Margaryan, Quentin Bammey, Christian Sandor, Vicky Kalogeiton
bullets: Addresses the need for online video editing without future-frame access, training, or technique-specific constraints.
Analyzes self-attention in DMD-distilled autoregressive video diffusion models and identifies stable query/key alignment but evolving value features.
Caches source values in a single forward pass and selectively injects them during denoising from Gaussian noise.
Across multiple autoregressive backbones, achieves real-time editing with improved source preservation and tonal fidelity at minimal overhead.

AR-Edit (right) runs on an autoregressive backbone [67, 21, 40], processing frames causally: it caches source value features in one pass and injects them at denoising pure noise conditioned on the target prompt.

papers.abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .
authors: Zhongyi Zhang, Jingyu Xiao, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
bullets: Introduces a benchmark of 124 real-world webpages across 7 domains and 33 animation types, paired with reference videos and original static assets.
Provides a two-dimensional evaluation protocol measuring static appearance fidelity and animation fidelity across aligned frames.
Finds that webpage animation reconstruction is harder than reproducing static visual appearance.
Shows that explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve coding-agent reconstruction quality.
Reports that rapid, continuous motion is more difficult to reproduce than discrete state transitions.

papers.abstract: Dense video object captioning (DVOC) localizes, tracks, and describes object trajectories within a video. Existing methods process each camera view independently, producing separate camera-local tracklets and captions for the same person across cameras. These outputs lack a unified description and leave complementary appearance evidence across views unused. We therefore formulate cross-view DVOC (CVDVOC), which associates these tracklets into scene-level global trajectories and generates one caption for each trajectory from synchronized views. To support this task, we construct CRTrack-Cap from CRTrack by auditing text-identity links and converting usable referring expressions into canonical captions. It retains 425 global trajectories and 838 local tracklets across 13 scenes, with canonical captions for 335 identities. We adapt CHOTA to the cross-view setting as CV-CHOTA to jointly evaluate tracking and caption quality. Our reference framework combines View-Exclusive Cross-Camera Association (VECA) for grouping tracklets with Conflict-Evidence Gating (CEG) for integrating caption evidence using its reliability and disagreement across views. Against three single-view methods adapted with MvMHAT for cross-view association, our framework achieves CV-CHOTA scores of 83.43 and 33.48 on the scene-disjoint in-domain and cross-domain tests, respectively. Together, CRTrack-Cap and our framework provide a benchmark and a strong baseline for describing the same person consistently across camera views.

papers.abstract: We address geometric video alignment for the same scene captured by multiple freely moving cameras. Existing methods, which are based on image stitching or video stabilization, are typically limited to two cameras or must assume the restrictive setting of a fixed linear ordering of the cameras. We propose MViS, a lightweight test-time optimization framework for joint multi-view alignment with temporal consistency. MViS uses a spatial-transformer-inspired net to jointly process frames from all views within a short temporal window and predict per-view, per-time homographies. Optimization proceeds in two stages: geometry-guided alignment followed by appearance-based refinement, with both stages enforcing multi-view and temporal consistency across the sequence. The method requires no scene-specific hyperparameter tuning, handles arbitrary and time-varying view-intersection graphs, and remains robust under rapid camera motion. On a standard two-view video benchmark, MViS matches or surpasses the state of the art. To facilitate evaluation in more complex scenarios, we introduce an annotated dataset with more than two freely moving cameras and establish the first benchmark for this setting. Project page: https://bgu-cs-vil.github.io/MViS-project/ .
authors: Shira Ifergane, Roy Amoyal, Shahar Benishay, Oren Freifeld

papers.abstract: The task of weakly supervised video anomaly detection is challenging. Existing approaches mainly model video frame features and determine whether anomalies are present based on their magnitudes. In this work, we propose a novel method that incorporates external knowledge into training to improve model performance, robustness, and generalization. We leverage textual prompts and a large language model (LLM) to establish prior information for the specific task, and employ dictionary learning to normalize and compress this information. Moreover, during experiments, we observed inconsistencies in the textual descriptions extracted from similar video frames by image caption models. To address this, we devise a method that leverages an LLM and auxiliary information to ensure consistency in the textual descriptions of similar frames within a video. Finally, we introduce a feature processing approach that incorporates prior knowledge and cross-modal attention mechanisms. This approach learns the relationships and characteristics among different modalities to construct more accurate and reliable feature representations, thereby improving the accuracy and stability of downstream tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses other state-of-the-art approaches.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of detecting anomalies from video-level supervision, where existing methods rely mainly on frame-feature magnitudes.
Uses textual prompts and an LLM to provide task-specific prior knowledge, then normalizes and compresses it through dictionary learning.
Improves consistency among textual descriptions of similar frames using LLMs and auxiliary information.
Integrates prior knowledge with cross-modal attention to learn relationships across modalities and build more reliable representations.
Experiments report that the method outperforms other state-of-the-art approaches, though no specific datasets or metrics are provided.

papers.abstract: While MLLMs can often identify what happens in a video, they still struggle with fine-grained spatio-temporal reasoning, which requires precise grounding when and where the supporting evidence appears and composing such evidence into a coherent reasoning chain. This challenge is exacerbated by the lack of scalable data construction and evaluation pipelines that provide granular, verifiable supervision linking reasoning steps to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.To address this gap, we present V-STORM, a structure-aware framework that transforms videos into Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs (STSGs) and derives Grounded Chain of Thought (GCoT) from validated evidence paths, making each reasoning step traceable to structured and verifiable spatio-temporal evidence.Under this framework, we construct a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark, both featuring GCoT annotations that link reasoning to explicit spatio-temporal evidence.Experiments reveal a clear separation between evidence localization and evidence composition: current MLLMs can often identify relevant spatio-temporal cues, yet still fail to integrate them into correct multi-step reasoning, exposing a bottleneck that answer-only evaluation largely obscures. Moreover, fine-tuning with V-STORM substantially improves both answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness, validating its effectiveness as supervision for faithful and evidence-grounded video reasoning. Our dataset, benchmark, and source code will be publicly released.
authors: Dian Jiao, Yuqian Yuan, Jiaqi Zhu, Mingjian Gao, Siwen Tan, Yunqi Cao, Jinhui Li, Sijing Li, Zhenxuan Fan, Haoyang Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Siliang Tang
bullets: Addresses MLLMs’ difficulty composing precise temporal and spatial evidence into coherent multi-step reasoning.
Represents videos as Spatio-Temporal Scene Graphs and derives grounded reasoning chains from validated evidence paths.
Introduces a 260K-sample training set and a 3K-sample human-verified benchmark with grounded chain-of-thought annotations.
Finds that MLLMs often localize relevant evidence but struggle to compose it correctly, a weakness hidden by answer-only evaluation.
Fine-tuning with V-STORM improves answer accuracy and grounding faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive (AR) modeling is arguably the only way to extend a fixed-length video diffusion model to longer or even streaming videos. However, existing AR diffusion methods use only the previously predicted chunk as context for the next, discarding the intermediate predictions that constitute the chunk's generation history. In contrast, conventional AR models such as LLMs condition on the entire history of preceding tokens. To this end, we propose Trajectory Forcing (TraF), an AR diffusion method that exploits the denoising trajectories of previous video chunks as context. TraF operates under two training regimes: (1) with ground-truth videos, where pseudo-trajectories are constructed from Gaussian interpolations and re-predicted by the model, and (2) with a teacher model, where real trajectories are obtained from the student's own denoising rollout. The first regime naturally provides a strong initialization for the second. On the 5-second VBench benchmark, TraF achieves a Total score of 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing (+0.84) and Causal Forcing (+1.11), with Quality and Semantic improving simultaneously. On 30-second generation---6$\times$ the training horizon---TraF achieves the highest overall quality among all compared methods.
authors: Bohan Wang, Shuo Chen, Yunzhi Li, Zhaozheng Chen, Junzhe Zhang, Hanwang Zhang
bullets: Existing autoregressive diffusion methods retain only the previous video chunk, discarding its generation history.
TraF uses previous chunks’ denoising trajectories as context for generating subsequent chunks.

On 5-second VBench, TraF scores 85.15, outperforming Self Forcing and Causal Forcing while improving both quality and semantics.
It achieves the highest overall quality among compared methods for 30-second videos, six times the training horizon.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering forces multimodal large language models to reason under strict visual-token budgets, creating a tradeoff between broad temporal coverage and fine-grained spatial detail. Uniform sampling preserves coverage but often obscures decisive local cues, while caption-based or frame-similarity retrieval operates over lossy proxies that can miss motion, state changes, and before-after relations. We recast long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem: given a fixed budget, decide how much to spend on global context versus high-resolution local evidence, and where in the video to draw that local evidence from. We introduce AdaAlloc, a training-free inference framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between a global video overview and localized visual detail. AdaAlloc first plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to locate candidate evidence segments and refines them into a compact temporal memory. The selected policy controls both frame sampling density and resolution, combining sparse, lower-resolution global frames with denser, higher-resolution local frames drawn from the refined memory. The final answerer reasons over the allocated global context and refined local evidence. Across LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench, AdaAlloc improves over budget-matched uniform sampling by up to 10.5 percentage points and outperforms the compared frame-selection and agentic methods on their reported benchmarks.
bullets: Recasts long-video reasoning as a visual-token allocation problem under a fixed budget.
Plans a global/local allocation policy, then uses temporal grounding to refine candidate evidence segments into compact memory.
Combines sparse low-resolution global frames with dense high-resolution local frames from refined memory.
Outperforms budget-matched uniform sampling and frame-selection/agentic methods on LVBench, MLVU, VideoMME, and LongVideoBench.

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses long-video understanding and multimodal LLM reasoning under token budgets, with a novel token allocation framework.
papers.title: AdaAlloc: Adaptive Visual Token Allocation for Long-Video Question Answering
papers.tldr: AdaAlloc is a training-free framework that adaptively allocates visual tokens between global context and localized detail for long-video QA, improving accuracy over uniform sampling by up to 10.5 points.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in video diffusion models have achieved remarkable photorealistic RGB synthesis, yet generating videos with a native alpha channel remains an open challenge. Existing approaches often rely on matting-style data and non-native RGBA designs, causing them to specialize in real-object scenes and to degrade severely on visual-effect content whose semi-transparency is spatially non-local and non-elliptical. We present UniRGBA, a unified framework whose key insight is that RGBA generation does not require a dedicated alpha encoder or complex latent-space restructuring---a minimal, targeted extension of the existing RGB pathway is sufficient. UniRGBA-VAE extends a causal video VAE to 4-channel RGBA via zero-initialized channel expansion, symmetric selective layer unfreezing (5% trainable), and a six-term progressive reconstruction loss anchored by a KL reference loss that prevents latent drift, followed by a two-stage schedule that introduces a lightweight GAN objective. We then apply standard DoRA to the pretrained DiT, reusing the unified 4-channel latent without any alpha-specific architectural changes. On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, UniRGBA substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA reconstruction while preserving RGB fidelity. For generation, UniRGBA outperforms Wan-Alpha on RGBA text-to-video tasks and matches or surpasses the original pretrained Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics, demonstrating that native alpha support can be integrated without compromising the underlying RGB prior or the model's architectural versatility.
authors: Lei Xu, Zhuo Li, Yongyi Jin, Aoyu Wang
bullets: Addresses failures of matting-based, non-native RGBA methods on visual effects with spatially non-local, non-elliptical transparency.
Extends a causal video VAE from RGB to RGBA using zero-initialized channels, selective unfreezing, progressive reconstruction losses, and a staged GAN objective.
Adapts the pretrained DiT with standard DoRA while reusing the unified four-channel latent, without an alpha-specific architecture.
On a visual-effect RGBA benchmark, it substantially outperforms Wan-Alpha for reconstruction and improves RGBA text-to-video generation.
Preserves RGB fidelity, matching or surpassing the original Wan2.1 backbone on RGB-only metrics.

Wan-Alpha (top), TransPixeler (middle), and Ours (bottom, DoRA on Wan2.1-T2V-14B) are stacked, all rendered on a checkerboard background to visualize transparency. papers.abstract: Video generation models can produce highly realistic videos while generating physically inconsistent object motion. This limitation suggests that visual modeling alone may not provide a transferable representation of physical dynamics. We introduce MotionCore, a framework for learning physical dynamics via a learnable partial differential equation solver and focuses on rigid-body motion. We introduce a latent neural simulator learning to predict the evolution of object-level physical states from observed motion. Its predictions are then converted into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model. The generator serves as a visual interface: it provides appearance and scene detail, while the learned dynamics model specifies the physical trajectory. To preserve this trajectory through the interface, MotionCore combines a diffusion-matching objective with a low-capacity decodability constraint on object identity and position. We evaluate MotionCore on public physical-consistency benchmarks and on paired data with known trajectories. Results indicate that MotionCore improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience in the evaluated rigid-body settings, while maintaining comparable visual quality. A controlled ablation protocol compares learned dynamics with an analytic prior and studies the choice of latent evolution processor.
authors: Zheng Wang, Zhengwei Gong, Yuanzhi Liang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Targets physically inconsistent object motion in otherwise realistic video generation.
Learns object-level state evolution with a neural PDE solver focused on rigid-body dynamics.
Converts predicted trajectories into spatially aligned latent controls for a controllable video diffusion model.
Uses diffusion matching plus a low-capacity decodability constraint to preserve object identity and position.
Improves physical consistency and trajectory obedience on evaluated benchmarks while maintaining comparable visual quality; scope is limited to rigid-body settings.

(c) Free-motion proposal. (d) Surface operator. (e) Collision operator: learned contact probabilities and coefficients enter a closed-form impulse update. papers.abstract: Reconstructing natural visual experience from cortical population activity is a central challenge in neural decoding, particularly for calcium imaging, where signals are noisy, temporally filtered, and paired neural-video data are limited. Here we present Ca2REAL (Calcium Activity to Reconstruct Events, Appearance, and Layout), a neural-to-video framework that conditions a pretrained video diffusion model through separate layout and semantic controls derived from calcium activity. Using measured responses from 7,863 V1 neurons in one mouse, Ca2REAL reconstructed held-out natural-movie clips with 81.4% all-pairs stimulus-identification accuracy, with its clearest gains over deterministic baselines in perceptual and semantic measures. We further evaluated the framework in a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons assembled from encoding-model-predicted responses across 11 independently recorded datasets. Perturbation and ablation analyses showed that reconstruction depends on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure, with layout and semantic pathways providing complementary spatial and identity information. Temporal analyses further showed improved preservation of semantic dynamics across reconstructed clips. These results show that large-scale cortical population activity constrains the spatial, semantic, and temporal structure of natural visual experience, providing a generative framework for high-fidelity neural reconstruction of dynamic visual scenes.
authors: Yukai Huang, Haoyu Albert Wang, Jiawei Zhang, Jialun Ma, Jiayao Ding, Yiran Lin, Xingyu Chen, Ziqi Gao, Yuguo Yu
bullets: Addresses noisy, temporally filtered calcium signals and limited paired neural–video data for visual reconstruction.
Separately derives layout and semantic controls from neural activity to condition a pretrained video diffusion model.
Using 7,863 V1 neurons, achieved 81.4% all-pairs identification accuracy on held-out natural-movie clips.
Virtual-population analyses across 11 datasets indicate reconstruction relies on distributed, stimulus-specific population structure.
Perturbations and temporal analyses show complementary layout/semantic information and preserved semantic dynamics.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 Overview of the data pipeline and Ca2REAL architecture. a, Dynamic Sensorium data acquisition for the primary measured experiment. Awake, head-fixed mice viewed natural movies presented at 30 Hz while locomoting on a cylindrical treadmill, and V1 calcium activity was recorded with two-photon imaging. b, Neural-response synthesis with digital-twin encoding models. A spatiotemporal neural encoder maps each movie to the corresponding population response through a shared visual feature extractor, temporal processing, and population-specific readout. c, Neural and visual preprocessing. Movie frames were centrally cropped and resized to the generator resolution, while calcium responses were normalized neuron-wise using training-set statistics before decoding. d, Ca2REAL architecture. A multiscale temporal front end provides features to two neural-control pathways. The layout pathway predicts a low-resolution movie for spatial control of Wan2.1-VACE, whereas the semantic pathway predicts global and temporally ordered visual tokens that are adapted to the generator conditioning space.

Fig. 3 Neural-to-video decoding from a stimulus-aligned virtual population of 116,705 neurons. a, Construction of the virtual population. Encoding models fitted to 11 independently recorded neural datasets predicted responses to common movie stimuli, and the predictions were concatenated across neurons. The lower panels show the contribution of each dataset and the cortical-area composition of the virtual population. b, Representative held-out target clips (GT) and reconstructions generated by Ca2REAL and baseline methods from the 116,705-dimensional encoding-model-predicted responses. Selected frames from one representative clip in each target cluster are shown. c, Quantitative comparison over 946 held-out segments.

Fig. 2 Natural-movie reconstruction from measured V1 calcium activity in a single mouse. a, Representative held-out target clips (GT) and reconstructions generated by Ca2REAL and baseline methods from measured responses of 7,863 V1 neurons. Selected frames from one representative clip in each of the four target clusters are shown. b, Quantitative reconstruction performance on 178 held-out measured clips.

Fig. 4 Complementary roles of the layout and semantic conditioning pathways. a, Representative reconstructions from measured and virtual-population activity using the full Ca2REAL model or with the layout or semantic pathway blocked at inference time. b, Mean oriented paired change in reconstruction performance relative to the full model after blocking either pathway. Signs are oriented so that negative values indicate worse performance for both higher-is-better and loweris-better metrics. Results are shown separately for the measured V1 population (n = 178 clips) and the virtual population (n = 946 clips).

Fig. 5 Distributed and stimulus-specific neural dependence of Ca2REAL. a, Effect of removing each source population relative to matched-size random neuron deletions (blue point, source-population removal result; gray line, matched-random 5–95% range; gray tick, median). b, Reconstruction performance as a function of the fraction of retained neurons. c, Robustness to progressive corruption of neuron identity. d, Robustness to replacing neural responses with responses evoked by a different stimulus. e, Robustness to random neuron dropout. f, Structured neuron-identity and cross-sample perturbations compared with magnitude-matched Gaussian perturbations. g, Effect of cross-sample substitution as a function of target–donor similarity defined in frozen SigLIP2 space; the outcome is SigLIP2-based all-pairs identification, and significance was assessed by a cluster-aware permutation test of the global Spearman trend. h, Denoising-objective pairing sensitivity at fixed diffusion noise level (σ = 0.7) in the full model and the model trained without Lpair, quantified by ∆pair = Lshuffled − Lmatched; asterisks indicate paired Full versus No-Lpair comparisons. For b–h, vertical bars indicate bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.

Fig. 6 Ca2REAL preserves temporal semantic dynamics. a, Semantic trajectory spread retention (points, medians; thin bars, interquartile ranges; thick bars, bootstrap 95% CIs; dashed line, ideal ratio = 1). b, Semantic path-length retention, with conventions as in a. c, Within-clip temporal identification accuracy (dashed line, chance level = 0.5). d, Paired temporal-identification advantage of Ca2REAL over each baseline (points, mean paired differences; bars, bootstrap 95% CIs; dashed line, zero). Blue/red denote measured/virtual populations. Significance tests were Holm-corrected; asterisks denote significance and ns denotes non-significance.
Table 2 Reconstruction metrics. Arrows indicate whether higher (↑) or lower (↓) values indicate better reconstruction.

Table 1 Measured-response substitution tests functional compatibility with the virtual-population decoder. All-pairs identification accuracy after replacing available synthetic responses with matched measured activity or control responses on the full test set (n = 946 clips). ∆ denotes the change relative to the fully synthetic condition.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on static visual understanding benchmarks, yet their ability to act in dynamic environments remains less well understood. We introduce AtariBench, a controlled benchmark that evaluates VLMs across 20 Atari 2600 games, requiring models to make sequential decisions from high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams. By decoupling fast in-game dynamics from wall-clock inference speed, AtariBench focuses on whether models can perceive rapid visual state changes, reason over spatiotemporal dynamics, and ground actions in the current observation. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations in state-of-the-art VLMs: models often fail to infer object motion and direction, exhibit brittle sequential decision-making, and over-rely on textual interaction history despite newly appended visual feedback. We further introduce a separability analysis to identify which in-game scores provide reliable signals of model competence, and use the benchmark to study how memory design and prompting strategies affect performance. Overall, AtariBench exposes a persistent gap between passive visual perception and active decision-making, providing a lightweight and rigorous testbed for developing VLMs that can reason and act in dynamic environments.
authors: Mingjia Huo, Yao Fu, Bo Chang, Yaqing Wang, Dawei Zhu, Dylan Zhang, Xinyang Yi, Lichan Hong, Ed H. Chi, Hao Zhang, Jiaxi Tang
bullets: Benchmarks VLMs on 20 Atari 2600 games using high-temporal-resolution gameplay streams.
Separates in-game dynamics from inference speed to test spatiotemporal perception, reasoning, and action grounding.
Finds failures in tracking object motion and direction, brittle sequential decisions, and over-reliance on textual history over new visual feedback.
Analyzes which game scores reliably reflect competence and examines the effects of memory design and prompting.
Highlights a persistent gap between passive visual understanding and active decision-making in dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of InstaGen. (a) Queries and keys are clustered into groups. (b) Centroid scores give each key group a probability π of being used by each query group. (c) The top key group is always kept; the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to π and weighted by 1/π. (d) Queries in a group share the same keys, so attention runs over dense blocks in one kernel.

Figure 4: InstaGen approximates attention more accurately than prior sparse methods. Left: relative L2 error of one self-attention call from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B against exact attention. InstaGen (uniform, 16+16, no warm-up) keeps the error low everywhere at 32% density, while SVG2 (p=0.9, warm-up counted as zero error) leaves large errors in individual heads and layers despite computing 46%.

Figure 5: Warmup ablations on Wan2.1-T2V-14B (720p, 81 frames, 50 steps). InstaGen with uniform sampling runs its first 0, 5, 10 or 15 of 50 steps at full attention (warmup), ranging from 4+4% to 32+32% budget. At 561 frames dense takes 162 min, SVG2 82.8 min (1.97×), and InstaGen 61.9 min (2.62×) with warm-up and 57.3 min (2.83×) without.

Right: PSNR against attention density, the share of attention computed over the whole generation. papers.tldr: InstaGen accelerates video diffusion by replacing inefficient top-block selection with group-shared importance sampling, improving reconstruction quality at comparable compute.

papers.abstract: Video Anomaly Detection (VAD) aims to temporally localize abnormal events in videos. Most existing approaches rely on dataset-specific training and curated annotations, limiting generalization in open-set scenarios. Recent zero-shot methods based on Large Vision- Language Models (LVLMs) alleviate this dependency but often lack temporal continuity and structured reasoning. We propose Cog-VADU, a fully training-free framework that reformulates VAD as a sequential cognitive reasoning task. Cog-VADU introduces Chain-of- Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP), which unrolls an LVLM into a recurrent reasoning chain across video segments. By propagating structured rationales over time, the model maintains implicit temporal memory, enabling robust discrimination between com- plex anomalies and high-motion normal activities. To improve reliability, we further design a cross-modal re-ranking stage that aligns textual rationales with visual embeddings, enforcing semantic consistency and temporal coherence for refined and stable predictions. Extensive experiments on multiple public VAD benchmarks demonstrate that Cog-VADU achieves competitive zero-shot performance. Moreover, cross-model evaluations show that CoADTP consistently enhances reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic manner, pro- viding interpretable and generalizable anomaly understanding for real-world applications.
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization and weak temporal reasoning of dataset-specific and existing zero-shot VAD methods.
Uses Chain-of-Anomaly Detection Thought Prompting (CoADTP) to propagate structured rationales across video segments as implicit temporal memory.
Applies cross-modal re-ranking to align textual rationales with visual embeddings, improving semantic consistency and temporal coherence.
Reports competitive zero-shot performance across multiple public VAD benchmarks.
Cross-model evaluations indicate that CoADTP improves reasoning-based anomaly detection in a model-agnostic way.

figures.caption: Figure 19: Qualitative comparison on a video reasoning benchmark. Our training-free framework CogVADU (blue) correctly identifies the anomaly by reasoning over temporal visual inconsistencies, detecting that the second puppy’s nose and tongue morph unnaturally across frames. In contrast, training-based VAD approaches (orange), including HAWK Tang et al. (2024), HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b), and VAD-R1 Huang et al. (2025), either hallucinate unrelated changes (e.g., ear color or fur texture) or fail to localize the correct anomaly despite similar visual evidence. This example highlights the advantage of reasoning-driven anomaly detection in capturing subtle semantic inconsistencies that are not easily modeled by conventional training-based approaches.

Figure 1: Comparison of video anomaly detection paradigms. (a) Vision-only methods rely on supervised training and produce anomaly scores without semantic reasoning. (b) Multimodal LLM-based VAD generates anomaly confidence and provides post-hoc explanations. (c) Cog-VADU employs a frozen LVLM with structured prompting and temporal cues to perform joint, training-free anomaly detection and reasoning.

Figure 6: Qualitative comparison on VANE. Cog-VADU generates structured, evidence-grounded reasoning (Observation → Anomaly → Reasoning → Answer), correctly identifying the anomaly (B). In contrast, prior multimodal VAD methods, including RL-based VAD-R1 Bharadwaj et al. (2025), often produce weakly grounded explanations.

Figure 13: Case 1 — Visually anomalous, semantically normal. Comparison of four state-of-the-art VAD methods on an open-web arm wrestling video (ground truth: Normal). URDMU Zhou et al. (2023a) produces a strong false alarm (peak ≈ 0.999); HolmesVAD Zhang et al. (2024b) hallucinates an unrelated “man in a blue shirt” scene; HAWK Tang et al. (2024) fabricates a basketball court context; and HolmesVAU Zhang et al. (2025b) contradicts its own reasoning by labelling recognized wrestling activity as “anomaly events.” In contrast, Cog-VADU correctly identifies the professional-wrestling context and outputs a calibrated score of 0.15 (Normal).
Figure 2: Comparison of prior-aware prompts for zero-shot VAD.

Figure 10: Structural analysis of annotation distributions under the proposed unified protocol. (a) Anomaly perception word cloud illustrating semantically enriched anomaly categories introduced through re-annotation, including subtle, contextual, and effect-based states that were under-represented in the original benchmarks. (b) Temporal relation word cloud highlighting causal, escalation, and aftermath relations, emphasizing the necessity of modeling complete cause-effect chains rather than isolated trigger events. Together, these visualizations provide linguistic and structural evidence that the original annotations are biased toward trigger-centric labeling, while our unified protocol captures temporally consistent and semantically grounded anomaly states.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.abstract: Localized AI manipulations in long-form videos often affect brief events within otherwise authentic content, making video-level classification insufficient for forensic analysis. Existing audio-visual deepfake benchmarks largely focus on short talking-head clips, while long-form temporal forensics remains predominantly visual. We introduce AV-FABLE, a dual-timeline benchmark for sparse manipulations in open-scene long-form audio-visual videos. AV-FABLE contains 16,650 pristine--manipulated twin pairs (998 hours) created with 27 editing configurations, with separate audio and visual timelines that enable modality-specific temporal localization and expose errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation. On AV-FABLE, zero-shot prompting of audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) yields near-chance detection and poor temporal localization. In contrast, supervised readouts of their frozen perception features recover strong forensic signals, suggesting manipulation evidence is encoded in these representations but not effectively exposed through language outputs. Motivated by this observation, we propose NFSR(Native Forensics via Separated Readouts), which reads frozen AV-LLM features with separate audio and visual temporal decoders. NFSR achieves the best audio-visual localization performance in-domain and across all three out-of-distribution settings, including transfer to held-out videos from an external long-video forensic benchmark. AV-FABLE, code, and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Introduces a dual-timeline benchmark for localized manipulations in open-scene, long-form audio-visual videos.
Includes 16,650 pristine–manipulated twin pairs spanning 998 hours and 27 editing configurations.
Zero-shot AV-LLM prompting performs near chance for detection and poorly for temporal localization.
NFSR uses separate audio and visual temporal decoders over frozen AV-LLM features, achieving the best localization in-domain and across three out-of-distribution settings.
The benchmark exposes errors hidden by joint-timeline evaluation and is intended for public release with code and model weights.

papers.abstract: Masked discrete diffusion models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive generation, but iterative sampling can be costly, and intractable sequence likelihoods complicate reward fine-tuning. We introduce IDRF, a framework for reward fine-tuning of few-step masked discrete diffusion generators. Starting from a standard reverse-KL-regularized objective, IDRF replaces the intractable sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization. With an optimal auxiliary denoiser, we prove that the population inverse-distillation loss upper-bounds the sequence-level KL divergence to the reference distribution. IDRF optimizes a trajectory-based surrogate of this loss without reference-model rollouts, so the student keeps its own few-step sampler. We view few-step generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and optimize reward with a clipped policy-gradient objective over the student's trajectories. Across DNA, image, and text generation, IDRF achieves high reward with up to $32\times$ fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.
bullets: Targets expensive iterative sampling and intractable sequence-level KL regularization in masked discrete diffusion.
Replaces the sequence-level KL penalty with inverse-distillation regularization and proves an upper bound under an optimal auxiliary denoiser.
Optimizes a trajectory-based, clipped policy-gradient objective over the student’s own few-step sampler.
Across DNA, image, and text generation, achieves high reward with up to 32× fewer denoising steps than the reference while mitigating reward hacking and preserving sample quality.

The reward of x0 gives the policy-gradient loss LR, and the student minimizes LR + λLID.

papers.abstract: Vision models pretrained for frame-level appearance often struggle to infer hidden physical properties from motion. We study center-of-mass (CoM) localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies from short monocular videos, where surface cues and point tracking are unreliable under self-occlusion. We propose STATERA, which adapts a pretrained video backbone (V-JEPA) with mostly frozen weights and a lightweight temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories. To support this task, we introduce the HiddenMass Benchmark, comprising 50K MuJoCo trajectories and a 63-sequence real-world test set with physically calibrated CoM ground truth. In simulation, STATERA-50K-Sigma improves normalized CoM error from 41.7% (DINOv2) to 25.2%. In zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, we observe a fundamental trade-off in supervision: phase-aware targets can induce bimodal predictions, while phase-agnostic targets can collapse toward statistically safe centroids. Nevertheless, our phase-aware STATERA-50K-Crescent is the only evaluated method that demonstrates consistent movement toward the true hidden offset. While this leads to a monocular vector overshoot artifact that marginally increases absolute Euclidean error compared to a static geometric centroid, it improves physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%. These results suggest that frozen temporal representations can better separate inertial dynamics from visual geometry for hidden-parameter estimation.
bullets: Targets CoM localization for opaque, asymmetric rigid bodies where visual geometry and tracking are unreliable.
Adapts pretrained V-JEPA features with a temporal tubelet mixer to predict per-frame CoM heatmaps and trajectories.
Introduces HiddenMass Benchmark: 50K simulated MuJoCo trajectories and 63 real-world sequences with calibrated CoM ground truth.
Reduces normalized simulation CoM error from 41.7% to 25.2% and improves real-world physics capture from 2.6% to 41.0%.
Zero-shot transfer remains challenging: phase-aware supervision moves predictions toward hidden offsets but can cause overshoot, while phase-agnostic targets may collapse toward centroids.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Qualitative Kinematic Trajectories. A comparison of 2D predicted paths during multiaxis tumbling within a static observation window. (Left) Spatial models (e.g., DINOv2) suffer from visual-kinematic aliasing, tracking high-contrast surface distractors instead of momentum. (Right) STATERA-50K-Crescent successfully isolates the smooth Newtonian parabolic arc of the hidden mass, directionally aligning with the verified Ground Truth despite a Euclidean vector overshoot.

Figure 2: STATERA Architecture. A 16-frame video sequence is processed via a partially-frozen V-JEPA 2.1 backbone. Temporal tubelets are mixed using a 1D Convolution before passing through the Spatial Preservation Decoder. The network bifurcates to output a continuous spatial heatmap (Head A) and a regularizing 1D Z-Depth scalar (Head B).

Figure 6: The Vector Overshoot Artifact. (Left) An architecturally complete model (1K-Anchor) correctly learns to bound the hidden mass phase within realistic 3D physical constraints. (Right) Ablating the absolute 1D Z-Depth regularizer (1K-No-Z-Depth) causes the 2D spatial extractions to lose physical scale constraints, leading to a severe, unregularized Euclidean explosion far beyond the physical boundaries of the rigid body.

Figure 1: Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematic Tracking. (Left) The HiddenMass-50K training environment featuring procedurally generated asymmetric masses. (Right) Zero-shot inference on real-world video sequences. While spatial baselines collapse to the visual centroid, STATERA successfully identifies the directional phase of the offset Center of Mass. The prediction pulls away from the visual center along the true kinematic vector (noting an empirical Euclidean overshoot inherent to the 2.5D spatial projection).

Figure 4: Curriculum Label Smoothing. Target probability distributions across training epochs. By mathematical design, at Epoch 0 (κ = 0), both targets initialize as identical broad Gaussian rings (σ = 12.5). Over the curriculum, the phase-agnostic baseline (Sigma) decays into an isotropic impulse (σ = 3.0), omitting phase data. Conversely, the phase-aware SOTA (Crescent) scales its Von Mises angular mask (κ → 50.0), forcing the network to continuously optimize for rotational torque direction.

Figure 5: Visual-Kinematic Aliasing (Bimodal Split). During high-torque rotations where groundtruth phase is highly ambiguous, models trained on static phase-aware targets output high-variance, bimodal probability heatmaps. The network essentially “hedges its bets” between two physically plausible mass locations, resulting in expectation collapse and severe temporal jitter.

Figure 7: HiddenMass Benchmark Profile. The Unified HiddenMass Score (HMS, orange) is calculated as a weighted composite: 25% Kinematic Accuracy, 25% Tracking Stability, and 50% Physics Disentanglement, explicitly penalizing statistical reward-hacking. Low Disentanglement (teal) reveals that DINOv2 and STATERA-50K-Sigma are deceived by visual and heuristic aliasing, defaulting closer to the geometric centroid. STATERA-50K-Crescent actively breaks this heuristic, achieving substantial positive physical disentanglement and securing the highest overall HMS (59.6).

Table 2: Zero-Shot Real-World Transfer (N=63). STATERA-50K-Sigma achieves the lowest spatial and jitter errors. However, unclamped Disentanglement analysis reveals DINOv2 and STATERA50K-Sigma struggle to fully disentangle the offset. STATERA-50K-Crescent remains the only architecture to achieve substantial positive disentanglement toward the hidden mass. Point trackers were evaluated via an idealized Dynamic Surface Centroid Proxy (initializing a uniform point grid around the object’s initial bounding center and gracefully falling back to the geometric center upon track death).
Table 1: In-Domain Simulation Performance (10,000 Sequences). Evaluated on the held-out MuJoCo validation set. Lower is better for all metrics.
Table 3: Temperature Pareto Sweep. The impact of the Soft-Argmax temperature (τ ) on physical capture versus Euclidean error. Evaluated on STATERA-50K-Crescent.

papers.selection_reason: Video representation learning for physical property estimation from motion, fitting video understanding and temporal reasoning.
papers.title: STATERA: Hidden Mass Estimation via Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Kinematics using Frozen Temporal Tubelets
papers.tldr: STATERA uses mostly frozen video representations plus a lightweight temporal mixer to estimate hidden centers of mass from monocular motion, achieving strong simulation performance and meaningful zero-shot transfer to real objects.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation offers efficient generation with diffusion and flow models, but preserving quality with only a few sampling steps remains challenging. Distribution-matching methods via score distillation provide a strong foundation, yet they rely on accurately tracking the student's changing distribution. At intermediate generation steps in few-step sampling, student-score estimation can be difficult, and commonly used estimators may describe a different distribution from the one used to update the student. Flow matching allows a more flexible approach to supervision through velocity fields constructed from the student's sampling process. Building on this perspective, we introduce Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), which uses a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields and turn their disagreement into feedback for learning. VAD unifies score distillation, Fisher-based matching, and moment matching, also explaining existing heuristic MMD updates and delivering new training objectives. We further develop VA-TDM, which follows trajectory distribution matching: providing supervision for partial denoising along the student trajectory. Beyond this, VA-TDM combines transition-aware online velocity learning and dual-form VAD supervision across intermediate student transitions. Extensive results show that VA-TDM is powerful for learning few-step generators, achieving state-of-the-art four-step performance in both text-to-image and text-to-video generation across various backbones and scaling effectively to 33B MiniMax-H3. In particular, our VA-TDM-H3 notably outperforms the few-step Fast-H3 and is closer to the original many-step H3 according to human preference.
authors: Yihong Luo, Tianyu Pang, Tianyang Hu
bullets: Addresses quality loss and unreliable student-score estimation in few-step distillation.
Introduces Velocity Adversarial Distillation (VAD), using a learned critic to compare student and teacher fields.
Unifies score, Fisher-based, and moment matching while motivating new training objectives.
Uses trajectory distribution matching with online transition-aware velocity learning and dual-form supervision.
Achieves state-of-the-art four-step text-to-image and text-to-video results, including scaling to the 33B MiniMax-H3 model.

papers.title: VA-TDM: A Unified View for Improving Few-Step Diffusion Models by Velocity Adversarial Distillation
papers.tldr: VA-TDM improves few-step diffusion and flow generation by adversarially matching student and teacher velocity fields throughout the student’s denoising trajectory.

papers.abstract: Generative video models are increasingly used as visual world simulators, yet their primary strength lies in rendering plausible pixels rather than reasoning about how a world should evolve. Coherent world evolution requires more than visual fidelity: when an event occurs, a model must infer its consequences for the entities in the world and then render the resulting state. For example, after a wild beast appears, the model should not only depict the wild beast, but also infer whether a nearby person should flee, take cover, or fight back based on the realized scene. Existing diffusion-based video models lack an explicit mechanism for maintaining world state and reasoning over such event-conditioned consequences, often producing visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent outputs. To make this reasoning gap concrete and measurable, we propose a new problem, Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, which requires a model to render an event, reason about its consequences for the evolving world state, and reveal a causally plausible outcome as the world continues to evolve, even out of sight. As a baseline reference solution, we introduce EvoWorld, a brain-renderer collaboration framework in which a vision-language model serves as the world brain: it observes generated segments, maintains an evolving account of the world, and reasons about plausible state transitions, while a segment-autoregressive video renderer realizes them visually. We further introduce EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for training and evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency. Experiments show that EvoWorld substantially improves event-conditioned causal evolution over recent models while preserving visual quality and consistency, establishing a reference point for reasoning-guided, autonomous world evolution beyond the current field of view.
authors: Yequan Bie, Dengyang Jiang, Zhixuan Chen, Xiaozhuan Liang, Haoxuan Che, Quande Liu, Xi Chen, Hao Chen
bullets: Introduces Out-of-Sight Causal Evolution, requiring models to render events, infer their consequences, and reveal plausible outcomes later—even off-screen.
Uses a vision-language “world brain” to track evolving state and reason about transitions, paired with a segment-autoregressive video renderer.
Provides EvoWorld-Data and EvoWorld-Bench for evaluating event realization, causal reactions, and revisit consistency.
Experiments report improved event-conditioned causal evolution while preserving visual quality and consistency.
Targets limitations of existing diffusion video models, which often produce visually plausible but behaviorally static or causally inconsistent scenes.

papers.abstract: Scene Graph Anticipation (SGA) predicts object relationships in future video frames. Continuous-time SGA models evolve each subject-object pair with an independent Neural ODE, so relationships sharing an entity cannot influence one another during integration, and nothing prevents mutually exclusive predictions, such as "sitting on" and "standing on", for the same pair. We introduce CoupledSGA, which links such relationships through a Relationship Interaction Graph with graph attention inside the ODE vector field, and adds a Structural Consistency Loss ($\mathcal{L}_{SC}$) based on a matrix of mutually exclusive predicates. Developing CoupledSGA revealed a limitation of the evaluation protocol. With-Constraint evaluation keeps one predicate per group for each subject-object pair, so its R@K and mR@K cannot capture the within-group violations targeted by $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$: we prove they are unchanged whenever each group's winning predicate and its score are held fixed. We further show that the gradient of $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ depends on predicate scores rather than ground-truth labels: for two-predicate rules it amplifies the ordering the model already holds, and when all scores in a group are equal it suppresses predicates in more exclusion rules more strongly, explaining why the penalty can lower recall while improving consistency. On Action Genome, activating $\mathcal{L}_{SC}$ after two warm-up epochs reduces R@20 from 42.21% to 35.18% while lowering the No-Constraint contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07% (matched-budget R@20: 40.48% CoupledSGA vs. 44.78% SceneSayerODE). CoupledSGA is a testbed, not a state-of-the-art claim: With-Constraint recall captures the cost of enforcing structural consistency but not the improvement. We recommend reporting No-Constraint results alongside a contradiction rate for methods that constrain predicate co-activation.
authors: Zeno Nongmaithem, Anushttha Srivastava, Anshit Sinha, Apoorv Sisodia, Suman Chowdhury, Prerana Mukherjee, Rajesh P. Barnwal
bullets: Independent Neural ODEs in continuous-time SGA cannot model interactions among relationships sharing an entity and may produce mutually exclusive predicates together.
CoupledSGA adds graph-attention coupling through a Relationship Interaction Graph and a Structural Consistency Loss based on mutually exclusive predicates.
The authors prove With-Constraint R@K and mR@K cannot reflect within-group violations when each group’s winning predicate and score remain fixed.
On Action Genome, the consistency loss reduces contradiction rate from 45.92% to 4.07%, but R@20 falls from 42.21% to 35.18%; matched-budget R@20 is 40.48% versus 44.78% for SceneSayerODE.
The paper recommends reporting No-Constraint results with contradiction rates; CoupledSGA is presented as a testbed rather than a state-of-the-art method.

papers.title: Coupled Scene Graph Anticipation: When With-Constraint Recall Hides Structural Inconsistency

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.
authors: Shuai Dong, Kanghui Tian, Linghan Chen, Wenqi Shao, Hongrui Wu, Haowen Hou, Yongfu Zhu, Xuehui Wang, Ziyue Wang, Wenpu Liu, Weichu Xie, Yuqi Xu, Congcong Wang, Kaiwen Tuo, Caoyuan Ma, Taiqiang Wu, Ji Zhao, Wenzheng Chang, Dianyi Wang, Siyuan Wang, Zhongyu Wei, Yu Qiao, Jiaqi Wang
bullets: Streaming video models must repeatedly choose whether to respond or keep observing, but trajectory-level credit can reinforce redundancy or suppress useful follow-ups.
TurnWise computes turn-level group-relative advantages from silence-completed prefix scores and each decision’s remaining return.
Turn-mean policy optimization gives response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of token output length.
The framework requires neither a learned critic nor additional rollouts.
Experiments report improved performance over prior RL methods for streaming video understanding.

papers.abstract: Online reasoning video segmentation (Online RVS) requires a model to segment query-referred objects as a video streams in, using only the frames observed so far. Existing formulations largely assume a fixed target set throughout the video, overlooking a fundamental property of streaming reasoning: as new events occur, the objects that satisfy a query may change over time. To address this, we propose a new task, Generalized Reasoning Video Segmentation (GRVS), where the target set depends on query-relevant events accumulated over the observed video history. As new evidence accumulates, the target set can evolve from empty to one or multiple objects, requiring a model to continuously maintain target validity while localizing the valid objects currently in view. To evaluate GRVS, we build Isekai, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 videos and 197 queries across 11 temporal query families, with 12,569 scoring points whose target sets are causally annotated over time. We further propose Sekai, an online framework with two complementary components: an Event Memory Reasoner (EMR) that maintains query-relevant events and evolving target states in structured memory, and a Memory-Grounded Decoder (MGD) that identifies valid targets from this memory and localizes them in the current frame. Experiments show that Sekai significantly outperforms existing online RVS methods, achieving 50.33 J&F and improving over the strongest baseline by 3.2 points. Code, example annotations, and evaluation scripts are available at https://github.com/zenastangbi/Sekai.
authors: Zhengtao Liu, Jinrong Xu, Shiu-Hong Kao, Huixin Sun, Yicong Li
bullets: Problem: Existing online video segmentation assumes a fixed target set, while streaming events can change which objects satisfy a query.
Method: The Event Memory Reasoner maintains query-relevant events and target states; the Memory-Grounded Decoder selects and segments valid objects in each current frame.
Benchmark: Isekai contains 60 videos, 197 queries, 11 temporal query families, and causally annotated target states across 12,569 scoring points.
Result: Sekai achieves 50.33 J&F, outperforming the strongest baseline by 3.2 points.
Scope: The task focuses on online, causal reasoning where target sets may evolve from empty to one or multiple objects.

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
authors: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
bullets: Targets the trade-off among pose localisation, temporal motion quality, and energy use in non-event-driven video.
Uses a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder for spatial evidence and MAM to estimate joint motion, align past heatmaps, and fuse them adaptively with current predictions.
Evaluated on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset using localisation, motion-error, and estimated arithmetic-energy metrics.
Compared with an architecture-matched ANN using MAM, it reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% with a 1.12-point PCK_HB(0.5) decrease.
Adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46%, respectively, with minimal computational and parameter overhead.
