papers.selection_reason: Improves video reasoning in multimodal LLMs via latent visual evidence generation, directly relevant to video understanding and multimodal large language models.
papers.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
papers.tldr: VideoLVR lets multimodal models revisit compact latent visual evidence during video reasoning, reducing visual forgetting without greatly expanding context.

papers.abstract: Automatic soccer event spotting supports highlight generation, video indexing, and sports analytics, but existing methods depend on large annotated datasets and soccer-specific training. We present a zero-shot framework that detects, classifies, and temporally localizes events in full-length soccer broadcasts without task-specific parameter training. Each match is segmented into overlapping clips represented by a compact visual storyboard and the aligned commentary transcript, which a general-purpose multimodal model processes jointly. On three manually annotated matches containing 130 events, the best configuration achieves 72.0% F1@5s and outperforms SoccerNet-trained CALF and NetVLAD++ in a cross-dataset setting, while the storyboard representation reduces inference cost by 72% compared with individual frames. We further analyze the effects of model family, input representation, and prompt optimization, and introduce an evidence-grounded excitement-scoring stage that ranks detected events with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.
authors: Sadia Kamal, Mahmudul Hasan, Tony Braskich
bullets: Addresses the need for soccer event detection without large annotated, soccer-specific training datasets.
Processes overlapping clips using compact visual storyboards aligned with commentary transcripts.
Achieves 72.0% F1@5s on 130 events across three manually annotated matches and compares favorably in a cross-dataset evaluation.
Storyboards reduce inference cost by 72% versus using individual frames.
Adds evidence-grounded excitement scoring with natural-language explanations for highlight selection.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Multimodal Event Spotting in Soccer Broadcasts
papers.tldr: A zero-shot multimodal framework spots, classifies, localizes, and ranks soccer events in full-match broadcasts using visual storyboards and commentary, without task-specific training.

papers.abstract: Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.
authors: Zhongrui Gui, Junyu Xie, Tengda Han, Weidi Xie, Andrew Zisserman
bullets: Studies identifying principal characters without cast lists, actor photos, or pre-built character banks.
Defines character naming: linking a dialogue-mentioned name to the corresponding visible character.
Uses cinematic cues including shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, references, gaze, and temporal continuity.
Provides a dataset and annotations for character naming and first appearances, plus a video-and-dialogue model.
Introduces progressive character-bank construction and compares the model with proprietary multimodal language models.

figures.caption: Figure 11: Example of the constructed character bank for Meet the Parents. We show another example of a character bank constructed by our streaming pipeline. Our method correctly identifies the most prominent characters, but errors remain for the bottom three entries. These characters often appear in complex multi-person scenes, making reliable name binding more difficult. In addition, transcription errors can introduce noisy name variants; for example, Fonker and Falker should both be resolved to Focker for Greg Focker.

Figure 2: Example annotations from the MCN dataset. The MCN dataset provides manually annotated timestamps for each character’s first visual occurrence and first naming, along with ground-truth name-to-face correspondences for the Character Naming task.

Figure 10: Example of the constructed character bank for Juno. We show the character bank constructed by our streaming pipeline. Each row (apart from the last two) corresponds to one character entry and includes representative face tracks, the predicted canonical name with confidence, and discovered aliases. The example illustrates that the bank captures major characters with clean visual clusters and resolves name variations, such as mapping Mama Bear to Juno, Bren to Brenda, and McGovern to Mac. Some naming errors remain, typically due to noisy or ambiguous character-name associations.

Figure 4: Qualitative results for Character Naming. Examples are from Four Weddings and a Funeral and Jerry Maguire. In each case, our default “Qwen3VL-4B-Thinking (SFT + RL)” model reasons jointly over subtitles and video frames to link a queried name to the correct face — in the first, by following a verbal introduction to a later podium shot; in the second, by resolving direct address across a shot–reverse-shot exchange.

Figure 6: Qualitative results for character naming. We associate character names with their facial appearances in movies, mirroring how audiences infer who is who while watching. Characters may be introduced through diverse cues, including direct address by other characters (top), visual reasoning with common knowledge (middle), and third-party reference (bottom). In each case, the model grounds the name to the correct colored box by combining the spoken cue with visual evidence such as gaze, gesture, and scene role. Correctly linking character identities is central to movie understanding, enabling coherent character tracking across scenes. The examples are taken from Sleepless in Seattle, Four Weddings and a Funeral and Meet the Parents.

Figure 7: Comparison of reasoning efficiency on character naming. We compare our model against Qwen3.5-9B on the same scene. Our model produces a concise, well-grounded answer that directly links the spoken cue (“Congratulations, Walter”) to visual evidence (gaze and handshake direction), correctly identifying the orange box as Walter. In contrast, the baseline generates a lengthy chain of thought with repeated re-examinations and self-verifications, yet arrives at an incorrect mapping (green). This illustrates that longer reasoning does not guarantee better grounding: our model achieves more accurate character naming with substantially fewer tokens.

Figure 8: Examples of failure cases for both our model and Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview. We show three examples in which Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, the strongest proprietary baseline, fails. These cases suggest that it struggles to capture subtle actions that are important for character naming. In the last example, Gemini is given the original audio rather than the erroneous subtitles for inference. The examples are taken from Four Weddings and a Funeral and Jerry Maguire.

Figure 5: Examples from the MCN dataset. Six character-naming annotations illustrating the range of problem types covered: direct address with shot–reverse-shot structure, direct address with eyeline match, direct address over the telephone, on-screen text, and OCR-based reasoning. Clips are drawn from Moneyball, Gangs of New York, Sleepless in Seattle, The Help, Four Weddings and a Funeral, and The Ides of March.

Table 2: Character naming accuracy on the MCN test set. We report overall accuracy (including none labels) and known accuracy (restricted to queries with a valid face track). Our fine-tuned Qwen3VL-4B-Thinking closes most of the gap to proprietary frontier models despite being substantially smaller in terms of model size.

Table 4: Results on the MCN First Occurrence dataset. We report mean Temporal IoU (mTIoU) against two reference intervals, first visual occurrence and first naming, and Principal Character Recall (PCR@K) on the final character bank forK∈{5,10,15}. papers.abstract: Injecting new subjects naturally during streaming video generation requires integrating newly supplied visual references into the existing video while preserving established subjects and the scene. Encoding references independently of the current scene provides little guidance for this integration, while keeping their features in persistent memory can interfere with established context. We propose ReferStream, a framework that requires no additional training and combines reference construction using the current scene with transient cache injection. Joint Latent places reference latents in target regions of the latest scene latent, allowing reference features to be extracted in context. Cache Restoration uses these features to condition the injection chunk, then restores the overwritten global cache entries while retaining the newly generated history. This procedure incorporates new visual conditions without retraining the generator or revising emitted frames. We further introduce ReferStream Bench, a new benchmark with scheduled reference arrivals, evolving instructions, and explicit annotations of subject presence for InShot and MultiShot generation. Evaluation follows the event schedule and measures both the fidelity of new subjects and the preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality, text adherence, and count accuracy. Experiments on ReferStream Bench show higher scores for text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy than the compared baselines, including offline methods given all references in advance. Project page: https://xushuolin.github.io/ReferStream/.

Reports improved text adherence, subject similarity, and count accuracy over compared baselines, including offline methods.
Evaluates both new-subject fidelity and preservation of established subjects, alongside video quality and text adherence.

papers.abstract: Video captioning aims to preserve visual information through compact descriptions, predominantly using natural language. However, precisely expressing fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics in natural language often leads to lengthy and potentially ambiguous descriptions. In this work, we explore Code as Video Caption, a paradigm where executable programs serve as a complementary representation of visual content through graphical primitives, layout rules, and functions of time. To examine whether code captions effectively preserve video information, we compare them with natural language captions on downstream question answering and video reconstruction tasks. Our results show that code captions achieve superior reasoning accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Despite these advantages, realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate faithful code captions. To systematically assess this capability, we introduce CodeCap-Bench, which comprises 323 videos spanning five categories of structured 2D content, along with fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework. Extensive experiments reveal that while leading proprietary MLLMs demonstrate promising code captioning capabilities, they still struggle to faithfully capture complex temporal dynamics, with open-source models lagging substantially behind.
authors: Jiafu Tang, Yifan Xu, Eric Tang, Junjie Zhao, Shipeng Luo, Te Sun, Haoxuan Hu, Yiyan Ji, Xinlong Chen, Zihao Wang, Yang Shi, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Jiaheng Liu

papers.abstract: Recent advances in diffusion models have achieved remarkable success in restoring high-quality images in a zero-shot manner. Unfortunately, extending this success to video restoration is challenging due to the substantial computational resources required to pre-train video diffusion models. A rising trend seeks to address video restoration by utilizing a pre-trained image diffusion model, initiating restoration from either frame-wise independent or identical Gaussian noise. Yet, these approaches often fall short, as such simple noise initiations fail to capture and utilize the inherent temporal correlations within degraded video frames. In this work, we propose taming noise initialization for zero-shot video restoration, which preserves the intrinsic temporal correlations by generating initial noises directly using DDIM inversion on the corrupted video frames themselves. Building on this, we introduce an adaptive noise blending strategy that suppresses degradation patterns encoded during DDIM inversion while gradually steering the noise toward a Gaussian distribution. To further emphasize temporal consistency, we propose measurement-guided trajectory attention to better align features across frames. Extensive experiments on multiple video restoration tasks demonstrate that our method outperforms existing zero-shot approaches, consistently achieving superior results on the DAVIS, REDS4, and Set8 datasets.
authors: Chong Wang, Zixuan Fu, Hao Cheng, Siyuan Yang, Alex C. Kot, Bihan Wen
bullets: Problem: Frame-independent or identical Gaussian initialization fails to capture temporal correlations in degraded videos, while training video diffusion models is costly.
Method: Generate initial noise from corrupted frames via DDIM inversion to preserve temporal structure.
Adaptive noise blending suppresses inverted degradation patterns while progressively moving noise toward a Gaussian distribution.
Measurement-guided trajectory attention further aligns features across video frames.
Experiments across multiple restoration tasks on DAVIS, REDS4, and Set8 show consistent improvements over existing zero-shot approaches.

After that, the temporal correlation is further exploited by measurement-guided trajectory attention during the sampling process.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for enhancing the video reasoning capability of Large Multimodal Models (LMMs). Despite its empirical effectiveness, we show that outcome-level optimization can introduce an undesirable shortcut amplification effect, whereby models increasingly favor text-prior answers even when they are not supported by the visual evidence. To characterize this behavior, we investigate the training dynamics of video RLVR through the lens of perceptual uncertainty, analyzing how predictive uncertainty evolves under video-conditioned and text-only contexts. Our analysis identifies a perceptual uncertainty collapse phenomenon, in which RL training continuously sharpens the model's answer distribution while the uncertainty reduction attributable to visual evidence progressively diminishes. A further gradient-direction analysis reveals that such confidence enhancement becomes increasingly less aligned with visually grounded uncertainty reduction and is instead dominated by text-prior compression. Motivated by these findings, we propose Bifocal Self-distillation Policy Optimization (BSPO), a self-distillation framework that regulates policy updates with two complementary distributional signals. Specifically, BSPO derives empirical reasoning principles from intra-group correct and incorrect rollouts to identify reasoning-sensitive tokens, and introduces shortcut-aware visual perturbation to penalize predictions that remain invariant when task-relevant visual evidence is weakened. By adaptively reweighting the original RL advantage, BSPO preserves the task-solving benefits of RLVR while promoting updates that are both reasoning-sensitive and visually grounded. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of BSPO in improving video reasoning performance and strengthening visual faithfulness.
authors: Jiafeng Liang, Xianhao Ou, Tao Ren, Rongchuan Mu, Runxuan Liu, Dandan Tu, Ming Liu, See-Kiong Ng, Bing Qin
bullets: RLVR may make models increasingly confident in text-prior answers unsupported by video evidence.
Perceptual uncertainty collapse occurs as visual evidence contributes less to uncertainty reduction during training.
Gradient analysis links this confidence growth more to text-prior compression than to visual grounding.
BSPO combines self-distillation from correct/incorrect rollouts with shortcut-aware visual perturbations to guide policy updates.
Experiments show improved video reasoning performance and stronger visual faithfulness.

papers.abstract: Distribution-matching distillation enables high-quality image generation in only a few denoising steps. However, distilled student models often map different initial noise samples to similar outputs under the same prompt. To locate where diversity is lost, we compare the teacher and student along the sampling trajectory. The largest measured reduction in the response to different initial noises occurs during the first, high-noise step. When we replace the first step with the teacher's corresponding trajectory and leave the final three student steps unchanged, most of the output diversity returns. This suggests that the first step is a key point for restoring diversity. Motivated by this finding, we introduce \emph{ReSeed}, a post-distillation method that adds a seed-response bias adapter only to the first student step and aligns its velocity with the teacher's first-interval secant velocity. All student weights and later denoising steps remain unchanged. We evaluate ReSeed on three text-to-image models (SD3-Medium, SD3.5-Medium, and FLUX.1-dev) and one text-to-video model (Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B). For a distilled 4-step FLUX.1-dev model, \emph{ReSeed} requires only $0.00196\%$ additional trainable parameters relative to the base model and is trained on 8,000 prompt--noise pairs, while keeping the distilled student fully frozen and requiring no target images, perceptual losses, or adversarial losses. It improves DINO diversity by $48.3\%$ while maintaining competitive visual quality. These results show that substantial diversity can be recovered through a lightweight, data-efficient tuning of only the first denoising step, without finetuning the full student model.
authors: Wenwu Tang, Dong Wang, Yun Cheng, Olga Saukh
bullets: Diversity is lost primarily during the first, high-noise denoising step.

papers.abstract: Despite significant progress, current models struggle to generate comprehensive video captions, constrained primarily by coarse-grained supervision, which often fails to capture spatial-temporal dynamics and the underlying logical intent. To address this issue, we introduce MVRCap, a novel framework that reformulates video captioning as a reinforcement learning task steered by structured verification. Central to our approach is a Fine-Grained Verifiable Reward mechanism, serving as dense supervision to enforce rigorous visual-semantic alignment. Specifically, we construct this reward system anchored by three complementary pillars: a Hierarchical Concept Coverage Reward utilizing our newly constructed MVRCap-QA dataset to ensure multi-dimensional completeness and semantic depth, a Factuality Verification Reward to enhance factual consistency, and a Conciseness Constraint to maximize semantic density. Furthermore, we curate the high-quality MVRCap-SFT dataset, providing structured annotations across six key dimensions, to serve as a robust foundational initialization for the RL policy in this training pipeline. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MVRCap achieves state-of-the-art performance on authoritative benchmarks including VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG.
authors: Weihuang Lin, Xianing Chen, Zhibin Wang, Congzhi Zhang, Yiwei Ma, Jiayi Ji, Miao Chen, Jun Song, YuCheng, Bo Zheng, Xiaoshuai Sun, Rongrong Ji
bullets: Addresses coarse-grained supervision that misses videos’ spatial-temporal dynamics and logical intent.

Combines hierarchical concept coverage, factuality verification, and conciseness rewards.
Uses the MVRCap-QA dataset for coverage evaluation and MVRCap-SFT for structured policy initialization.
Reports state-of-the-art performance on the VDC, CAPability, and VC4VG benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs), which route predictions through a layer of human-interpretable concepts, have substantially improved the interpretability of visual classification by exposing an explicit, language-based rationale for each prediction. Most existing work focuses on static images, and temporal dynamics in videos have been underexplored in conceptual representation. We propose a framework that extends concept-based image recognition to procedural video understanding. It represents a multi-step video as a temporal sequence of segment-level concept score vectors and feeds this sequence into a Transformer encoder to predict the class label. We also explore a way to estimate the contribution of each concept for further interpretability. We evaluated three concept sets of different granularities on cooking and household-activity videos and found that coarser-grained concepts are sufficient for classifying these videos, which implies that fine-grained textual descriptions may be unnecessary.
authors: Ryoya Yoshiyama, Bowen Wang, Yuta Nakashima
bullets: Extends Concept Bottleneck Models from static images to multi-step video understanding.
Represents videos as temporal sequences of segment-level concept score vectors.
Uses a Transformer encoder to predict video classes.
Estimates each concept’s contribution to improve interpretability.
Evaluation on cooking and household-activity videos suggests coarse-grained concepts are sufficient.

papers.abstract: Interactive world generation requires models to follow successive commands while preserving relevant history and action consequences. We present Hy-Nomas, a video world model with an 8B diffusion backbone that supports free-form text instructions and continuous camera control across multiple interaction turns. It generates variable-length segments conditioned on current inputs and cached history. Our central design aligns structured video captions with action-aware causal attention: descriptive context remains accessible across segments, while action instructions are restricted to their intended temporal windows. A vision-language Prompt Enhancer (PE) translates user requests and multimodal interaction histories into structured conditions for the next segment. A multi-stage curriculum progressively introduces causal generation, text interaction, camera control, and training on model-generated histories, followed by diffusion distillation. In human evaluation, Hy-Nomas shows superior performance over existing world models. We release model weights, code and benchmarks, together with a lightweight adaptation workflow, to support reproducible research on interactive world generation.
authors: Qiaoling Chen, Jiaxiang Cheng, Xueqing Deng, Tiankai Hang, Ji Hou, Jiaqi Li, Yifan Liu, Tao Lu, Junshu Tang, Yu Tang, Yao Teng, Yu Tian, Heng Wang, Weizhi Wang, Xiyao Wang, Xilun Wu, Mingyu Yang, Yangbin Yu, Rui Zhao, Longjun Cao, Linghao Chen, Haoyi Duan, Jiaming Han, Mingji Han, Enhua Jiang, Shunkai Li, Yanzhe Liang, Qinwei Ma, Cong Wang, Lei Wang, Bing Wu, Ke Xing, Ray Ying, Zhentao Yu, Key Zhang, Yuan Zhou, Zhengguang Zhou, Kai Zou

Generates variable-length video segments conditioned on current inputs and cached interaction history.
Uses action-aware causal attention to preserve descriptive context while limiting actions to their intended time windows.
A vision-language Prompt Enhancer converts user requests and multimodal histories into structured next-segment conditions.
Human evaluations report better performance than existing world models; weights, code, benchmarks, and an adaptation workflow are released.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Overview of the model architecture. A structured multi-segment prompt, a video clip, and a camera trajectory are encoded into text, video, and camera tokens, respectively. Text and video tokens are processed by N = 54 dual-stream MMDiT blocks. Within each block, segmentwise causal attention with 3D RoPE allows tokens to attend to the current and preceding segments, while diffusion timestep embeddings modulate both streams. The two streams pass through separate MLPs, and camera cross-attention further conditions the video stream on camera tokens. During autoregressive generation, keys and values associated with both text and video tokens are stored in the KV cache as context for subsequent segments. The 3D VAE decoder maps denoised video latents to RGB frames. Purple, blue, and green denote the text, video, and camera streams, respectively.

Across each training stage, adaptive sampling adjusts the training distribution in response to weaknesses identified from evaluations of earlier stages.

The VLM annotates segments sequentially, maintains subject identities, interleaves scene and camera descriptions chronologically, and records subject actions separately with timestamps. Figure 4: Structured caption format. Video-level fields define perspective, style, and shared subject profiles. papers.abstract: Video models answer from sampled frames and may miss the decisive moment. A common remedy is to commit to an answer, re-examine the video, and confirm or revise it, a loop now mainly learned with reinforcement learning (RL). We find that RL erodes the initial answer, a phenomenon we term confidence erosion, where confidence means the label-verified reliability of the initial answer instead of self-reported certainty: because errors can be repaired later, a correct initial answer earns less reward, and the initial answer stalls even as the final answer's gain over it rises. We propose the principle confident first, reflective second: the initial answer must stay reliable on its own, above a floor set by a reference policy, and reflection may only add to it. Our method, CoFire, implements this principle with one mechanism for each erosion channel: reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference. CoFire reaches 67.0% mean accuracy on Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method, and improves initial-answer and final accuracy over outcome-reward RL by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average: a stronger initial answer carries through to a stronger final one.
authors: Zihao Lin, Jingyuan Liu, Yucheng Zhang, Yuguang Yao, Lifu Huang
bullets: RL-based reflection can cause confidence erosion: correct initial answers are undervalued because later correction is rewarded.
CoFire enforces a reference-policy reliability floor for the initial answer and allows reflection to add, not replace, its value.
It addresses reward incentives, parameter drift, and gradient interference as sources of erosion.
CoFire achieves 67.0% mean accuracy across Video-MME, MLVU, and LongVideoBench, 1.7 points above the strongest compared 7B method.
Compared with outcome-reward RL, it improves initial and final accuracy by 4.1 and 3.7 points on average.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of COFIRE. Top: G rollouts of one policy answer (Spre), choose how to check (Sgate), and confirm or revise (Srev). Bottom: one mechanism per erosion channel: λ rises below the initial-answer accuracy floor (incentive), verified reference answers anchor the decision token (drift), and only the conflicting part of the reflection gradient is removed (interference).

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.
Evaluates 37 closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, alongside human evaluation.
Humans achieve 68.5% video-only accuracy, compared with 50.0% for the strongest evaluated MLLM, Qwen3.6-27B, in zero-shot evaluation.
Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: Video Large Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in video understanding and reasoning, but processing long visual sequences incurs substantial computational, latency, and memory overhead. This survey examines training-free inference acceleration, focusing on reducing inference costs while preserving task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence. We organize existing methods by their intervention stages in the inference pipeline, covering input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding. Post-training quantization (PTQ) is discussed separately as a cross-stage extension with varying calibration requirements. We analyze how intervention position affects evidence preservation and computational savings, and why local efficiency improvements may not translate into end-to-end acceleration. We complement this analysis with quantitative evidence from prior studies and our own experiments under a shared evaluation setting to assess accuracy-latency trade-offs.
authors: Yuqi Li, Chuanyue Yan, Neil Rodrigues, Xianglong Wang, Xiaoqin Feng, Junming Liu, Xi Xiao, Zhongwei Cheng, Wei Li, Lin Chen, Yingli Tian
bullets: Video VLMs face high computation, latency, and memory costs on long visual sequences.
Methods are categorized by intervention stage: input, visual encoding, projector, prefill, and decoding.
Post-training quantization is treated as a cross-stage approach with different calibration requirements.
The survey examines how intervention location affects preservation of task-relevant spatiotemporal evidence.
Prior results and shared-setting experiments assess accuracy–latency trade-offs and highlight that local gains may not yield end-to-end speedups.

papers.abstract: Dyadic relationship recognition aims to identify the latent social relationship between two individuals from their multimodal interactions. Existing methods typically project heterogeneous cues into a shared representation and optimise a flat classification objective, overlooking that relationships may rely on different interaction patterns. For instance, distant relationships can often be inferred from direct behavioural correspondence, whereas close relationships are better reflected by coordinated affective, behavioural, and multimodal responses. To address this limitation, we propose HiRe-DRR, a Hierarchical Multimodal Interaction Reasoning framework that organises relationship evidence from three complementary perspectives: feature level, interaction type, and relationship hierarchy. HiRe-DRR decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations and constructs homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions. We further introduce the Mixture-of-Interaction Transformer (MoI-Former), which treats diverse interactions as specialised experts and employs relation-aware sparse routing to identify relationship-relevant evidence while preserving contextual interaction information. The proposed Hierarchical Conditional Loss (HC-Loss) exploits the hierarchical nature of social relationships through coarse-to-fine supervision, enabling structured relationship reasoning. Extensive experiments on three dyadic relationship benchmarks demonstrate that HiRe-DRR outperforms recent representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods. Our routing analysis further reveals that distant relationships tend to rely on low-level homogeneous interactions, whereas closer relationships focus on high-level heterogeneous interactions. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/tw-repository/HiRe-DRR.
authors: Wang Tang, Fethiye Irmak Dogan, Linbo Qing, Ce Zhu, Hatice Gunes
bullets: Addresses the limitation that different social relationships depend on different interaction patterns.
Decomposes facial, bodily, acoustic, and textual cues into low- and high-level representations with homogeneous and heterogeneous cross-participant interactions.
Uses MoI-Former with relation-aware sparse routing to select relevant interaction evidence while retaining context.
Applies HC-Loss for coarse-to-fine supervision aligned with relationship hierarchies.

Experiments on three benchmarks show improvements over representative image-, video-, and multimodal methods; routing analysis links distant relationships to low-level homogeneous interactions and closer relationships to high-level heterogeneous interactions.

papers.abstract: Long-video question answering is challenging since the answer often hinges on a few decisive moments scattered throughout the video, while memory constraints force Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to sample frames at extremely low rates, resulting in sparsity that risks omitting key evidence. Though aggressively enlarging the context size is intuitive, we argue that performance remains fundamentally constrained by the bias, \emph{i.e.}, the misleading cues caused by spurious \textit{linguistic} correlations and salient yet irrelevant \textit{visual} observations. In this paper, we first introduce {S-MME}, a benchmark designed to systematically diagnose shortcut-biased behavior in MLLMs. To mitigate this failure, we further propose a training-free framework, Counterfactual Long-video Evidence-Aware Reasoning (CLEAR). By treating the full video-question pair as a complete view, CLEAR estimates bias effects via augmented views by only keeping the question or locally salient visual clips. Then, we intervene hidden states to mitigate the discrepancy at inference such that the correct answer can be predicted confidently. With experimental studies across five benchmarks, we show that our method is generalizable and can be integrated in different MLLMs, yielding consistent gains in prediction and robustness. We hope CLEAR can offer a complementary direction in test-time scaling for long-video understanding.
authors: Xusheng Liang, Jianqiao Sun, Hao Zhang, Yulei Niu, Hengshuang Zhao, Jiawei Ma
bullets: Long-video QA is difficult because sparse frame sampling can miss decisive evidence, while spurious cues can still mislead models.
S-MME benchmarks shortcut-biased behavior from misleading language correlations and salient but irrelevant visual content.
CLEAR estimates bias using question-only and locally salient-clip views, then intervenes on hidden states at inference.
Experiments across five benchmarks show consistent gains in prediction and robustness across different MLLMs.
CLEAR is presented as a complementary test-time scaling approach; the abstract does not specify detailed limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of CLEAR. (a) The full-video path produces the final answer, while questiononly and salient-view probes reveal spurious linguistic correlations and salient-yet-misleading visual observations. The salient view is formed by selecting top-K locally relevant clips according to query-conditioned visual attention. (b) CLEAR extracts the hidden state of the shared decision token z at selected late decoder layers, and constructs residual vectors rql = hf l − hq l and rsl = hf l − hs l from the restricted-view probes to the full-video state. These residual vectors are injected into the full-video path to steer its hidden state away from shortcut anchors before final decoding.

Figure 2: Construction pipeline of S-MME. We first mine candidate questions with explicit long-video evidence requirements, then use restricted views to identify shortcut-consistent distractors, followed by human validation of answer uniqueness, evidence sufficiency, and shortcut plausibility.
Figure 4: Effect of intervention location. Latelayer intervention performs best, with the last block achieving the highest accuracy.

Figure 1: MLLMs often fail despite the presence of decisive evidence, either by following spurious linguistic correlations or by over-relying on salient but misleading visual observations. CLEAR diagnoses these shortcut-biased trajectories with controlled probes and steers the full-video representation toward evidence-consistent prediction.
Figure 5: Context scaling analysis. CLEAR consistently improves accuracy and reduces ShortErr under the same frame budget.
Figure 6: Qualitative effect of CLEAR on open-ended video QA.

papers.abstract: Recent advancements in text-guided 3D editing, particularly with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), have shown promise but still lag behind the flexibility of 2D editing tools. Existing methods face a critical trade-off between preserving multi-view consistency and allowing structural modifications. Image-based editors can also struggle to apply the intended edit to objects viewed from unusual angles. To address these limitations, we introduce VidEdit3D, a framework that reformulates 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. By drawing a parallel between camera movement in static 3D scenes and temporal dynamics in video, we leverage the robust spatiotemporal priors of pre-trained Video Diffusion Models (VDMs) to encourage semantic and structural coherence across views. Specifically, we propose Trajectory-Guided Rendering (TGR) to select informative keyframes and construct smooth video clips aligned with VDM input requirements. To propagate edits from an anchor view to these clips, we develop Flow-Aligned Video Editing (FAVE), a training-free framework incorporating an Editing Consistency Guidance (ECG) mechanism. ECG contrasts source and edited image conditions at a shared latent state, using scheduled source-image amplification to strengthen adherence to the edited reference while maintaining original scene context. Finally, we introduce Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement (RS-GS) to strictly confine geometric and appearance updates to target primitives, reducing background attribute leakage. Experiments demonstrate stronger instruction alignment and better multi-view consistency than the baselines.
authors: Yanming Yang, Chenxi Song, Tong Zhao, Juntao Xu, Wenhao Rao, Yiwen Chen, Yiwei Wang, Chi Zhang
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between structural editability and multi-view consistency in existing 3D and image-based editors.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Rendering to select keyframes and create smooth camera-aligned video clips.
Applies Flow-Aligned Video Editing with Editing Consistency Guidance to propagate an anchor-view edit across views.
Uses Region-Selective 3DGS Refinement to limit geometry and appearance changes to target regions and reduce background leakage.
Experiments show stronger instruction alignment and improved multi-view consistency than baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of VidEdit3D. We reformulate 3D scene editing as a trajectory-based video editing task. The pipeline consists of three key stages: (1) TGR: We organize selected views into smooth video clips. (2) FAVE: Given a user-edited anchor frame, we propagate the edit across the clip using a pretrained VDM. This module incorporates ECG for semantic alignment and a self-attention-based mask for background preservation. (3) RS-GS: We lift the 2D edits back to 3D via inverse rendering to confine updates to the target Gaussians.

Fig. 3. Qualitative comparison of reference-guided scene editing. VidEdit3D inserts accessories, removes a vase, and localizes appearance changes to the requested objects. Source and edited results are shown at matched viewpoints, with insets providing a second view.
Fig. 7. More results. Each task shows a source image followed by two edited views.

Fig. 9. Edits with user-provided accessory references. User-provided images specify the hat and mask, sunglasses, and AI pendant used in the edited anchor. Each row shows the source, the reference image, and three views rendered from the edited 3D scene.

Fig. 1. Flexible and consistent 3D editing with VidEdit3D. The baseline (left) shows inconsistent appearance, incomplete headset insertion and vase removal, and misplaced glasses. VidEdit3D (right) propagates the anchor edit across views, producing coherent appearance changes and localized object insertion and removal while preserving nearby content.

Fig. 11. Field of view affects the balance between unchanged context and target resolution. Wider views retain surrounding context and better sustain the jersey and gold-material edits, at the cost of target resolution. The localized 3D edit (bottom left) remains stable. Video editing (bottom middle and right) is unaffected by this appearance fading: temporal continuity provides stronger frame-to-frame correspondence and better matches the video diffusion model’s learned prior, allowing the target appearance to persist. Rows show source and edited frames.
Fig. 10. Failure-mode and scope analysis: occlusion, imperfect anchors, thin structures, and segmentation.

Fig. 5. Effect of RS-GS region selection. Without restricting Gaussian updates, recoloring the armchair also alters the adjacent sofa. VidEdit3D preserves the sofa appearance while completing the red-chair edit. Colored boxes mark corresponding regions enlarged below.
Fig. 8. More results (continued). Each task shows a source image followed by two edited views.

papers.abstract: Generating videos of a specific subject from a few reference images remains challenging when the camera reveals surfaces that are not visible in the input. Early subject-to-video (S2V) methods condition on a single reference image and must therefore infer the subject's unseen appearance and geometry as the viewpoint changes. To address this limitation, recent methods extend S2V to multiple reference views, providing more information about the subject from different viewpoints. However, they do not explicitly specify the 3D structure that connects these observations. In addition, existing training data do not guarantee that viewpoint changes preserve the same underlying 3D subject. We present OmniShowcase, built on two components: (i) a fully automated data synthesis pipeline that produces training videos along diverse camera trajectories, with viewpoint variation driven by underlying subject geometry, even spanning full 360-degree orbits; and (ii) a geometry-conditioning method that provides the video model with a turntable of surface-normal maps reconstructed from the reference views without requiring temporal alignment with the generated frames. We construct Showcase-4K, a corpus of 3D-asset-based videos covering twelve camera motions across 88 trajectory configurations with reconstruction-derived surface-normal conditioning, and ShowcaseBench, a held-out evaluation set with the source meshes and camera parameters used to render each video. Experiments show state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency while maintaining competitive video quality and motion. Project page: justin4ai.github.io/OmniShowcase
authors: Junyeong Ahn, Geonwoo Kim, Kinam Kim, Gihwi Kim, Hoonjin Jung, Hyojin Jang, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses unseen subject surfaces and inconsistent 3D structure during viewpoint changes.
Uses an automated pipeline to synthesize videos with geometry-driven camera motion, including full 360° orbits.
Conditions generation on surface-normal maps reconstructed from reference views without requiring temporal alignment.
Introduces Showcase-4K for training and ShowcaseBench for evaluation with known meshes and camera parameters.
Reports state-of-the-art subject identity and 3D consistency with competitive video quality and motion.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of OmniShowcase. From N=4 reference views, we reconstruct 3D geometry and render a surface-normal turntable. The reference images and normal condition are injected into the reference pathway of a LoRA-tuned image-to-video diffusion transformer. The model uses appearance information from the reference views and 3D structure from the normal condition to generate the target video without per-subject optimization.

Figure 2: Automated 3D-consistent data synthesis pipeline. From a curated 3D asset (Deitke et al., 2023), Blender renders the target orbit and four reference views. (a) The target is composited into a prompt-driven scene by video inpainting (Jiang et al., 2025); (b) the four views are reconstructed in 3D (Li et al., 2026) and rendered as the surface-normal turntable used as the condition. Every stage runs without human intervention.

Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of training data. Uni3C (Cao et al., 2025) is an image-to-video model, so every surface the camera path uncovers is generated. Ours renders the subject from a 3D asset and generates only the background.

Figure 10: 3D reconstruction from generated video. The subject is segmented out of each method’s generated orbit and lifted to a coloured point cloud, the same reconstruction evaluated by GT-CD, shown here from four viewpoints so the geometric differences are visible directly. Baselines recover a thin shell of the surfaces their orbit actually sweeps, while ours closes the volume.

Figure 7: Additional qualitative comparison. Four further subjects under diverse camera trajectories, with the same method ordering as Figure 5. Each block pairs the four reference views and the prompt, whose +[tag] suffix names the trajectory (Appendix G.2), with generated frames from every method.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison with baselines. 3DB denotes 3DreamBooth. Given a teapot and a jar of peach gummies, we compare OmniShowcase against four baselines. Red boxes mark where identity or 3D structure breaks down.
Figure 6: Conditioning ablation. Given a biplane and a bulldozer, we compare the three conditioning variants against ours. Marked regions highlight where identity or 3D structure breaks down.
Figure 8: Trajectory and scene control. One subject driven by several camera configurations, including arc, zoom-in and truck, with the background also varied by the prompt for each trajectory.

Figure 9: Trajectory control in a fixed scene. The same subject and background under different camera configurations, from full orbits to an arc and a zoom-out, where only the camera trajectory changes between rows. Inference only.

Figure 13: Failure cases. Left two. The upper one is prompted in the usual static style and settles into an averaged pose that matches none of the references, while the lower one is asked to follow the motion in step with the orbit and tangles in 3D at the transitions between poses.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation is essential for deploying modern video diffusion models. Among existing approaches, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) has emerged as a highly promising paradigm by achieving strong output-space fidelity without adversarial training, while remaining flexible across various student architectures. We observe, however, that DMD fundamentally relies on an output-space objective, lacking explicit regularization on the model's internal representations. As the distillation step count aggressively shrinks, this output-only supervision becomes insufficient, causing the distilled student to degrade in both fine-grained spatial structures and coherent temporal dynamics. To address this limitation, we introduce Self Flow Forcing (SF$^2$), which incorporates a predictive representation loss into the DMD framework without altering its output objective. By providing the student and an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) teacher with heterogeneous noise levels, we establish an information asymmetry. This formulation forces the student to predict the teacher's internal representations from a more corrupted input, effectively integrating self-supervised representation alignment into distribution matching. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SF$^2$ effectively mitigates temporal flickering and consistently improves both spatial fidelity and motion quality. Furthermore, the proposed mechanism is architecture-agnostic - seamlessly supporting both bidirectional and causal models - and requires no external feature extractors, introducing minimal computational overhead.
authors: Junyi Chen, Haiyu Zhang, Zhoujie Fu, Tengfei Wang, Chunchao Guo
bullets: DMD’s output-only supervision can fail at very low step counts, harming fine spatial detail and coherent motion.
SF² adds a predictive representation loss while preserving DMD’s original output objective.
A student receives a more corrupted input than its EMA teacher and predicts the teacher’s internal representations.
Experiments report less temporal flickering and consistent gains in spatial fidelity and motion quality.
The method is architecture-agnostic across bidirectional and causal models and needs no external feature extractor.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of SF2. From the student’s denoising trajectory, the cleanest prediction drives the standard DMD loss LDMD, while two intermediate states (xt, xs) with t > s feed the SF2 branch: a spatial mask mixes them into an asymmetric, highly corrupted input for the student, while the EMA teacher sees only the cleaner xs. Hidden states from asymmetric layers are aligned via learnable projectors with a stop-gradient cosine loss Lrep. The teacher is updated by EMA and requires no external pre-trained features.

Figure 6: Quantitative evaluation on interactive video generation. We evaluate the adherence of the generated video to the input camera and action conditions. Compared to the WorldPlay baseline, SF2 achieves notably higher translation, rotation, and action accuracy across training steps, demonstrating that a stronger internal representation leads to more precise state transitions in interactive environments.

Figure 7: Qualitative camera trajectory alignment. Reconstructed 3D point clouds and camera trajectories from the generated videos. The trajectory produced by SF2 (blue) tightly tracks the input condition (green), whereas the WorldPlay baseline (red) exhibits severe drift. This visualizes how the stronger internal representation of SF2 enforces strict adherence to complex control signals.

Figure 2: Qualitative comparison on causal few-step T2V generation. Top row: multi-step bidirectional Wan2.1 teacher. Rows 2–5: few-step distilled causal students (CausVid, Self-Forcing, Causal-Forcing, SF2). The four panels expose four facets of representation-level coherence that the rep loss is designed to compress into the student: articulated-motion plausibility (top-left), event irreversibility (top-right), object persistence (bottom-left), and scene-structural stability (bottomright). SF2 satisfies all four, whereas baselines fail in distinct ways on each.

Table 2: Quantitative comparison with existing methods on VBench [17] and VisionReward [46]. Models are grouped by sampling regime — bidirectional multi-step, distilled bidirectional, autoregressive multi-step, and distilled autoregressive — and bold marks the best score within each comparable group. Throughput is in FPS and latency in second, both measured on a single H100. All distilled models (in both distilled groups) share the same Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B backbone.

Table 4: Full hyperparameters for the three SF2 instantiations. The SF2 branch is identical in spirit across settings; the only paradigm-dependent quantities are the masking ratio ρmax and the chunk size Fb (causal only). All bidirectional models use K=4 denoising steps; the causal student also uses K=4 unless otherwise noted.
Table 1: Per-cycle training-time breakdown (% of one cycle). One cycle = 1 generator update + 5 critic updates. The SF2branch is only ∼6% of the cycle.

Table 3: Probing representation quality via re-rendering and frame-level coherence. We report PSNR / SSIM / LPIPS against the generated frames, plus VBench Temporal Flickering and Background Consistency. SF2 improves over vanilla DMD on every reconstruction and coherence metric at matched Dynamic Degree, despite using no 3D supervision during training.

papers.tldr: Self Flow Forcing strengthens few-step video diffusion distillation by adding self-supervised internal-representation prediction to DMD, improving spatial fidelity and temporal coherence with minimal overhead.

papers.abstract: Uniform frame sampling can miss brief evidence in sparse-event videos when the VLM sees only K frames. We propose EARS (Evidence-Aware Retrieval via Sound and motion), a training-free, query-free front-end that ranks frames using optical-flow motion and audio energy, then applies temporal non-maximum suppression for diversity. The evidence score alone has frame-level AP 0.39; used only to select frames for the VLM, EARS with temporal diversity reaches localization AP 0.94, compared with 0.88 under Uniform sampling. In the updated matched study, at K = 1 EARS reaches XD-subset F1 0.660 versus 0.614 for centered Uniform (the paired interval includes zero); earlier backbone studies use separate protocols. On mostly-silent UCF-Crime, however, EARS slightly trails Uniform. A single configuration is used across both benchmarks; the new controls do not repeat the original held-out search. EARS therefore targets low-budget videos whose salient evidence aligns with motion or audio; on dense narratives or stealthy events, uniform or semantic selection remains preferable, and cheap modality statistics cannot reliably route between them. bullets: Targets sparse-event videos where uniform sampling may miss brief evidence under a frame budget.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised temporal action localization (PTAL) aims to recognize and localize action instances in untrimmed videos using only point-level annotations. Existing pseudo-label-based methods have made substantial progress in PTAL. However, confidence-based initialization can overlook well-localized proposals. Meanwhile, existing methods either keep pseudo-labels fixed during detector training or update them without fully exploiting alternative boundary evidence from the original proposal pool. These limitations constrain supervision quality, thereby hindering detection performance. To learn high-quality pseudo-labels, we propose a framework that integrates prior-guided initialization with consensus-guided refinement during detector training. Our framework comprises two modules: Prior-Guided Initialization (PGI) and Consensus-Guided Refinement (CGR). PGI combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to establish instance-specific reliability for initial pseudo-label selection and candidate retention. CGR continually uses the retained original candidates to construct boundary targets, combining their consensus with evolving detector predictions to refine pseudo-labels throughout training. Experiments on four benchmarks demonstrate that our method achieves competitive detection performance compared with existing methods. In particular, our method achieves 68.5\% average mAP over tIoU thresholds 0.1--0.7 on THUMOS14, surpassing PseR by 3.7 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/zhenyingfang/LHQP
bullets: Addresses missed well-localized proposals and weak pseudo-label updates in existing PTAL methods.
Prior-Guided Initialization combines proposal confidence with point-derived priors to select reliable initial pseudo-labels and retain candidates.
Consensus-Guided Refinement uses retained original proposals and evolving detector predictions to refine action boundaries throughout training.
Evaluated on four benchmarks, achieving 68.5% average mAP across tIoU 0.1–0.7 on THUMOS14, 3.7 points above PseR.

papers.abstract: Effective video agents must learn not only how to answer, but also where to look next. Transferring this capability to smaller models is challenging because each observation serves two purposes: supporting an answer and guiding the search for further evidence. Textual descriptions may capture what is currently visible while omitting cues needed for subsequent acquisition. We introduce Latent Agentic Reasoning for Video Analysis (LARVA), a framework that distills multi-round video agents through jointly learned latent reasoning and visual observations. Rather than communicating through captions, an observer passes compact continuous representations to a reasoner that selects the next acquisition action or produces the final answer. Crucially, action and answer supervision propagate through this interface, training the observer to communicate information useful for downstream decisions. Observation reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment provide auxiliary supervision from textual teacher trajectories. Across five video-understanding benchmarks, LARVA achieves strong performance with 4B and 7B backbones. On VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, the 7B model outperforms a textual CoT student trained on the same teacher trajectories by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. These results highlight the value of jointly learning how agents represent evidence and act on it when distilling video-understanding capabilities.
authors: Junzhang Liu, Hao Yuan, Qi Zhang, Yiming Wu, Long Chen, Zhecan Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring agentic video understanding when observations must both support answers and guide future evidence acquisition.
Uses compact continuous latent representations between an observer and a reasoner instead of textual captions.
Jointly trains observation and reasoning through action/answer supervision, with reconstruction and reasoning-distribution alignment as auxiliary signals.
Evaluated with 4B and 7B backbones across five video-understanding benchmarks.
The 7B model surpasses a same-trajectory textual CoT student by 5.1, 2.5, and 3.7 percentage points on VideoHolmes, Video-MME, and LVBench, respectively.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative video models have improved visual realism, making detection increasingly dependent on subtle temporal inconsistencies. However, these signals are weak and spatially localized, while most of the video content is redundant. This creates a fundamental mismatch: existing detectors rely on heavy backbones to model full videos, which leads to high computational cost and limited scalability. In this work, we rethink AI-generated video detection from a representation perspective. Instead of modeling entire videos, we restructure them into compact temporal slice representations that isolate informative temporal evolution. We introduce a lightweight framework using frequency-aware temporal slice consistency learning, where informative spatial rows and columns are aggregated over time to form slice-domain inputs. This reparameterization suppresses redundant appearance while preserving discriminative temporal dynamics, enabling efficient and targeted detection. By constructing slices from both high- and low-frequency regions, our method exposes complementary temporal artifacts, including unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness. We instantiate this idea in a Temporal Slice Consistency Network, which integrates task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer to model cross-slice and cross-frequency dependencies. We further introduce AI-Artist, a new benchmark with artist-curated videos from recent high-fidelity generators, including Seedance and Kling. Experiments on GenVideo and AI-Artist show that our method achieves strong performance while requiring over 400$\times$ fewer model-forward FLOPs and 3.6$\times$ faster model inference than the strong video-based baseline ReStraV (2.9$\times$ faster end to end, including preprocessing), enabling scalable and practical deployment.
authors: Wei Shang, Zhiyuan Li, Shengfeng He
bullets: Targets the redundancy and high computational cost of full-video detectors, where generation artifacts are weak and spatially localized.
Aggregates informative spatial rows and columns over time into compact slices, suppressing appearance redundancy while preserving temporal dynamics.
Uses high- and low-frequency slices to capture complementary artifacts such as unstable details and abnormal motion smoothness.
Implements Temporal Slice Consistency Network with task-driven slice localization, hierarchical positional encoding, and a lightweight Transformer.
Evaluated on GenVideo and the new AI-Artist benchmark; reports strong performance, 3.6× faster model inference, and 2.9× faster end-to-end processing than ReStraV.

papers.abstract: Tube-wise video completion reconstructs temporal trajectories at spatial locations unobserved in every frame. We propose a two-stage framework combining regularized masked Kronecker product decomposition (KPD) with cross-fitted self-supervised residual learning. First, we estimate a compact structural backbone directly from observed entries using cyclic component-wise least-squares updates, spatial and temporal factor regularization, and regularizer-optimal scale balancing. The exact updates yield a nonincreasing objective. Second, we address the mismatch between in-sample fitting errors and the prediction errors encountered at missing tubes. We partition observed tubes into folds and construct residual targets using backbone models fitted without the corresponding target tubes. A lightweight 3-D convolutional neural network then predicts corrections from the backbone, visible residual context, observation mask, and local detail features. Exact data consistency preserves observed measurements. Experiments include ablations, sensitivity analysis, grayscale and RGB video completion, and structured missing patterns. Our method achieves the highest mean PSNR and SSIM at the higher tested sampling rates on the grayscale benchmark. On eight selected DAVIS RGB sequences, it achieves the highest mean missing-region PSNR and full-frame SSIM and the lowest mean missing-tube temporal-gradient MAE at every evaluated sampling rate.
authors: Qi Qi, Yanfei Wang, Yanjun Cui, Jun-e Feng
bullets: Targets reconstruction of spatial-temporal tubes missing across every video frame.

Reports strongest performance on the tested grayscale and DAVIS RGB benchmarks across the stated sampling settings, with ablations and sensitivity analyses.

papers.abstract: Intelligent operating rooms require accurate awareness of surgical workflow for better intra-operative decisions, teamwork, and surgical documentation. Therefore, accurately recognizing surgical phase during surgery is crucial. However, previous artificial intelligence-based methods provide fluctuating predictions for the transitions, restricting their clinical use. To address this challenge, we propose a clinically meaningful framework that integrates a Swin Transformer and Temporal Transformer Encoder (TTE) for effective surgical phase recognition and a parallel YOLOv11s network for real-time surgical instrument localization. To avoid phase flickering and to produce stable workflow predictions, a causal temporal smoothing is applied. The proposed framework is tested on the Cholec80 dataset for the simultaneous recognition of the surgical phases and instruments. The overall phase recognition accuracy of this model was 92%, and the macro average F1-score was 0.86. This performance surpasses CNN based methods such as EndoNet (81.7%) and SV-RCNet (85.3%), as well as temporal convolutional and transformer-based approaches including TeCNO (88.6%), Trans-SVNet (90.9%), and LoViT (91.5%). Besides, the module of instrument detection achieved mAP@0.5 = 0.863. The reliability of the results is confirmed, obtaining a high recognition rate of the workflows, and a high accuracy of the localization of the instruments. The proposed framework can serve as a foundation for intelligent surgical assistance, enriching situation awareness, and potential robotic surgery applications. Code will be made publicly available at: https://github.com/ac005sheekar/LapChol-Surgery-Swin-Cholec80

papers.abstract: Long-video generators increasingly retrieve past visual observations to prevent identity drift. The intuition is compelling: more access to history should make future video more consistent. But an image can be faithful to the past and wrong for the present. Does visual memory always improve the generated story? We investigate this question through VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study. Track-A measures which references are selected from 92 real films (16,548 segments), before generation and without generator confounds. Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed last-seen controls on 30 causally generated stories (2,824 segments) using a shared generator. Retrieval increases entity recall from 0.559 to 0.628-0.693 and improves similarity to past appearances, but decreases precision from 0.977 to 0.915-0.938 and forbidden-entity avoidance from 0.968 to 0.845-0.898. It can also reinforce obsolete appearances after the story changes them. Conversely, high long-gap recall can arise without memory when the prompt itself supplies the appearance; an appearance-stripping analysis exposes this confound. These results distinguish historical fidelity from current-story correctness and show why retrieval relevance or final-video consistency alone does not establish memory utility.
authors: Yuzhuo Chen, Huafeng Shi, Xinyu Wang, Yulong Xu, Yucheng Wang, Haoqin Hong, Guoxin Zhang, Zehua Ma, Weiming Zhang
bullets: Introduces VMem-Bench, a two-track diagnostic study of visual-memory retrieval.
Across 92 real films, Track-A evaluates which references retrieval systems select before generation.
Across 30 generated stories, Track-B compares four retrieval policies with no-memory and gold-informed controls using a shared generator.
Retrieval raises entity recall and similarity to past appearances, but lowers precision and forbidden-entity avoidance.
High long-gap recall may come from prompt-provided appearance details rather than memory, so retrieval relevance or final consistency alone is insufficient evidence of memory utility.

papers.selection_reason: Diagnostic study of visual memory in long-video generation, distinguishing historical fidelity from story correctness.
papers.title: More Memory, Better Videos? A Controlled Study of Visual Memory in Long-Video Generation

papers.abstract: Road anomalies such as collisions, violations, and sudden hazards demand more from video understanding than detection: a practical system must verify what happened, describe the scene, and explain the cause. We find these competences pull in opposite directions for vision-language models: closed-form questions reward precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended answers are scored by similarity to reference text, where matching the annotation style matters as much as reasoning correctly. We present Reason-or-Recite (RoR), a two-specialist framework for the Traffic Anomaly Reasoning track of the 2026 AI City Challenge. RoR (1) rewrites the official chain-of-thought annotations into a structured, temporally grounded schema and LoRA-tunes a 9B vision-language model on the enhanced traces; (2) fine-tunes a 4-bit-quantized 27B model on answers alone, absorbing the annotation style; and (3) selects between the two candidates per question with a training-free LLM judge. RoR ranks first on the in-domain leaderboard with mean score 0.6788.
bullets: Traffic anomaly video understanding requires verifying events, describing scenes, and explaining causes.
Closed-form questions favor precise, evidence-grounded reasoning, while open-ended scoring also rewards matching annotation style.
RoR LoRA-tunes a 9B model on structured, temporally grounded reasoning traces and fine-tunes a 4-bit 27B model on answer text.
A training-free LLM judge selects the better specialist response for each question.
RoR ranks first on the in-domain 2026 AI City Challenge leaderboard, scoring 0.6788.

papers.abstract: An action seen once and the same action seen three times receive the same action-recognition label, so that supervision does not require a model to count. Answers shared across histories that differ in event order, accumulation, or relations leave those distinctions unconstrained; we call this state under-specification. Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) addresses it by training on source-grounded probes of event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency; under the same recent-frame interface it improves OVO-Bench over a strict-matched generic temporal supervision baseline while remaining comparable on StreamingBench, with the largest gain in hallucination detection. Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) then adapts evidence access while keeping the learned model fixed, expanding from recent frames to sparse event and compact history views on demand. The two interventions separate representation from view selection: supervision particularly benefits hallucination detection and causal reasoning, access particularly benefits event recall and forward reasoning. Together they reach the best reported accuracy among the published systems compared here on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench at a fraction of the processed frames of exhaustive selection, and strict replay shows that most of the remaining gap to a three-view oracle is a correct answer that was later replaced. Streaming accuracy depends on what supervision asks the model to keep, what evidence inference exposes, and whether the model keeps a correct answer once it has one.
authors: Yihao Hu, Pan Wang, Yitong Lin, Zhihao Wen, Deyuan Liu, Hang Wang, Mingda Wan, Yiwen Zhao, Yutong Li, Yuchen Mao, Tao Lin
bullets: Streaming supervision can under-specify distinctions such as event order, accumulation, relations, and whether an answer is sufficiently supported.
Visible-State Supervision (ViSS) uses source-grounded probes targeting event identity, order, accumulation, relation change, and answer sufficiency.
Test-Time Causal View Search (TVS) expands evidence from recent frames to sparse events and compact histories without changing the learned model.
ViSS mainly improves hallucination detection and causal reasoning; TVS mainly improves event recall and forward reasoning.

Together, they achieve the best reported accuracy among compared published systems on StreamingBench and OVO-Bench, using a fraction of exhaustive-selection frames; answer replacement remains a key residual error.

papers.title: Supervising the Visible State: Separating Representation from View Selection in Streaming Video

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation can transfer large multimodal models to compact models for autonomous driving, but uniform token-level matching can dilute planning-relevant semantics and amplify teacher errors. We propose RSKD, a semantic-consistency-guided distillation framework that routes supervision according to both the task importance of an answer phrase and its semantic consistency with the teacher prediction. Task-critical semantic phrases are localized in the ground-truth answer, and a phrase-level consistency score controls the balance between Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) distillation and ground-truth supervision. Teacher information is emphasized only where it is semantically consistent, while semantically inconsistent phrases receive stronger ground-truth supervision. We evaluate RSKD on DrivingVQA, LingoQA, and MapLMv2. RSKD improves over the compared student-based baselines on DrivingVQA and LingoQA and remains competitive on MapLMv2.
authors: Chuchu Xie, Yang Zhong, Kangan Qian, Hao Ye, Kun Jiang, Diange Yang

papers.abstract: Humans have been shown to use a "straightened" encoding to represent the natural visual world as it evolves in time (H\'enaff et al. 2019). In the context of discrete video sequences, "straightened" means that changes between frames follow a more linear path in representation space at progressively deeper levels of processing. While deep convolutional networks are often proposed as models of human visual processing, many do not straighten natural videos. In this paper, we explore the relationship between network architecture, differing types of robustness, biologically-inspired filtering mechanisms, and representational straightness in response to time-varying input; we identify strengths and limitations of straightness as a useful way of evaluating neural network representations. We find that (1) adversarial training leads to straighter representations in both CNN and transformer-based architectures but (2) this effect is task-dependent, not generalizing to tasks such as segmentation and frame-prediction, where straight representations are not favorable for predictions; and nor to other types of robustness. In addition, (3) straighter representations impart temporal stability to class predictions, even for out-of-distribution data. Finally, (4) biologically-inspired elements increase straightness in the early stages of a network, but do not guarantee increased straightness in downstream layers of CNNs. We show that straightness is an easily computed measure of representational robustness and stability, as well as a hallmark of human representations with benefits for computer vision models.
authors: Anne Harrington, Vasha DuTell, Ayush Tewari, Mark Hamilton, Simon Stent, Ruth Rosenholtz, William T. Freeman
bullets: Studies how architecture, robustness, and biologically inspired mechanisms affect straightness in learned visual representations.
Finds adversarial training increases straightness in CNNs and vision transformers, but not necessarily for segmentation or frame prediction.
Shows straighter representations improve temporal stability of class predictions, including on out-of-distribution data.
Biologically inspired components increase straightness early in networks but do not consistently improve deeper CNN representations.
Positions straightness as a simple measure of representational robustness and stability, with task-dependent limitations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language models are shifting from offline passive understanding toward online proactive interaction. However, prevailing methods largely rely on explicit requests while miss the implicit user intent (e.g., "where should I click next?" while a user navigate a website), meanwhile fail to update the state simultaneously as user requests might update continuously. These limitations make them less suited to intent-aware interaction in practical. To address these challenges, we introduce StreamVibe-Bench, a new benchmark serving as testbed for user intent interaction, with 4.1K evaluation samples and 85K training samples spanning explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents. Building on this benchmark, we develop StreamVibe-VL, a streaming proactive model that infers implicit user intents from continuous observations and dynamically tailors its interactions as these intents evolve. We further introduce StreamVibe-Harness, which maintains user intents as persistent states with a fleixble lifecycles via a hierarchical memory to track the latest user intent and environmental state. Our experiments reveal three key findings: (i) StreamVibe-VL preserves strong general video understanding while improving response timing and answer quality by 10.7% over other baselines; (ii) existing proactive models remain limited in understanding user intent and deciding when to respond, especially under implicit and dynamic intents; and (iii) StreamVibe-Harness further improves response consistency and adaptation over sustained interaction, resulting in a 12.3% gain in proactive interaction.
authors: Chengzhi Liu, Yuxiang Lai, Yuzhe Yang, Yanqing Liu, Jiheng Hou, Yue Cao, Haonan Wang, Ruixi Fan, Lan Wang, Sheng Liu, Songyou Peng, Yale Song, Kevin Qinghong Lin, Xin Eric Wang, Jui-Hsin Lai, Youbao Tang
bullets: Addresses the inability of existing vision-language agents to infer implicit intent and update interaction states as requests evolve.
StreamVibe-Bench includes 4.1K evaluation and 85K training samples covering explicit, implicit, and dynamic intents.
StreamVibe-VL infers intent from continuous observations and adapts response timing and content dynamically.
StreamVibe-Harness uses hierarchical memory to maintain persistent user and environmental states across interactions.
The proposed systems report 10.7% better response timing and answer quality, plus a 12.3% gain in sustained proactive interaction.
