papers.abstract: Recently, point-supervised temporal action localization has attracted increasing attention due to its low annotation cost (only one frame per action instance) and competitive detection performance. However, since point annotations are less complete than proposal annotations, existing methods mainly rely on multiple instance learning for snippet-level classification, which leads to a performance gap compared to fully supervised models. To bridge this gap, we propose P2P-Former, a novel point-to-proposal Transformer-based framework that effectively connects point-level supervision with proposal-level learning for temporal action localization. In this work, we identify two key challenges in transitioning from point-level supervision to full supervision: (1) how to generate reliable proposals as pseudo ground-truth, and (2) how to effectively integrate point-level cues into the fully supervised paradigm. To address the first challenge, we propose a Point-aware Proposal Generation (PPG) strategy that refines the confidence of proposals produced by a base locator using a point-aware importance estimation function, and then performs optimal matching between point annotations and candidate proposals to select reliable proposals as pseudo ground-truth. To tackle the second challenge, we introduce a Point-guided Semantic Enhancement (PSE) module that aggregates prototypes from point-annotated features and injects them into snippet features through Transformer-based interactions. Moreover, we design a Point-to-Proposal Constraint Loss (PPCL) that enforces each predicted proposal to include the annotated point, thereby encouraging more accurate localization. Extensive experiments on the THUMOS14 and ActivityNet-1.3 datasets demonstrate that our method outperforms several existing state-of-the-art approaches.
authors: Yunchuan Ma, Laiyun Qing, Sai Xu, Guorong Li, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses the performance gap between low-cost point supervision and fully supervised temporal action localization.
Uses Point-aware Proposal Generation (PPG) to refine candidate proposals and match them with annotated points as pseudo ground truth.
Introduces Point-guided Semantic Enhancement (PSE) to transfer point-derived prototypes into snippet features via Transformer interactions.
Applies Point-to-Proposal Constraint Loss (PPCL) to ensure predicted proposals contain the annotated action points.
Experiments on THUMOS14 and ActivityNet-1.3 show improvement over several existing state-of-the-art methods.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed P2P-Former framework. A base action locator first generates coarse proposals, which are then evaluated using point-aware scoring and matched with point annotations via the Hungarian algorithm to obtain reliable pseudo labels. Point-labeled features are clustered to construct category prototypes, which are injected into a prototype-guided semantic enhancement block to enrich video tokens. The enhanced tokens are processed by a Transformer encoder and FPN, followed by classification and regression heads for temporal action localization. The model is trained with Lcls, Lreg, and the point-toproposal constraint Lp2p.

Figure 1: Comparison. (a) Existing methods rely on sparse point-level annotations for classification and derive proposals by thresholding class activation sequences, without explicitly learning temporal localization. (b) P2P-Former discovers high-quality action instances as pseudo labels, enabling joint classification and boundary regression for more complete action localization.

We provide four cases of temporal action localization from different action classes, including “River tubing”, “Applying sunscreen”, “Paintball”, and “Scuba diving”. Prediction errors are highlighted with red dashed boxes. The dark blue region represents the overlap between different predicted instances. The IoUs between our detection results and the ground truths are notably higher.

papers.abstract: Most action-conditioned video world models remain limited to a single player, while existing multiplayer models support only small, fixed groups of agents. We introduce FlockWorld, an artificial-life environment built on Reynolds's Boids algorithm for studying population-scale multi-agent video world models. Specifically, FlockWorld renders synchronized egocentric crops, assigns distinct colors to preserve camera-agent identity across views, exposes rule-derived accelerations as actions, and lets the number of camera agents be configured independently of the size of the surrounding population. We further introduce FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching on FlockWorld data to jointly generate synchronized egocentric videos for multiple agents. Our results suggest that joint generation benefits agent detection at density-matched settings and that diffusion forcing improves rollout fidelity. Together, FlockWorld and FlockDiT provide a controlled testbed for multi-agent video generation.
authors: Meryem Koksal, Yunzhe Wang, Volkan Ustun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of existing action-conditioned video world models, which typically support one agent or small fixed groups.
Builds an environment from Reynolds’s Boids algorithm with synchronized egocentric views, color-based agent identities, and configurable camera-agent and population sizes.
Introduces FlockDiT, an action-conditioned latent diffusion transformer trained with flow matching for joint multi-agent video generation.
The abstract reports improved agent detection in density-matched settings and better rollout fidelity with diffusion forcing.
Provides a controlled testbed rather than a claim of broad real-world performance; its scope is artificial-life simulation.

All rows share the same ground-truth context, so the leftmost column is identical and all subsequent frames are generated. The floor hallucinates camera-agent colors and does not reliably preserve the focal agent’s hue, whereas the diffusion-forcing model maintains the focal identity and renders most neighbors as uncolored boids.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in image editing have enabled fine-grained and highly controllable visual modifications. However, achieving similar levels of controllability in video editing remains an open challenge, particularly for precise local edits, dynamic temporal effects, and consistent lighting across frames.In this paper, we propose EditDistill, a framework that distills image-level visual transformations from edits to guide video editing.Specifically, given a source video and an edit prompt, we first generate an edited version of the initial video frame using an off-the-shelf image editing model. We then distill the visual transformation of this original-edited image pair into a compact representation termed an edit descriptor.This descriptor is injected into a video diffusion model through our lightweight fusion module, which steers the denoising process toward the desired edit. To align the video trajectory with the demonstrated image edit while preserving motion and layout, we train with edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses, and derive an equivalent inference-time guidance formulation under flow matching.Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves strong performance on standard benchmarks and produces high-quality video editing results across diverse scenarios. For more details and videos, please refer to the anonymous webpage: https://yu-shaonian.github.io/EditDistill-Web/.
authors: Guojun Lei, Hong Li, Hongbing Yang, Lixue Gong, Chi Wang, Zheng Dong
bullets: Addresses the challenge of precise local edits, dynamic effects, and consistent lighting in videos.
Generates an edited first frame, then distills the source–edited image transformation into an edit descriptor.
Injects the descriptor into a video diffusion model through a lightweight fusion module to steer denoising.
Uses edit-descriptor alignment and DINO structural consistency losses to preserve motion and layout.
Reports strong benchmark performance and high-quality results across diverse video-editing scenarios.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of EDITDISTILL. Stage I encodes the transformation between an image pair (Is, Ie) into the edit descriptor d. Stage II keeps the Wan2.1-I2V-14B video diffusion frozen and trains the inject modules to inject d into selected transformer blocks by lightweight feature fusion modules steering the diffusion denoising toward the desired edit to produce a temporally coherent video V e from the video V s.

Figure 5: Qualitative comparison. EDITDISTILL performs both local and global edits while keeping the main subject, background, and motion stable. In contrast, other methods may miss the desired edit, unintentionally change nearby regions, or produce unstable results across frames.

Figure 7: Stage I edit descriptor model. The Delta VAE encoder extracts a stochastic descriptor from the source and edited VAE latents by combining shared features, their explicit feature difference, and a multi-scale encoder. The Delta VAE decoder receives only the source latent and descriptor, and reconstructs the edited latent through descriptor-conditioned residual blocks with self- and cross-attention.

Figure 4: Descriptor attention. Cross-attention maps show that local edits concentrate on the regions that need to change, while global edits such as relighting or stylization produce broader but still structured responses. The descriptor behaves as a transformation operator rather than a fixed mask or copied target image.
Figure 6: Relighting comparison. The distilled descriptor captures a global lighting transformation and guides coherent relighting across frames while preserving scene geometry and motion.
Figure 8: Frame-wise descriptor attention. The same edit descriptor re-localizes to the relevant moving regions across different video frames.

Figure 2: EDITDISTILL encodes the visual transformation between image editing pair into a compact edit descriptor, and combines the edit descriptor alignment constraint with the DINO structural similarity loss to distill the image editing capability into the denoising trajectory of video editing.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation for autoregressive (AR) video generation commonly first initializes an AR student and then refines it with distribution matching distillation (DMD). This refinement process faces two challenges. First, although initialization already yields a reasonably capable student, DMD obtains the refinement direction indirectly by estimating the full student score before forming the teacher-student correction. Second, detached-history training prevents the generator from assigning credit to a current chunk for its influence on subsequent chunks. We introduce Leta, a few-step distillation framework that addresses these challenges with ScoreDelta and FutureCredit. ScoreDelta directly estimates the teacher-student correction from denoising residuals, while FutureCredit learns an auxiliary cross-chunk update signal from vector-Jacobian products (VJPs) of next-chunk teacher residuals. Leta combines these signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in a single forward pass during generator updates. Teacher evaluations and credit VJPs are used only for estimator training. For ScoreDelta, we establish population equivalence to score-difference estimation and a conditional approximation advantage under limited capacity in a fixed-feature linear model. In our controlled experiments, Leta improves over DMD by 0.9 points on VBench and 0.66 on VideoAlign. This advantage persists at a higher generator update frequency (a generator-to-estimator update ratio of G:E=1:1), where Leta improves over DMD by 1.6 on VBench and 0.35 on VideoAlign. Project page: https://scdzx.github.io/Leta/.
authors: Zixuan Duan, Yabo Chen, Xunzhi Xiang, Xin Zhang, Haibin Huang, Yin Chen, Chi Zhang, Qi Fan
bullets: Addresses two DMD limitations: indirect score estimation and detached-history training.
ScoreDelta estimates the teacher–student correction directly from denoising residuals.
FutureCredit learns cross-chunk credit using vector-Jacobian products of next-chunk teacher residuals.
Combines both signals into a joint teacher-guided update field in one generator-update forward pass.
Controlled experiments report gains over DMD on VBench and VideoAlign, including at a 1:1 generator-to-estimator update ratio.

papers.abstract: Camera motion recognition requires separating viewpoint changes caused by camera translation, rotation, or zoom from object motion and scene dynamics. Video-language models often rely on semantic cues and struggle with the geometric evidence needed for this task. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures such as V-JEPA offer strong spatio-temporal representations, but our experiments suggest that they underrepresent geometric cues in some regions. Under temporal-reversal supervision, V-JEPA improves overall but degrades on several motion families, whereas a weaker geometry-oriented VGGT predictor improves across all families. We refer to these geometrically underrepresented regions as geometric blind spots and propose Fovea-JEPA to identify and address them. Using V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert, we construct intervention pseudo-labels from their prediction errors to weakly supervise a blind-spot predictor. The predictor produces token-wise response maps, which are aggregated into a clip-level intervention score to guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features. This selective intervention introduces complementary geometric information while preserving reliable visual predictions. Experiments on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench demonstrate the effectiveness of Fovea-JEPA, with gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over previously reported state-of-the-art baselines, respectively. Code and models will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Xiangkun Shi, Hanhui Li, Shiyue Zhang, Chang Liu, Junwen Pan, Zhenbang Sun, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets geometric blind spots in video representations that hinder distinguishing camera motion from object and scene dynamics.
Uses V-JEPA as the base model and VGGT as a geometry expert to create error-based pseudo-labels for blind-spot supervision.
Aggregates token-level blind-spot responses into clip-level scores that guide adaptive fusion of visual and geometric features.
Reports gains of 9.67, 8.67, and 24.38 percentage points over prior state-of-the-art baselines on CameraMotionDataset, CameraBench, and ShotBench.
Scope: addresses camera-motion recognition through selective geometric intervention while preserving reliable visual predictions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Fovea-JEPA. Our dual-branch framework leverages visual-geometric complementary cues and hierarchical error-guided pseudo supervision to detect geometric blind spots. Subsequently, our framework adaptively retains robust visual semantic predictions or activates geometric compensation to correct visual prediction errors.

Figure 1: Motivation of Fovea-JEPA. Top: Fovea-JEPA estimates a blind-spot map Q and aggregates it into an intervention score q, which indicates whether intervention by a geometry expert (e.g., VGGT) is necessary. A high-q case activates geometric intervention to correct the V-JEPA prediction, whereas a low-q case preserves the original prediction. Bottom left: matchedbudget intervention controls. Applying intervention to high-q clips outperforms applying it to low-q or randomly selected clips, while retaining VGGT tokens with the highest q scores outperforms retaining those with the lowest scores or using random masks. Bottom right: Fovea-JEPA compared with state-of-the-art methods across three benchmarks.

Figure 3: Qualitative analysis of the learned intervention decisions. Each column pairs two clips with the same ground-truth camera motion. For high-q cases, q > τ activates the VGGT-guided intervention: the predictions from both V-JEPA 2.1 and VGGT are inexact, whereas Fovea-JEPA recovers the exact label set. For low-q cases, q < τ preserves the V-JEPA pathway, retaining its exact prediction despite an inexact VGGT prediction.
Figure 4: Clip-level intervention-budget analysis. The random curve is the expected same-budget accuracy.

papers.title: Fovea-JEPA: Overcoming Geometric Blind Spots in V-JEPA for Camera Motion Recognition
papers.tldr: Fovea-JEPA improves camera-motion recognition by detecting where V-JEPA misses geometric cues and selectively injecting information from a geometry-focused predictor.

papers.abstract: We introduce TrackTok, an efficient video tokenization framework that produces object-centric tokens, i.e., tokens that consistently encode the same semantic objects across time, even as it moves, deforms, or undergoes partial occlusion. Conventional patch-based or existing holistic tokenizers produce token identities often tied to fixed image locations. In contrast, our approach learns temporally persistent object-centric representations that bind visual features across frames into stable semantic units. This enables substantially more compact, continuous latent video representations, reducing the number of tokens required for downstream generative modeling with state-of-the-art flow models, while preserving the semantic structure needed for high-quality synthesis. Our tokenizer offers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. TrackTok achieves comparable class-conditional generative FVD on UCF-101 dataset at 8 times fewer latent tokens and better latency, and outperforms existing 1D tokenization baselines on frame prediction task on Kinetics-600 across low token budgets. These results suggest that object-aligned and temporally persistent tokenization is a promising direction for scalable video generation, where reducing latent token counts is critical for efficient modeling. Our code for this work is available at https://github.com/phamleyennhi/tracktok.
authors: Nhi Pham, Christopher Wewer, Bernt Schiele, Jonas Fischer, Jan Eric Lenssen
bullets: Addresses the instability of patch-based and holistic tokens whose identities are tied to fixed image locations.
Learns tokens that track the same objects across motion, deformation, and partial occlusion.
Produces compact continuous latent representations for downstream flow-based video generation.
Matches class-conditional FVD on UCF-101 with 8× fewer latent tokens and lower latency.
Outperforms 1D tokenization baselines on Kinetics-600 frame prediction at low token budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method Overview. TrackTok encodes an input video V into a 1D set of object-centric, semantically persistent, latent tokens Z . Its encoder E is composed of semantic feature extraction with V-JEPA 2.1 [16], the construction of input-dependent queries Q using centroids of k-Means clusters C, and a ViT performing attention based on semantic similarity instead of spatial position. The decoder D reconstructs the three-dimensional RGB video from the 1D latent set Z .

Figure 6: Token Impact Across Time. We sample four frames from the input clip together with reconstructed frames and token impact visualizations (c.f. Sec. 4.1). For each sample, we apply PCA on token features and map the top three components to RGB as color for the corresponding token impact mask. The visualization highlights the semantic object alignment and temporal tracking of tokens learned by TrackTok in contrast to AdapTok’s or LARP’s tokens, which are dominated by high-frequency textures and edges. Both baselines also show degraded reconstruction quality at 128 tokens. Furthermore, leveraging only V-JEPA 2.1 without our cluster queries (CQ) still results in tokens encoding fixed regions of the video. Refer to Appendix E for more uncurated examples.

Figure 5: Class-Conditional Generation on UCF-101 Across Token Budgets. We show samples for diverse action categories, including hand motions (rows 1–2), dynamic natural scenes (row 3), and human body pose sequences (rows 4–5). Even at 32 tokens, our generated videos retain recognizable object structure, motion coherence, and semantic consistency across frames, comparable to LARP with 32× as many tokens. We include more qualitative examples in Appendix E.

Figure 4: Left: UCF-101 reconstruction quality. Our rFVD remains stable while LARP and AdapTok significantly degrade at low token count. Right: Generation quality vs. latency, lower-isbetter. Ours at 32 tokens achieves 8× lower latency and comparable quality to LARP at 1024 tokens.
Figure 3: Frame Prediction on Kinetics-600, lower is better (gFVD). Ours outperforms baselines at low token regime.
Figure 8: Ablation Study. We provide (a) qualitative samples of the Fencing class and (b) quantitative ablation of the encoder design.
Figure 7: Object Alignment & Temporal Consistency. TrackTok’s tokens encode semantic units and track them consistently across frames.

Table 1: Class-Conditional Video Generation on UCF-101. We report generation FVD (gFVD) across methods under comparable token budgets, token-to-pixel (T/P) ratios, training data size, and number of trainable parameters. While prior methods achieve lower gFVD at moderate compression rates, TrackTok remains competitive even under extreme compression (128 tokens, 0.012% T/P), highlighting a favorable efficiency–quality trade-off in the low-token regime. † denotes models trained using the same setup as ours. Best and second best are highlighted per token budget.
Table 2: Object Discovery and Tracking. For equal token counts, TrackTok’s tokens are more strongly aligned with individual objects as well as more temporally consistent than those of baselines.

papers.title: TrackTok: Object-Centric Video Tokenization with Semantically Persistent Tokens
papers.tldr: TrackTok tokenizes videos into semantically persistent object-centric tokens, enabling efficient generation with far fewer latent tokens while maintaining video quality.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
authors: Sagnik Anupam, Utkarsh Lal, Aneesh Edara, Botong Zhang, Yao Tang, Jiatao Gu, Dinesh Jayaraman, Osbert Bastani
bullets: Evaluates VLMs on language-conditioned frame ordering, depthwise object ordering, and left-to-right pixel-coordinate ordering.
Uses stereo and wrist-camera images from real-world robots, with task difficulty controlled by the number of items to sort.

Introduces an autonomous pipeline for generating scalable training data.
Shows that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on this data improve ordering performance and transfer to downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Many robot manipulation videos do not indicate whether the task was successfully completed. RoboJev-27B is an open-weight vision-language model that takes a task instruction, 10 frames of a manipulation attempt, and (if available) final frames from auxiliary cameras and predicts whether the robot accomplished the task. RoboJev-27B is a variant of JEV-27B-VL, trained with a rank-32 LoRA adapter on the language model only (keeping the vision encoder frozen) using 52,598 episode records. It also uses a source-specific KL penalty that applies only to research data, anchoring predictions closer to the original model on those sources. It uses a calibrated two-token readout that outputs success/failure probabilities in a single forward pass. On 268 held-out episodes of the same robot model (SO-101), RoboJev-27B attains 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC. It also generalises to episodes collected by unseen labs/robots (AUROC = 0.890 over 459 episodes) as well as to clearly labelled community-collected episodes (accuracy = 93.3% over 135 episodes), where the base model attains an AUROC = 0.900 on the unseen-lab/robot subset with the same inputs. It takes 0.26 seconds per episode (median, serial) to infer on a single H100, which is about \$0.19 per 1,000 success predictions at \$2.69 per GPU-hour (not including media processing and serving costs). RoboJev-27B is released together with its inference code, along with a transparent evaluation: 20,628 predictions organized into 29 model/protocol entries are made available to facilitate browsing and to enable reproducible benchmarking of success detection. We also compare against strong API-based frontier VLMs, which take in fewer input frames (4 images from the primary camera only); note that this comparison is not strictly like-for-like because RoboJev-27B is given more frames at inference.
bullets: Addresses the lack of success labels in many robot manipulation videos.
Fine-tunes JEV-27B-VL with a language-only LoRA adapter, frozen vision encoder, source-specific KL regularization, and a calibrated two-token success/failure readout.
Uses 10 manipulation frames plus optional auxiliary-camera final frames as input.
Reports 95.2% balanced accuracy and 0.993 AUROC on held-out SO-101 episodes; cross-lab/robot AUROC is 0.890.
Released with inference code and 20,628 predictions across 29 evaluation entries for reproducible benchmarking; comparisons with frontier VLMs use fewer frames and are not strictly like-for-like.

papers.abstract: While interactive video world models require autoregressive generation, directly adapting pretrained bidirectional video diffusion models into autoregressive ones with teacher forcing can disrupt their visual priors and degrade autoregressive generation quality. In this paper, we introduce Mix Forcing, a causal pre-training paradigm for interactive video world models, implemented with the Mixture-of-Bidirectional-and-Autoregressive (MoBA) attention. Mix Forcing jointly trains a video diffusion model with both teacher forcing and bidirectional training, yielding a strong causal initialization for few-step post-training. In self-attention, Mix Forcing leverages teacher forcing to learn causal next-chunk prediction for autoregressive rollout, while using bidirectional attention to preserve pretrained visual priors. To support online text interaction, Mix Forcing further adopts a chunk-wise cross-attention design that conditions each video chunk on a shared environment prompt and its own local prompt, without exposing future instructions to the current chunk. Following causal pre-training on a 14B image-to-video model, we apply consistency and distribution matching distillation to obtain a four-step autoregressive generator. Experiments on our internal benchmark and public benchmarks, including WBench and SANA-WM-Bench, show that our model achieves state-of-the-art visual quality and timely event following with precise camera control. Notably, our model supports high-fidelity long-horizon generation without quality degradation even over one-hour rollouts. Project page is here: https://zelingao98.github.io/mixforcing
authors: Zelin Gao, Hao Ouyang, Jiapeng Zhu, Qiuyu Wang, Jingye Chen, Zichen Liu, Xing Zhu, Yujun Shen, Yinghao Xu
bullets: Addresses the degradation of visual priors when adapting bidirectional video diffusion models to causal, autoregressive generation.
Introduces MoBA attention, jointly combining teacher-forced causal prediction with bidirectional training for causal initialization.
Uses chunk-wise cross-attention to condition video on shared environment context and local instructions without revealing future prompts.
Applies consistency and distribution-matching distillation to produce a four-step autoregressive generator.
Reports state-of-the-art visual quality, event following, and camera control, with high-fidelity rollouts lasting up to one hour on reported benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Video world models are expected to generate videos that accurately follow specified camera trajectories while maintaining consistent 3D structures. However, existing models are predominantly trained on densely sampled videos with small inter-frame camera motions. When applied to sparse, large step trajectories, they often produce frozen frames, inaccurate camera motion, and severe geometric drift. We attribute this degradation to a mismatch between the gradual viewpoint transitions seen during training and the large viewpoint changes required at inference time. To address this problem, we propose Dense Trajectory Teacher Distillation (DTTD), a post-training framework that transfers a model's generation capability from dense trajectories to large camera motions. Given a sparse trajectory, DTTD interpolates additional camera poses to construct a dense trajectory covering the same path. The frozen base model then generates reliable teacher videos along this familiar dense trajectory, and pose aligned teacher observations are used to evaluate candidate videos generated under the original sparse trajectory. In this way, the model serves as its own generation teacher, requiring neither additional video data nor a stronger external video generator. We further combine dense teacher supervision with geometry aware rewards that assess cross frame consistency and camera trajectory following, and use the resulting preferences for offline preference optimization. To stably expand the model's motion range, we introduce a cumulative curriculum that progressively incorporates larger motion steps while retaining simpler trajectories to reduce capability forgetting.
authors: Shuofeng Sun, Linqing Zhao, Haibin Yan
bullets: Existing models often fail on sparse, large-step camera trajectories, producing frozen frames, inaccurate motion, and geometric drift.
DTTD interpolates sparse camera paths into dense trajectories that the frozen base model can reliably generate.
Pose-aligned dense teacher videos supervise candidate outputs generated on the original sparse trajectory, without extra data or an external teacher.
Geometry-aware rewards measure cross-frame consistency and trajectory following for offline preference optimization.
A cumulative curriculum progressively increases motion difficulty while retaining simpler trajectories to limit capability forgetting.

papers.abstract: Video spatial reasoning requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to understand how objects are arranged and related across viewpoints. While these models can recognize objects in individual frames, integrating these observations to solve complex spatial tasks remains challenging. We examine route planning as a representative task and observe that existing models become substantially less accurate as the number of required turns increases, with several models achieving accuracy close to random guessing on routes requiring three or more turns. This finding suggests that recognizing landmarks alone is insufficient: models must also connect observations across viewpoints and track how landmarks are arranged in a shared space. Motivated by this observation, we introduce GeoLift, a training-free framework that uses feed-forward 3D reconstruction to map objects detected in individual frames into a shared metric 3D scene. GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained geometry models for scene reconstruction. It then uses shared geometric regions, called superpoints, to associate observations of the same object across views without a learned matcher. The reconstructed 3D map enables explicit computation of spatial relations and multistep routes, and provides geometric evidence for estimating distances and sizes. With all model weights frozen, GeoLift improves Qwen3-VL-4B's average score on VSI-Bench from 55.4% to 64.1%, including an increase in route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, and achieves 59.8% accuracy on MindCube. These results show that connecting frame-level object grounding through a shared 3D map can improve complex spatial reasoning without task-specific training.
authors: Xinglin Li, TingTing Long, Jingzhi Zhou, Jiajing Chen, Jian Yang, Jin Xie
bullets: Existing MLLMs struggle to connect landmarks across viewpoints, with accuracy dropping sharply on routes requiring three or more turns.
GeoLift combines a frozen MLLM for 2D grounding with pretrained feed-forward geometry models for training-free 3D reconstruction.
Shared geometric regions called superpoints associate the same objects across views without a learned matcher.
The resulting 3D map supports explicit spatial-relation and multistep-route computation, plus distance and size estimation.
It raises Qwen3-VL-4B’s VSI-Bench average from 55.4% to 64.1% and route-planning accuracy from 30.9% to 53.6%, while reaching 59.8% on MindCube.

VGGT-Omega and MoGe-2 recover global geometry and metric scale, allowing the 2D groundings to be lifted into a shared 3D reference. Geometric superpoints and superpoint agreement associate observations of the same instance across views without a learned matcher. The resulting view-consistent map supports a toolbox of deterministic spatial operations, including occupancy-grid construction and A* route search. Geometry can also be provided as a hint together with the video for queries that require visual interpretation.

Figure 1: From local 2D observations to explicit 3D spatial reasoning. papers.abstract: Marine video understanding is crucial for a wide range of real-world applications. However, existing marine video datasets suffer from limitations, including the limited number of data samples, fine-grained text descriptions, and detailed visual attributes. To address these limitations, we introduce a large-scale, video-text dataset featuring rich, in-the-wild visual attributes tailored for complex marine environments. Our dataset comprises 2,000 video-text pairs annotated with 13 attributes covering up to four objects per scene, object visual/geometric properties, behaviors, environmental context, and camera motion, spanning diverse lighting conditions, times of day, and 7 countries. From these annotations, we generate 16,080 video-question pairs (12,080 multiple-choice, 4,000 open-ended). Furthermore, we benchmark both proprietary and open-source video-LLM models on video question answering and video captioning tasks. We find that (i) proprietary models often achieves superior performances; (ii) VLMs handle object motion well but struggle with complex camera motion; (iii) closed-source models struggle to perceive camera motion; and (iv) VLMs struggle to reason in static cameras.
authors: Quang-Trung Truong, Thanh-Nghia Nguyen, Phu-Phong Vo, Jaeyeon Kim, Cheng Chen, Jie Zhang, Binh-Son Hua, Duc Thanh Nguyen, Ivor Tsang, Sai-Kit Yeung

papers.abstract: Advertisers routinely create multiple duration variants of ads to meet marketing budgets and viewer preferences, a labor-intensive and costly process. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel at general video understanding, their ability to perform specialized editorial tasks remains unexplored. We introduce AdShot, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs on shot selection for ad clipping. It contains 823 professionally edited ad pairs (30-sec sources and 15-sec edits) across 194 brands and 17 industries, annotated with shot-level boundaries and content features (action, emotion, information, imagery). We evaluate 13 state-of-the-art video-only MLLMs and 2 audio-visual MLLMs (7B-72B parameters) on shot selection accuracy (Precision, Recall, F1), duration constraints (15s), and content preservation, including an audio ablation. We find: (1) model architecture matters more than scale, with smaller models often matching or exceeding larger ones; performance is strongest for target ads with 6-10 shots; (2) models exhibit a mean absolute duration error of 5.39s, with most tending to overshoot the 15s target, though they can still substantially reduce human editing effort; (3) all models exhibit systematic content biases, favoring information-rich and emotion-focused shots while under-selecting action and imagery. We publicly release our benchmark to facilitate research at the intersection of multimodal AI and computational advertising.

papers.abstract: Precise camera control is essential for cinematic character video generation, yet existing methods struggle to follow large-angle trajectories with combined rotation, translation, and radius variation from arbitrary initial azimuths. Such viewpoint changes also reveal character regions unseen in the initial frame, causing geometric distortions, appearance degradation, and identity drift. To systematically study these coupled challenges, we introduce CLACT, a large-scale Character-centric dataset and benchmark covering diverse Large-Angle Camera Trajectories, with accurate camera geometry and multi-view character observations for training and evaluation. We further propose WorldCast, a framework for world-consistent character video generation under diverse large-angle camera motions. Specifically, we back-project the initial frame into a 3D point cloud using estimated depth, align the point-cloud scale with the target camera trajectory, and render it along the trajectory to obtain explicit geometric guidance and coverage masks. To complement the incomplete character information, we introduce Geometry-Aligned Memory Attention (GAMA). Using relative camera poses estimated jointly from the initial frame and multi-view character anchors, we express anchor and target-view geometry in a common coordinate frame. GAMA uses this geometric alignment to guide the retrieval and injection of view-relevant character features during generation. Evaluations across diverse large-angle camera trajectories demonstrate accurate trajectory following while preserving character geometry, appearance, and identity.

papers.abstract: Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.

papers.abstract: Short-form video combines speech, imagery, and on-screen text, creating challenges for systematic content analysis. We present a five-stage multimodal framework for measuring creators' themes and communication strategies at scale. The framework integrates platform metadata, speech transcripts, and vision-language descriptions of sampled frames, then applies large language models to generate predefined indicators and open-ended labels. An audited keyword scheme consolidates thematic labels, while creator-weighted aggregation gives each account equal weight regardless of posting volume. We demonstrate the framework on 9,852 TikTok videos from sixteen creators, retaining 7,311 videos for analysis across seven themes and seven communication indicators. Automated profiles reveal substantial differences in creators' use of education, humor, and responses to current events. Validation against two independent expert annotators yielded a mean framework-expert agreement of Cohen's $\kappa = 0.40$ across the six binary indicators, close to the $\kappa = 0.42$ the two experts achieved with each other, though agreement varied substantially across individual indicators. The framework provides a modular approach to comparative analysis of creator communication, combining scalable annotation with transparent aggregation and construct-specific validation.
authors: Julie R. Ancis, Michael Fire, Omer Tarshish
bullets: Addresses the challenge of systematically analyzing speech, imagery, and on-screen text in short-form video.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video question answering requires a model to continuously monitor an incoming stream and autonomously decide when to speak, what to say, and whether to emit a response. Existing streaming systems face a fundamental difficulty: retaining long visual histories is costly, whereas discarding them can lead to missed events and repeated responses. We propose \textbf{ProV-Mem}, a training-free proactive memory framework built around a frozen VLM backbone. ProV-Mem decomposes the proactive decision into three lightweight memory tiers: a temporal-trigger memory controls when to query the backbone and recovers from prolonged silence, an instructional memory guides what to say through a fixed prompting prior for concise and visually grounded generation, and an episodic memory determines whether to emit by filtering near-duplicate responses. Under an idealized conditional-sufficiency assumption, we derive a stagewise approximation bound relating the decomposed process to a full-state joint policy. We further introduce Cost-Aware Area Under the Curve (\textbf{CAUC}), which extends PAUC by explicitly discounting redundant, overly frequent, and unnecessarily long emissions. Experiments on the four scenarios of ProactiveVideoQA show that ProV-Mem achieves the best CAUC across all scenarios and the best PAUC on WEB, EGO, and TV, while maintaining low per-response inference latency.
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between retaining costly long visual histories and discarding information needed for timely, non-redundant responses.
Uses temporal-trigger memory to decide when to query, instructional memory to guide concise grounded answers, and episodic memory to filter near-duplicate emissions.
Provides a stagewise approximation bound under an idealized conditional-sufficiency assumption.
Introduces CAUC, a cost-aware metric that penalizes redundant, overly frequent, and overly long responses.
On ProactiveVideoQA, achieves the best CAUC in all four scenarios and the best PAUC in three, with low per-response latency.

papers.abstract: Controlling the camera relative to a moving subject in an existing video is challenging: behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view require the camera to adapt to the subject's changing position and orientation, making the desired trajectory difficult to specify in advance. Existing camera-controlled video-to-video methods typically rely on explicit trajectories or reference motions, which do not directly express these dynamic camera--subject relationships. We introduce semantic camera motion control, a novel video-to-video task in which a reference video and a target motion label specify the desired subject-relative camera behavior without an explicit target trajectory. Our method, SemCam, learns to realize this behavior while preserving source content. It combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation with motion-conditioned modulation, while a background-consistency loss encourages fidelity in regions visible in both reference and target videos. We construct 661 paired videos covering eight semantic camera behaviors and evaluate on a separate 109-scene benchmark using subject-relative motion metrics, appearance measures, and a user study. SemCam achieves a semantic-motion success rate of 68.6%, compared with 45.3% for Vista4D, the strongest evaluated baseline, while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of specifying camera motion around subjects whose position and orientation change over time.
Uses a reference video plus a target motion label to express behaviors such as maintaining a frontal view.
Combines shared-basis low-rank adaptation, motion-conditioned modulation, and a background-consistency loss.
Evaluated on 661 paired videos and a separate 109-scene benchmark covering eight semantic camera behaviors.
Outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline on semantic-motion success while maintaining comparable subject identity preservation.

papers.abstract: The rapid growth of video data has created an urgent need for efficient video understanding systems that can handle long and continuous visual inputs, posing significant challenges for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) due to severe memory bottlenecks. Moreover, existing compression methods often overlook the explosive accumulation of approximation errors. To address this issue, we propose Video-MemComp, a training-free and sensitivity-aware context management framework for memory-constrained streaming video understanding. Our method theoretically decomposes compression error into orthogonal local approximation error and layer-wise structural sensitivity via a first-order Taylor expansion. To minimize local approximation error, we perform token aggregation in a pre-RoPE safe zone with an attention-conserving logit bias, mitigating geometric distortions caused by RoPE rotations. To manage layer-wise structural sensitivity, we dynamically allocate the KV cache budget based on offline gradient priors and online context entropy, prioritizing high-sensitivity layers. Video-MemComp outperforms or achieves performance comparable to full-cache and state-of-the-art compression methods on benchmarks including MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema. Notably, it improves the overall accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-3B from 62.3% to 64.1% while reducing the KV cache to an equivalent of 6,000 tokens per layer, saving over 90% of KV memory.
authors: Yonghui Niu, Yuhao Ji, Chang Nie, Jiao Zhang, Yilong Li, Junlan Feng, Ran He, Caifeng Shan, Chaoyou Fu
bullets: Targets memory bottlenecks and error accumulation in long-context streaming video understanding.
Uses a first-order Taylor expansion to separate local approximation error from layer-wise structural sensitivity.
Aggregates tokens in a pre-RoPE safe zone with attention-conserving logit bias to reduce geometric distortion.
Dynamically allocates KV-cache budgets using offline gradient priors and online context entropy.
Matches or exceeds full-cache and existing compression methods on MLVU, VideoMME, and EgoSchema; Qwen2.5-VL-3B rises from 62.3% to 64.1% with over 90% KV-memory savings.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Overview of our Video-MemComp Framework. Guided by Taylor expansion (top), we split global memory compression into two objectives. 1) Minimizing Local Approximation Error El (middle): Pre-RoPE Aggregation merges redundant tokens based on inter-frame filtering and intra-frame merging. Intra-layer KV Pruning selects key-value pairs using a dialogue-aware Proxy Query Qproxy. 2) Managing Structural Sensitivity Sl (bottom): A Tri-Hybrid Budget Allocation dynamically assigns the total memory budget Btotal using offline structural sensitivity, online information density, and uniform regularization to protect critical layers from aggressive pruning.

Figure 1 Our architecture. While standard Video-LLM models suffer from linear O(T ) memory growth, VideoMemComp maintains strictly O(1) memory via a Taylor-expansion-guided hybrid strategy, enabling efficient streaming video understanding. Specifically, we decompose the error via Taylor expansion into local approximation error El and layer-wise structural sensitivity Sl. To minimize El, we adopt Attention-Preserved Pre-RoPE Aggregation and Intralayer Sparsity-based KV pruning. Meanwhile, Sl is used to guide layer-wise budget allocation.

Figure 2 Performance on MLVU with Qwen2-VL-7B. Our method outperforms strong baselines across all memory budgets, and even surpasses the Full KV baseline at 6K, 12K, and 24K KV budgets, showing that Video-MemComp removes redundancy while preserving key semantics. See Section E.1 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 5 Accuracy-Memory trade-offs on Qwen2.5-VL-3B (VideoMME Long Video). Conversely, KV Compression (Orange) demonstrates robustness under strict memory constraints. Our Hybrid Method (Green) achieves the optimal Pareto frontier across all budgets, balancing redundancy removal with attention preservation. See E.4 in the supplementary material for details.

Figure 6 Hyperparameter landscape of budget allocation. See F.3 in the supplementary material for details.

The landscape reveals a convex optimization zone, where the peak represents the optimal trade-off between aggressive redundancy filtering and semantic preservation. Notably, overly aggressive temporal pruning (low θinter) causes irreversible performance degradation. See F.4 in the supplementary material for details.

papers.abstract: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.
authors: Tianchi Xu, Yalin Zheng, Yangxin Zhu, Ruonan Ren, Zheng Fu, Yunlong Wang, Yuanxin Zhong
bullets: Addresses the subjectivity, sparsity, and poor scalability of keyframe-based progress annotations.

NimCritic uses Joint Video-Progress Learning, Historical Progress Perturbation, and contrastive Video-Progress Alignment to predict dense progress.
Matches or exceeds leading process reward models, achieves about 65% higher terminal success accuracy than GVL on VPB, and about 97% recall on RoboArena rollout retrieval.

papers.abstract: Deploying Vision-Language Models for video anomaly detection confronts a fundamental constraint. Their semantic reasoning demands computational budgets incompatible with the scale of real-world video streams. We present Signal-Aware Adaptive Fusion (SAAF), a framework that achieves efficient zero-shot anomaly detection through three key innovations. First, we introduce a dual-signal adaptive sampler operating in semantic embedding space: a delta signal captures sudden events via frame-to-frame cosine distance, while a drift signal detects static and gradual anomalies through deviation from rolling temporal context. Their OR-gated combination with adaptive EMA-based thresholding provides comprehensive anomaly coverage without training data. Second, we propose a threshold-gated cascaded architecture where lightweight frame-level scoring precedes expensive video-level temporal analysis, invoking it only when confidence warrants additional context. Third, we design a signal-aware weighted fusion mechanism that dynamically adapts score combination based on which signal triggered frame selection. Across four benchmarks, SAAF delivers competitive accuracy at substantially lower cost. Among training-free zero-shot methods, SAAF sets a new state of the art on XD-Violence (92.07%), MSAD (86.70%), and ShanghaiTech (80.54%) AUC-ROC, with XD-Violence and MSAD also surpassing supervised baselines. SAAF sustains 44.95, 48.61, and 41.06 FPS on XD-Violence, UCF-Crime, and MSAD, a 2.43$\times$, 2.63$\times$, and 2.22$\times$ throughput improvement over the prior best zero-shot method. Code: https://github.com/kdawoud91/SAAF
authors: Khaled Waleed Dawoud, Muhammad Haris Khan
bullets: Uses frame-to-frame semantic changes (delta) and temporal-context deviations (drift) to detect sudden, static, and gradual anomalies without training data.
Employs EMA-based adaptive thresholds and OR-gated sampling for broad anomaly coverage.
Cascades lightweight frame scoring before expensive video-level analysis, reducing unnecessary computation.
Dynamically fuses scores according to the signal that triggered frame selection.
Achieves competitive accuracy across four benchmarks and reports 2.22×–2.63× throughput gains over the prior best zero-shot method on three datasets.

Stage 4 propagates and refines sparse anchor scores to produce dense frame-level predictions.

papers.abstract: Video reasoning requires understanding how events unfold over time, yet videos with accurate temporal annotations are expensive to collect. Self-play offers an alternative by letting a model generate and solve its own tasks without manual annotation. However, existing video self-play methods train on fixed sets of recorded videos, so they cannot alter the underlying event dynamics and rely on noisy pseudo-labels derived from the model's own outputs, such as majority voting, that risk reinforcing shared model errors. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Tempo-Zero, a self-improvement framework that closes a loop of executable environments, execution-verified self-play, and environment evolution, where executing a program renders a video with the ground-truth option and interval of every question. A single policy plays both Questioner and Solver, proposing questions and answering them with timestamped evidence lines, and is trained on execution-grounded rewards instead of model consensus. The Solver's performance steers a curriculum over tasks and difficulty levels, and the policy selects rule changes that enrich the event dynamics of later rounds. Despite being trained solely on simple programs, without supervised fine-tuning or external video data which prior methods typically require, Tempo-Zero outperforms the base models and recent self-play baselines on average across twelve real-world video benchmarks at different model scales, with particularly strong gains on temporal grounding tasks. Project page: https://alchemist-jo.github.io/tempo-zero/

papers.abstract: The 3rd WEAR Dataset Challenge asks for an activity label for every one-second window of four unseen participants. Each window has 15 VideoMAEv2 frame embeddings, the accelerometer signal of one random limb, and the windows are shuffled. This report is an empirical analysis of one system built after the challenge deadline. Window classifiers are stacked with features averaged over per-participant graphs of video neighbours and scored successor candidates, and a mean-field style decoder with a soft count constraint per activity labels all windows of a participant together. The setting is offline and transductive, and the count constraint relies on each activity being performed once. In a participant-wise simulation with participant-level bootstrap intervals, stacking added 0.051 macro F1 over stage-1 fusion and the count constraint 0.011 (95% interval 0.006 to 0.017). A quadratic seam distance ranks the true same-limb successor first among about 720 candidates in 83.9% of cases, but adding it to the link model changed macro F1 by -0.0001 (-0.0006 to 0.0005). With the decoder settings and the mixing weight chosen inside the folds and the mislabelled spans left out of training, the system scores 0.936 in simulation (0.940 for participants who performed each activity once); the submitted configuration scores 0.938 (0.943). Per-participant scores range from 0.80 to 0.97. These results come from a non-nested stacking protocol that uses unlabelled features transductively, so they are not a fully inductive estimate. An oracle that averages the final unary scores over the true segments reaches 0.973, and 79% of the remaining errors involve the null class. On the private leaderboard, which no choice used, the selected Kaggle submission scored 0.9231 (public 0.9254, with bounds partly tuned there), and a later one with bounds chosen in simulation scored 0.9247 (public 0.9253).
bullets: Stacking graph-based video-neighbour and successor features improved macro F1 by 0.051 over initial multimodal fusion; the count constraint added 0.011.
A mean-field-style decoder jointly labels each participant’s shuffled windows, assuming every activity occurs exactly once.
Quadratic seam matching identified the true same-limb successor first in 83.9% of cases but changed macro F1 by only -0.0001.
The simulated system scored 0.936 macro F1, while private leaderboard scores were 0.9231 and 0.9247 for two submissions.
Remaining errors were concentrated in the null class; results are limited by a non-nested, transductive stacking protocol and the once-per-activity assumption.

papers.title: An Error Budget for Shuffled Multimodal Windows in the 3rd WEAR Challenge: Stacking, Count Constraints and Seam Matching

papers.abstract: Continuous visual world simulation requires coupling evolving scene geometry with temporally persistent appearance. We present UniWorld, a unified framework that integrates depth trajectories and reference appearance within a shared video generation model. The central design maintains visual and geometric histories on a common timeline. Noise-aligned overlapping continuation places generated history at the prescribed sampling noise level and commits only newly generated latents. Rolling depth latent state preserves the corresponding geometric controls, incrementally reads newly available geometry, and keeps the conditioning fixed within each sampling window. Together, these mechanisms ensure exact preservation of latent history while bounding the active depth state by the window size. We evaluate continuous generation, paired history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scene categories. The same generator supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, while cached and incremental execution paths produce bitwise-identical outputs. Appearance changes and geometric control branches operate through the same interface without modifying committed history. The measured steady-state DiT execution path achieves real-time generation throughput, demonstrating the efficiency of UniWorld for continuous visual world simulation.
authors: Xin Zhang, Yabo Chen, Shuaiwei Wang, Zixuan Duan, Haibin Huang, Feng Xu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coupling temporally persistent visual appearance with changing scene geometry.
Uses noise-aligned overlapping continuation to preserve generated latent history while committing only new content.

Supports estimated, native, and on-demand simulator depth, with cached and incremental execution producing identical outputs.
Evaluations cover continuous generation, history interventions, and long-horizon behavior across diverse scenes; the steady-state DiT path achieves real-time throughput.

papers.abstract: Humans efficiently process multimodal streams spanning hours to years, building persistent, fine-grained spatiotemporal memories that support reasoning about and predicting long-horizon events. In contrast, existing benchmarks focus on short- and medium-context tasks, and most foundation models struggle to preserve fine-grained information over long horizons. To evaluate and improve long-horizon spatiotemporal reasoning, we introduce the LongVideo dataset and the 4DMemoryBench. LongVideo comprises about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions covering visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning across diverse context lengths. We further develop the 4DMemory Harness, which integrates four complementary skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and a model-specific retrieval-augmented generation system. Evaluating 13 leading models, we find that standalone foundation models struggle with long-horizon tasks, while the 4DMemory Harness improves all of them by over 50\%. Compared to previous benchmark, the same models exhibit a performance drop of more than 10\% on 4DMemoryBench. We hope 4DMemory will facilitate the development of spatiotemporal agents capable of addressing complex, long-horizon tasks.
authors: Yanhao Jia, Yi Zhu, Yiran Zhong, Weigao Sun, Feida Zhu, Pengkun Jiao, Sihan Yang, Ming Ma, Steven Hoi, Erik Cambria
bullets: LongVideo contains about 900 hours of video and over 5,000 manually reviewed questions spanning visual, textual, and spatiotemporal reasoning.
4DMemoryBench evaluates reasoning across diverse context lengths, targeting persistent memory over long video streams.
The 4DMemory Harness combines four skills, 22+ specialized tool models, and model-specific retrieval-augmented generation.
Across 13 leading models, the harness improves performance by over 50%, while models perform over 10% worse than on a previous benchmark.
The benchmark targets development of agents for complex, long-horizon spatiotemporal tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Motivation for 4DMemory Agent. (a) Traditional models with limited active context may lose access to earlier observations, leaving relevant evidence unavailable for temporal reasoning. (b) 4DMemory Agent coordinates persistent memory and task-specific skills through a harness to retrieve evidence and reason over events and their relations. 2024b; Bai et al., 2025). At the method level, adaptive spatiotemporal compression removes redundant frames and visual tokens, sparse memory consolidates dense observations into long-term representations, and query-adaptive hierarchical selection allocates computation across temporal granularities (Shen et al., 2025; Song et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). Together, these advances improve access to long-range evidence, but their gains are typically evaluated under different datasets, interfaces, and access conditions, making it difficult to isolate improvements in the base model, evidence acquisition, memory, and final reasoning. Moreover, these components are not readily composable across systems, since methods such as LongVU require access to the internal visiontoken pipeline, whereas LongVT learns its tooluse protocol through model-specific post-training of Qwen2.5-VL-7B rather than through a modelagnostic plug-in interface (Shen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026).

Figure 3: Overview of the LongVideo construction pipeline. Hours-level videos undergo audio-text screening, clip construction, and evidence refinement to obtain coherent clips with grounded captions. Visual evidence, audio captions, and transcripts are aligned to original source timestamps and organized into chronological multimodal evidence chains. QA pairs are then constructed from multiple evidence chains and checked for answer correctness, clip necessity, and potential shortcuts.

Figure 4: Illustration of 4DMemory Agent framework. (a) The harness builds persistent, question-independent memory of events, entities, and spatial relations, preserving source timestamps for reuse across questions. (b) A foundation model retrieves timestamped evidence and iteratively refines its queries and reasoning, with optional tools provided by a skill library.

papers.abstract: Point-supervised Temporal Action Localization (PTAL) aims to localize action instances using only a single annotated timestamp for each instance. Such sparse supervision offers limited guidance for modeling the structural organization of an action instance. Existing PTAL methods primarily infer action regions from classification responses, leaving the structural organization of multiple action-related parts within each instance insufficiently modeled. To address this problem, we propose DeformStruct, an instance-level deformable structure modeling framework for PTAL. DeformStruct progressively constructs the structure of each action instance through three stages. First, Structural Anchor Mining discovers multiple anchors from annotated points and action-responsive regions, providing structural nodes grounded in the current instance. Second, Deformable Part Alignment associates latent structural parts with these anchors through deformation-aware matching, allowing their temporal supports to adapt to instance-dependent variations. Third, Relational Structural Organization explicitly models the relative temporal relations among the aligned parts, forming a relational representation that characterizes how different action-related parts are organized together. Extensive experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID demonstrate consistent improvements in point-supervised temporal localization and validate the effectiveness of deformable structural modeling.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Yonghao Dong, Jie Wang, Gang Hua
bullets: PTAL uses only one timestamp per action instance, providing limited structural supervision.
DeformStruct progressively builds instance structure through anchor mining, deformable part alignment, and relational organization.
The method adapts part temporal supports to instance-specific variations and models relations among aligned parts.
Experiments on THUMOS14, ActivityNet-v1.3, GTEA, and BEOID show consistent localization improvements.
The approach is scoped to point-supervised temporal action localization and depends on sparse point annotations.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed DeformStruct framework. Given pre-extracted video features and point annotations, a Transformer Encoder first produces the encoded feature sequence XE . DeformStruct progressively models each action instance through three stages: Structural Anchor Mining discovers multiple action-related anchors, Deformable Part Alignment adaptively aligns latent parts with these anchors to accommodate temporal variations, and Relational Structural Organization models the relative temporal relations among the aligned parts to characterize their structural configuration. Finally, the Transformer Decoder predicts candidate action segments, and the framework is jointly optimized with localization and structural objectives.

Fig. 7. Qualitative comparison of our proposed method with QROT [14] and HR-Pro [7] on THUMOS14 [10]. We provide two test videos with action classes of GolfSwing and HighJump, respectively. It can be seen that our detection results show higher IoUs with the ground truth.

A complete action instance may contain multiple temporally distributed action-related stages, whose locations, durations, and relative configurations vary across instances. Existing holistic modeling tends to overlook such regional evidence, temporal variation, and structural relations. Our DeformStruct instead models the action as a deformable structure composed of multiple action-related parts, adaptively aligning them to instance-specific temporal evidence and capturing their structural relations.

papers.abstract: Video moment retrieval aims to localize a query-relevant temporal segment in an untrimmed video. Existing methods typically perform video-text alignment in Euclidean space, where representations are embedded in a flat geometry. However, accurate moment localization requires organizing query-relevant evidence across multiple grounding states, where target regions, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors exhibit distinct temporal structures and relevance patterns. Such Euclidean representations lack an explicit geometry to jointly capture these relationships, motivating us to explore structured temporal evidence organization from a geometric perspective. Specifically, we propose Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO), a geometric framework that organizes query-aware temporal memory in hyperbolic space. HTEO maps temporal representations into a Poincar\'{e} ball and organizes temporal evidence through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR). REO adjusts temporal tokens' radial positions to encode the structural differences among temporal evidence, while OAR enhances query-conditioned semantic alignment through orthogonal rotation. The organized representation is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space and injected into the decoder through a lightweight residual memory update, enabling hyperbolic geometric cues to be incorporated into standard Transformer decoders while preserving the original cross-modal memory. Furthermore, we introduce radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to explicitly guide temporal evidence organization and query-conditioned semantic alignment, respectively. Extensive experiments and analyses across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HTEO improves temporal localization while providing an interpretable geometric organization of temporal evidence.
authors: Mengnan Liu, Sanping Zhou, Kun Xia, Jiaxuan Lin, Gang Hua, Le Wang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of modeling target moments, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors with flat Euclidean representations.
Uses a Poincaré-ball memory with Radial Evidence Organization for temporal structure and Orthogonal Angular Refinement for query-conditioned alignment.
Projects the organized features back to Euclidean space and adds them through a lightweight residual memory update.
Introduces radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to guide the learned organization.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show improved temporal localization and interpretable evidence structure.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO) framework. Given a video-query pair, HTEO first constructs query-aware temporal memory through multimodal feature fusion and maps it into a Poincaré ball via the exponential map. In hyperbolic space, temporal evidence is organized through Radial Evidence Organization (REO) and Orthogonal Angular Refinement (OAR), where REO regulates the radial structure to capture different temporal grounding characteristics, and OAR refines angular directions to enhance query-conditioned semantic relevance. The organized memory is then projected back to the Euclidean tangent space via the logarithmic map and incorporated into the decoder through a lightweight residual update for moment localization. The bottom panel illustrates the detailed geometric operations.

Fig. 4. Visualization of hyperbolic radius-angle organization for temporal evidence modeling. (a) The radius-angle feature space shows the geometric separation among target, boundary, and background tokens. (b) The angular similarity curves demonstrate that angular direction provides query-conditioned relevance cues. (c) The temporal evolution of radius reveals structural variations around different temporal evidence regions and boundary transitions.

Fig. 8. Qualitative comparison of HTEO with TR-DETR and LD-DETR on the QVHighlights dataset. HTEO achieves more accurate temporal localization with better alignment to GT. The queries are displayed as provided in the original dataset.

Fig. 1. Motivation of hyperbolic temporal evidence organization for video moment retrieval. (a) In flat Euclidean memory, query-relevant tokens and contextual distractors may exhibit similar feature distances, making them difficult to distinguish based on flat similarity alone. (b) Such ambiguity can lead to false response peaks on distracting background regions, resulting in inaccurate temporal localization. (c) HTEO organizes query-aware temporal evidence in hyperbolic space through radius-angle geometry, where angular direction captures query-conditioned relevance and radial distance provides structural cues for temporal evidence organization. By introducing geometry-aware organization, HTEO enhances the discrimination between relevant evidence and semantically similar distractors, leading to more structured temporal representations for moment retrieval.

Fig. 6. Qualitative analysis of false peak correction using hyperbolic angular refinement. Four representative validation samples are shown where Euclidean similarity produces distractor-induced response peaks. Hyperbolic angular organization shifts dominant responses toward the ground-truth moments and suppresses irrelevant activations.

Fig. 7. Visualization of temporal evidence organization in Euclidean and hyperbolic spaces. Compared with flat Euclidean representations, hyperbolic geometry yields more structured distributions of target, boundary, and background tokens, indicating improved evidence separability. The query texts are displayed as provided in the original dataset.
Fig. 3. Visualization of hyperbolic radius-angle behavior.

Fig. 5. Illustrative analysis of inside-outside response gaps. The left panel compares the maximum query-conditioned responses inside and outside the ground-truth interval, while the right panel shows the corresponding per-query inside-outside response gaps.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based analysis of intraoperative laparoscopic videos has the potential to improve surgical decision-making and precision. However, effective surgical assistance requires models that can generalize across diverse intraoperative tasks. Here we present LapaFM, a foundation model for laparoscopic surgery trained on more than 20,000 minutes of surgical videos using a multi-stage continual learning strategy that mitigates catastrophic forgetting and inter-task interference. LapaFM learns multimodal visual representations and supports multiple tasks, including smoke removal, surgical phase recognition, instrument and polyp segmentation, and lesion identification. The model was evaluated on 13 retrospective and two prospective cohorts collected from different imaging devices. LapaFM consistently outperformed task-specific models and existing foundation models across datasets, and also generalized to gastrointestinal endoscopy tasks, including polyp detection and classification. Notably, it recovered over 90% of smoke-obscured frames and achieved clinician-level or superior performance in lymph node metastasis prediction and prospective polyp classification.

papers.abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.

papers.abstract: Despite the promising development of deep learning for video anomaly detection (VAD), explainability (XAI) of these models remains a challenge. Explainable and privacy-protecting VAD builds transparency and trust that facilitates adoption of computer vision systems, including safety and security monitoring. However, anomaly explainability in privacy-preserving VAD systems is underexplored. In this study, we present the XAVAD approach, a unified descriptive anomaly XAI for an anonymized VAD, that integrates flexible zero-shot anonymization, anomaly type categorization, visual localization, and scene context description. We provide empirical and qualitative assessments of multifaceted explanations integrated with full-body visual anonymization for privacy protection. We adopt a multimodal CLIP embedding for videos, using improved LLM-assisted prompting and pool-scoring mechanisms for anomaly-type identification. We enhance Grad-ECLIP for spatial anomaly heatmap localization, leveraging computation and accuracy through our novel prompt-guided patching autofocus mechanism. We employ VLMs to generate context and reasoning descriptions of detected anomalies through curated prompt engineering. We have evaluated the accuracy and computational cost of XAVAD on several publicly available CCTV and video datasets. Our experiments demonstrate substantial gains of our XAVAD over state-of-the-art benchmark approaches and provide insights into privacy protection trade-offs in XAI for VAD. We further present ablation studies and assessments across diverse configurations and modeling alternatives to demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods.
