papers.abstract: Code-based video generation offers fine-grained control, targeted editing, and component reuse compared with direct video generation. This approach requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to translate visual and temporal requirements into executable programs that produce complete videos. However, existing code-based benchmarks primarily target specialized tasks, leaving complete video creation across diverse creative categories and input modalities insufficiently evaluated. We introduce Code2Video-Compass, a general-purpose benchmark for code-based video generation across text-to-video (T2V), image-to-video (I2V), and video-to-video (V2V) settings. Code2Video-Compass comprises 2,104 tasks spanning 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and three complexity dimensions covering construction, dynamic animation, and state dependency. It combines tasks curated from textual instructions and visual references with corresponding T2V, I2V, and V2V tasks derived from complete professional and user-created videos. We propose a dual-level evaluation framework combining 12 objective metrics and five subjective metrics. Objective evaluation covers operational performance, video quality, text-video alignment, and reference fidelity, while subjective evaluation uses an MLLM judge to evaluate instruction following and holistic video quality. Extensive evaluation of 15 recent proprietary and open-weight MLLMs from nine families reveals that even leading models face challenges in reliably generating high-quality complete videos aligned with textual and visual requirements, with performance generally declining as construction, dynamic animation, and state-dependency complexity increases. We anticipate that Code2Video-Compass will advance reliable, coherent, and controllable code-based video generation and inspire broader progress in programmatic visual creation.
authors: Zhenghan Chen, Zekai Shao, Xin Lin, Leting Cheng, Siming Chen
bullets: Addresses the lack of broad evaluation for complete code-based video creation beyond specialized tasks.
Includes 2,104 tasks across 10 categories, 24 subtypes, and construction, dynamic-animation, and state-dependency complexity dimensions.
Covers text-to-video, image-to-video, and video-to-video generation, using textual instructions and visual references from professional and user-created videos.
Combines 12 objective metrics with five subjective MLLM-judged metrics for operational performance, quality, alignment, fidelity, instruction following, and holistic quality.
Evaluation of 15 MLLMs shows persistent difficulty producing high-quality, requirement-aligned videos, with performance declining as task complexity increases.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have substantially improved spoken interaction and video understanding. Existing online and streaming benchmarks primarily assess causal multimodal perception through timestamped question answering, whereas real-world interaction requires models to continuously identify task-relevant multimodal cues and decide whether, when, and how to respond. This leaves open how well current models can sustain real-time interaction throughout an evolving multimodal stream. To address this gap, we introduce DIVE, a benchmark for evaluating full-duplex interaction with visual engagement under continuous and realistic multimodal streams. It organizes six tasks into three complementary interaction scenarios. (1) Proactive Intervention evaluates whether models can identify emerging visual or semantic cues and intervene at the appropriate moment. (2) Continuous Engagement evaluates sustained participation through continuous visual tracking and visually grounded query interaction. (3) Interaction Coordination evaluates how models coordinate listening and speaking under overlapping and multi-party interactions. DIVE contains 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and precise temporal metadata. Its evaluation protocol separates response quality, participation decisions, and response timing. We evaluate representative real-time models using response quality, window response rates, and reaction latency. Experiments show that leading real-time models achieve sub-second average response latency, yet their average window response rates remain at or below 53.77%. Response quality varies substantially across models and tasks, with adapting ongoing responses to newly arriving information remaining particularly challenging. We hope DIVE facilitates progress toward more natural and capable real-time multimodal interactive systems.
authors: Yuhang Chen, Guangyue Liu, Shilong Liu
bullets: Targets a gap in streaming benchmarks that focus mainly on timestamped question answering rather than deciding whether, when, and how to respond.
Defines six tasks across proactive intervention, continuous engagement, and coordination during overlapping or multi-party interaction.
Provides 525 audio/video samples with fine-grained human annotations and temporal metadata.
Separately evaluates response quality, participation decisions, and timing using response quality, window response rate, and reaction latency.
Leading models respond in under a second on average, but window response rates reach at most 53.77%; adapting responses to new information remains difficult.

papers.abstract: As streaming video generation advances, enabling real-time interaction with generated video is becoming increasingly important. We introduce StreamEval, a unified benchmark for interactive streaming video generation spanning five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing. StreamEval comprises 300 scripted test cases lasting 15-300s, each specifying initial assets, incrementally arriving multimodal requests, and explicit requirements for state changes and content preservation. Performance is assessed along four evaluation dimensions: task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination, instantiated through ten task-specific metrics on a 0-100 scale. Evaluating 37 distinct models across 300 test cases, we find that high visual quality and identity retention do not necessarily coincide with reliable request execution or sustained state consistency. In particular, request execution remains challenging: the highest task-specific scores are 36.90 for Following among seven avatar-performance models, 25.93 for Following in text-conditioned world generation, and 15.00 for Edit Success among three reported reference-editing models. These findings identify reliable request execution under timing and preservation constraints as a central challenge for advancing omni-modal real-time interactive systems. The leaderboard is available at https://streameval.ai
bullets: Covers five tasks: avatar dialogue, avatar performance, world generation, instruction editing, and reference editing.
Uses 300 scripted 15–300-second test cases with incremental multimodal requests, initial assets, and explicit preservation requirements.
Evaluates task execution, state consistency, visual fidelity, and audiovisual coordination through ten task-specific metrics.
Results from 37 models show that visual quality and identity retention do not guarantee reliable request execution or sustained consistency.
Request execution scores remain low across evaluated tasks, highlighting a key bottleneck for real-time interactive systems.

papers.abstract: Object counting in videos remains a poorly characterized capability of multimodal large language models. Counting questions are included in many existing VideoQA benchmarks, but the ground-truth count distributions in these benchmarks are heavily skewed toward small values. Across the nine benchmarks we survey, the median ground-truth count is at most five, and the three most frequent values together account for between 45% and 93% of the videos. The resulting mean accuracy is then dominated by the most frequent counts; a value-dependent bias at a rare count contributes negligibly to the average and remains invisible. We introduce CountVideoBench, a benchmark of 2,600 synthetic videos covering 26 cardinalities in the interval [5, 50] (100 videos each), grouped into six clusters of consecutive counts that span the range while enabling near-neighbor comparisons. Each video contains a single class of static objects under a controlled camera motion, removing object motion and reducing recognition as confounds. We evaluate sixteen video-language models from nine architecture families in a zero-shot setting. No model exceeds 27.6% Exact Match. The dependence of accuracy on cardinality varies across models, ranging from monotonic decline to a non-monotonic peak-and-collapse pattern, which rules out increasing difficulty with cardinality as the dominant explanation of counting failure. Every model further concentrates its predictions on its own set of preferred integers, with accuracy peaks coinciding with these values and collapsing at adjacent counts. These findings highlight the need for balanced, diagnostic counting benchmarks to reliably assess this fundamental visual capability.
authors: Marc Chapus, Carlos Crispim-Junior, V\'eronique Eglin, Atilla Baskurt
bullets: Existing VideoQA benchmarks are dominated by small ground-truth counts, masking errors at rarer cardinalities.
The benchmark contains 2,600 synthetic videos with 26 balanced counts from 5 to 50, controlled camera motion, and single-class static objects.
Sixteen video-language models are evaluated zero-shot; none exceeds 27.6% exact-match accuracy.
Accuracy varies unpredictably with cardinality, including monotonic declines and peak-and-collapse patterns.
Models favor particular integers, with performance dropping sharply at neighboring counts, motivating balanced diagnostic benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous video editing from open-world resources remains a challenging problem in multimedia content creation. Retrieval-based methods are constrained by fixed source material and lack creative flexibility, while generative models struggle with long-horizon coherence and often diverge from user intent. Both paradigms fail to replicate the structured, multi-stage reasoning that underlies professional post-production. To address these limitations, we present Auto-Director, a tool-augmented multi-agent framework that mirrors professional editorial workflows: a Planning Agent decomposes abstract topics into fact-grounded scripts via retrieval-augmented planning; a Material Agent indexes open-world footage through shot segmentation and visual tagging; an Editor Agent assembles semantically aligned clips with MLLM-driven spatial adaptation; and a Critic Agent governs an iterative Reflect-and-Revise loop that checks scene-level alignment and pacing. To rigorously evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce VEdit-Bench, a benchmark of 100 expert-curated topics with human-annotated Golden Scripts and a five-dimensional metric suite covering Narrative Logic, Factual Accuracy, Semantic Alignment, Compositional Quality, and Stylistic Cohesion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Auto-Director significantly outperforms baseline methods in both automated metrics and human evaluation, effectively bridging the gap between amateurs and professional-grade video production.
authors: Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Addresses limited creative flexibility in retrieval-based editing and poor long-horizon coherence or intent alignment in generative approaches.
Uses four specialized agents: Planning, Material, Editor, and Critic, coordinated through retrieval, visual tagging, semantic alignment, and iterative revision.
Introduces VEdit-Bench, a benchmark with 100 expert-curated topics, Golden Scripts, and five evaluation dimensions.
Reports better automated-metric and human-evaluation performance than baseline methods, narrowing the gap between amateur and professional video production.

papers.abstract: Streaming video understanding requires a model to decide not only what to answer but also when to answer. Evidence arrives progressively, and recent benchmarks identify premature responses, issued before the queried event has concluded, as a recurring failure mode. Existing approaches often learn response timing through additional training, while training-free alternatives typically rely on scalar gating signals that do not explicitly represent when an answer becomes final. We organize chunk-wise streaming errors into three patterns: sampling variation can make an answer unstable, a stable answer may lack support in the observed video, or an answer may be supported by the current evidence while the event remains unfinished. We propose PACE (Plan, Attend, Check, and Emit), a training-free framework designed around these three failure modes. Given a question, PACE drafts a plan specifying what to observe and what will signal completion. As the stream unfolds, it invokes an off-the-shelf video LLM at informative moments, evaluates each draft for stability, grounding in its cited frames, and completion, and records verified observations in an event ledger. Experiments on ProactiveVideoQA and OVO-Bench Forward show that PACE improves over the official protocols by up to 5.9 average PAUC points and 6.2 average accuracy points across proprietary and open-source backbones, yielding state-of-the-art performance.
authors: Siqi Guo, Yuxia Chen, Wenbo Zhu, Yangguang Ji, Zhenxiang Jiang, Teng Zhong, Yu Zhang
bullets: Targets premature responses and other timing errors in streaming video understanding.
Uses a question-specific plan to identify observations and completion signals.
Checks draft answers at informative moments for stability, frame grounding, and event completion.
Maintains verified observations in an event ledger while the video stream unfolds.
Improves official protocols by up to 5.9 PAUC points and 6.2 accuracy points across evaluated benchmarks and backbones.

papers.abstract: Oddly Satisfying Videos (OSVs) can evoke strong viewer responses through repetitive motion, visual tactility, and ASMR-like sounds despite containing few explicit semantic emotion cues. This makes OSVs a challenging setting for Video Emotion Analysis (VEA), since most existing methods focus on semantic video content and under-model the physical sensory dynamics that shape viewer responses. To support Oddly Satisfying Video Emotion Analysis (OSVEA), we construct the Oddly Satisfying Video Dataset (OSVD), comprising 12,000 annotated 5-second clips. Each clip provides viewer-emotion labels under video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual conditions, together with explanations grounded in visual and acoustic sensory evidence. Building on OSVD, we propose PI-MLLM, a psychophysics-inspired multimodal large language model that integrates Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment (MSDA) and Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution (CAVA). MSDA uses auxiliary prediction objectives to align modality representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics. CAVA evaluates emotion scores across modality coalitions and applies Shapley attribution to identify the dominant modality and determine whether visual and auditory evidence is synergistic or conflicting. Experiments show that PI-MLLM improves both viewer-side emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality, suggesting the value of physical sensory cues to video emotion analysis.
authors: Yuheng Zhang, Jie Zhang, Yuecong Min, Yunwei Zhao, Meichen Liu, Qiankun Li, Shiguang Shan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of analyzing emotions in videos with few explicit semantic cues but strong sensory effects.
Introduces OSVD, a dataset of 12,000 annotated 5-second clips with video-only, audio-only, and audio-visual emotion labels and sensory-grounded explanations.
Uses Modality-Specific Dynamics Alignment to align representations with visual motion and acoustic energy-onset dynamics.
Uses Coalition-Based Audio-Visual Attribution with Shapley values to identify dominant modalities and audiovisual synergy or conflict.
Experiments report improved emotion prediction and sensory-grounded explanation quality.

MSDA aligns the visual representation with optical-flow dynamics and the audio representation with RMS loudness and onset strength. CAVA uses modality-conditioned emotion scores to estimate visual and auditory contributions and their interaction. The total objective combines generation, dynamics-alignment, coalitionclassification, and attribution losses.

Figure 1: Existing VEA methods rely on sensory-ungrounded semantic annotations and implicit multimodal fusion. Our approach addresses these limitations with psychophysics-aware sensory annotations and explicit multimodal modeling that preserves modality-specific dynamics and cross-modal relations for viewer-emotion reasoning.

Finally, the modality-specific reports are fused into audio-visual annotations and evaluated against human judgments.

papers.abstract: Moving from controllable videos to genuinely playable worlds requires persistent world state, executable game rules, and low-latency interaction. We outline a roadmap for the next generation of Matrix-Game that separates game execution from visual generation through an executable game harness, and introduce Matrix-Game 4.0 as the first system built on this design. A lightweight game engine maintains world state and executes interaction rules, a multimodal coding agent translates player ideas into game code and dynamic scene captions, and a renderer based on autoregressive video model transforms engine-rendered low-poly proxies into detailed visuals, conditioned on dynamic captions and memory references. This framework provides continuous guidance for visual generation and enables natural-language creation and modification of scenes and gameplay. Our renderer is trained on aligned low-poly and high-fidelity video pairs and distilled into a causal generator that generates in four-frame chunks with one or two denoising steps. Together with targeted inference optimizations, Matrix-Game 4.0 enables 480p, 60 FPS gameplay on a single NVIDIA RTX5090 with a key-press-to-display latency of 112ms. Single-step generation achieves 83FPS steady-state throughput with 18.2GiB of peak GPU memory usage. With fixed prompts, steady-state throughput also reaches 67FPS on an RTX5080 and 58FPS on an RTX5070Ti. We demonstrate customizable shooter and driving games with engine-enforced mechanics, and release code, model weights, and low-poly game assets to support research and creation of playable game worlds.

figures.caption: Figure 5: Architecture of the rendering model. The noisy latent of one chunk (one latent frame, four video frames) and the low-poly proxy encoded by TAEHV are concatenated into 148 channels and patchified into 405 tokens per latent frame at 480×864. Thirty causal DiT blocks apply self-attention over a KV cache that holds spatial-memory frames, reference frames, and the latest 20 chunks, cross-attention to the cached text keys and values of the dynamic caption, and a feed-forward network, each modulated by the timestep through AdaLN. The output head predicts a velocity, one or two flow updates produce the clean latent, and TAEHV decodes four frames. The finished chunk is then re-run at t = 0 without the control input to write its keys and values into the cache.

Figure 6: Overview of the inference optimizations. (a) Per-block GPU time on an RTX 5090, broken down by kernel category. (b) Decoding is moved ahead of the clean-KV update, so frames are output earlier. (c) Instead of shifting the whole KV window at every step, the ring cache writes the new frame into the oldest slot. (d) Self-attention is split into seven window ranges whose quantized keys and values are cached; the partial outputs are combined by log-sum-exp.

Figure 2: Roadmap of Matrix-Game V4: The multimodal coding agent and the game engine form the harness for the video generation model. The player sends ideas and requests to the agent and actions to the engine (1). The agent writes the world, turning ideas into game code and scenes for the engine, and translates the world, turning the state and events reported by the engine into text descriptions. The engine maintains the world state and the rules in code (2) and sends control signals as a structural rendering of the scene (3). The video generation model renders frames in real time from the text description, its past frames, and the structural rendering (4). The generated frame returns to the player as visual feedback (5).

Top: low-poly proxy frames of one CitySample driving clip; numbered markers are the visible objects that the engine reports for this frame, each linked by its instance ID to a semantic description. Below: the caption that the rule-based template produces for the same frame, without any vision-language model. Orange text comes from object states and events, and blue text from object positions and distances. As the car moves, parked vehicles leave the description, pedestrians change from standing to approaching, and newly visible objects are announced under “Changes”.

Figure 8: Game modes written with the coding agent, rendered in real time. Top: in the thirdperson shooter, the agent adds health and ammunition control, shield durability, a faster shotgun, a game-over condition, and simple sound effects. Middle: in the driving game, the agent implements a time trial with route checkpoints and collision penalties. Bottom: the same driving game turned into a pursuit mode, in which the player must intercept a target vehicle and stay close to it for five seconds. The engine evaluates every rule; the video model renders each frame from the engine output.

Figure 7: Re-rendering over 40-second held-out rollouts. For each game, the upper row is the low-poly proxy from the engine and the lower row is the frame generated by the distilled causal model at the same time step. papers.abstract: Long-horizon video generation requires retaining an ever-expanding history, but conditioning on its growing token sequence is costly. Existing methods restrict or compress historical context, potentially losing information needed for future generation. This work proposes ReCam, which groups local spatiotemporal blocks of historical latents into vectors and projects them directly into the high-dimensional hidden space of a Diffusion Transformer. The model learns to use the resulting memory tokens through native self-attention, reducing token count while retaining block-level access to the full history. To mitigate temporal drift during autoregressive rollout, we further introduce dual-pointer denoising with separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames. Among the evaluated methods, ReCam achieves the highest VBench-Long overall score of 80.1 and competitive static-scene revisitation performance on R2M-Bench. It also leads on all four consistency metrics for off-screen subject reappearance, including clothing consistency of 4.09 versus 3.03 for the best baseline.
authors: Yukuo Ma, Cong Liu, Junke Wang, Junqi Liu, Haibin Huang, Zuxuan Wu, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the cost and information loss of conditioning on growing video histories.
Groups local spatiotemporal latent blocks into vectors and projects them into a Diffusion Transformer’s hidden space.
Uses native self-attention for block-level access to the full history with fewer tokens.
Introduces separate noise schedules for recent context and target frames to improve autoregressive stability.
Achieves the top reported VBench-Long score (80.1) and leads all four off-screen subject reappearance consistency metrics.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of ReCam. Historical latents are grouped into local spatiotemporal blocks and projected into memory tokens by a lightweight MLP. The first frame remains a clean visual anchor. Native self-attention connects the historical memory and current chunk, while text cross-attention is applied only to the current chunk.

Figure 1 A coarse read on fine-grained history. We compare our method with other representative methods. Keyframe-based approaches, such as CaM [Yu et al., 2025], typically employ an external rule-based selector to retrieve a subset of frames as memory. In contrast, compression-based methods [Zhang et al., 2025] encode history into a compact representation through a separate reconstruction stage. Different from these approaches, ReCam allows the video model itself to learn how to represent history and how to retrieve it via its native attention mechanism.

Figure 6 Overview of the general-purpose video corpus. (a) Percentage of videos in each duration interval. (b) Word cloud of the 60 most frequent words in the captions after filtering out template terms such as “captures” and “environment”.
Figure 4 Efficiency and optimization. (a) Peak GPU memory and forward-pass time on one H100. (b) Dual-pointer loss approaches clean-context loss and remains below single-pointer loss.
Figure 5 Anti-drifting via dual-pointer denoising. Generated frames from clean context (top) and dual-pointer denoising (bottom), with time progressing from left to right.
Figure 7 Example history-generation prompts with the subject (a) initially present and (b) initially absent. Ellipses indicate omitted text.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed framework. Given an egocentric manipulation video, our framework uses a reference branch and an optimized generation branch for test-time action transfer. We apply Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in the early denoising steps to preserve hand-object structure, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in the mid-to-late steps to refine local correspondences and improve interaction realism.

Figure 6. The overview of EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench contains 350 reference manipulation videos and 1,400 target prompts, covering indoor/outdoor scenes, single-/two-hand interactions, and diverse manipulation categories. The benchmark evaluates whether generated videos preserve the reference action semantics while adapting to new visual contexts.

Figure 5. Gallery of proposed method. EgoACT can transfer a wide range of egocentric manipulation videos, covering diverse interaction categories, object types, and motion patterns. The generated videos preserve plausible hand-object structure, contact dynamics, and temporal coherence while adapting the reference action to new visual contexts.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.
Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. Compare with previous methods, our method preserves stable hand-object layout and object response.
Figure 10. More visual results.

Figure 4. Illustration of the proposed SCC. (a) Direct transfer injects the reference action without correction, which may lead to errors in weak hand-object interactions. (b) Applying correction throughout the whole denoising process over-constrains early generation, making it difficult to decouple transferable action from source observation. (c) Our SCC performs sparse correspondence calibration only in the mid-to-late denoising stages, where the action layout has been established and local interaction details can be refined, improving temporal consistency and hand-object realism.
Figure 11. More visual results.
Figure 12. More visual results.
Figure 13. More details about EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench covers diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios and is annotated by scene type, and object category.

Figure 7. User Study. B1–B5 denote VACE, Mask2IV, CosHand, InterDyn, and DiTFlow, respectively. Our method is consistently preferred by human evaluators, achieving the highest excellent/good ratio across all evaluated aspects.

Figure 2. Motivation. Motion transfer suffers from hand structural collapse and lacks physical interaction. Condition-guided generation preserves hand shape but produces physically implausible contact. Our method maintains both hand structure and realistic interaction.
Figure 9. Visual ablation. VSA suppresses structural collapse, while SCC improves local correspondence.

Figure 15. Attention Visualization. We visualize the crossframe attention maps before and after enabling VSA during the early denoising stage. Without VSA, attention is dispersed across irrelevant regions, failing to capture coherent hand-object structure. With VSA enabled, the attention concentrates on interactionrelevant areas such as hand, object, and contact regions, indicating that the generation trajectory is better aligned with the reference structural layout. This confirms that VSA effectively anchors the hand-object skeleton through velocity-guided alignment, resulting in more structurally consistent attention patterns.

papers.abstract: Endoscopic video contains state transitions induced by camera displacement, deformable tissue, and instrument interaction, yet existing pre-training methods treat dynamics implicitly. Inspired by action-conditioned joint-embedding predictive world models and by the observation that endoscopic optical flow contains both shared image-plane displacement and localized residual motion, we reformulate passive endoscopic video pre-training as causal motion-guided latent-state prediction. We present EndoWorld-JEPA, to our knowledge the first latent world-model pre-training framework designed for general-purpose endoscopic video representation learning. In place of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics, the model conditions prediction of the next latent state on motion observed up to the current state. Its Optical Motion-guided module separates dominant displacement from residual motion and converts the resulting evidence into an ordered temporal motion condition and spatial local-motion weights. Complementary global and motion-local predictors use these outputs: the temporal condition modulates both latent transitions, whereas the local weights define an auxiliary motion-local state that extends prediction from scene-level evolution to spatially selective dynamics. Patch-wise motion weighting emphasizes localized change while retaining anatomical context, and past-motion-window dropout randomly withholds the complete motion condition to reduce dependence on unreliable motion. This global--local formulation learns predictable visual--motion dynamics in representation space without reconstructing stochastic appearance artifacts. Evaluation shows that a common pre-trained checkpoint achieves strong transfer across four downstream benchmarks, supporting motion-guided global--local latent prediction as an effective pre-training paradigm for endoscopic video.
authors: Jie Wang, Shilong Yang, Tao Zhou, Juan Yu, Rong Qu, Jianfeng Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Linlin Shen
bullets: Addresses the implicit treatment of camera, tissue, and instrument-induced dynamics in existing endoscopic pre-training methods.
Uses observed motion instead of recorded actions, calibrated poses, or robot kinematics to condition next-state latent prediction.
Separates dominant image-plane displacement from localized residual motion to form temporal motion conditions and spatial motion weights.
Combines global and motion-local predictors, with motion-window dropout to reduce reliance on unreliable motion cues.
A shared pre-trained checkpoint transfers effectively across four downstream benchmarks, supporting the proposed paradigm.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of EndoWorld-JEPA, a causal motion-conditioned JEPA world model. Top: for the implemented K = 5 horizon, the OM block converts six consecutive observations ending at xst into five incoming optical flows, motion descriptors, a local-motion weight map, and a motion condition. Middle: the global–local JEPA block uses this five-transition motion history with the current state xst to predict local and global latent targets at xst+5. Bottom: the pretrained encoder and OM block are transferred with task-specific decoders for four downstream tasks.

Figure 3: Representative OM responses to a whole-view shift (top), a local-region change (middle), and their combination (bottom). Columns show preceding and current frames, dense flow ust , residual magnitude Rst , local map Mt, relative weights Nwt,i, and the weight overlay. Dense-flow hue follows the direction key, while intensity denotes displacement magnitude. Row annotations report ∥dst∥2 and P90(Rst). Residual magnitude and Mt share a within-row display range. Here, Nwt,i = 1 denotes uniform pooling; weight maps and overlays share the clipped 0.3–7.0 scale. Display scaling does not affect OM computation.

Figure 1: Comparison of three pre-training paradigms and their treatment of local dynamics. (A) Existing endoscopic video pre-training captures temporal context, but transitions remain implicit: invariance may attenuate change, masking models transitions indirectly, and observed motion does not condition prediction. (B) Medical world models rely on domain-specific data and transition conditions unavailable in passive endoscopy. (C) EndoWorld-JEPA couples an Optical Motion-guided (OM) block that derives motion guidance from unlabeled passive video with a causal global–local JEPA, requiring no recorded controls or calibrated poses. Bottom: a schematic comparison illustrates that existing video pre-training models localized dynamics only implicitly within global latent features, whereas the OM block produces an explicit local-motion map whose patch weighting emphasizes motion-relevant regions.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in predicting semantically and geometrically distinct futures from similar egocentric observation histories.
Uses fixation strength and recency to modulate a vision-language model via Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation for intention inference.
Maps intentions to contact, support, and placement fields with Anticipatory Contact Grounding.
Generates 6-DoF object trajectories and articulated motion for both hands using a diffusion-based model.
Introduces the phase-aware EgoAIM benchmark with fine-grained intention annotations; reports state-of-the-art intention and motion forecasting, with near-oracle performance in some phases.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Overview of Gaze2HOI. Hierarchical inference from egocentric observations to future hand-object interactions: (a) TGSM modulates VLM visual features with gaze cues to infer structured per-hand intentions. (b) ACG grounds inferred intentions into explicit 3D contact, support, and placement fields. (c) Conditional motion diffusion leverages semantic and geometric conditions to jointly forecast articulated hand motion and 6-DoF object trajectories.

Anticipatory Contact Grounding then combines the inferred intentions with object geometry and interaction history to localize likely contact regions, reducing geometric ambiguity. The resulting semantic and geometric cues guide coordinated hand-object motion forecasting.

Fig. 6. Illustration of gaze injection strategies. Each panel shows the image and corresponding prompt for the same egocentric observation. The TGSM overlay is for visualization only; gaze cues are injected through visual feature modulation.

Fig. 1. Egocentric hand-object interaction forecasting. Gaze2HOI forecasts coordinated interactions involving both hands and multiple objects across four phases: Establish Contact, Move, Manipulate, and Put Down. L and R denote the left and right hands, respectively.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.
RoboJudge-9B is fine-tuned with supervised learning and reinforcement learning, achieving the highest reported agreement on the benchmark with a Pearson correlation of 0.719.
The trained judge also improves performance on external benchmarks and is used to evaluate video generation models.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ROBOJUDGE. (A) We propose ROBOJUDGE-BENCH, which evaluates MLLMs as judges of embodied videos. (B) Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment serve as the two core evaluation dimensions for embodied judge models. (C) We benchmark 29 existing model judges, (D) and construct ROBOJUDGE-TRAIN, a 12K-video dataset for judge training, and fine-tune ROBOJUDGE-9B, which achieves the strongest overall agreement among model judges.

Figure 4: Qualitative failure cases of existing judges on ROBOJUDGE-BENCH. Each panel compares human and judge Physical Adherence (PA) and Instruction Alignment (IA) scores with sampled frames and judge reasoning. (A) GPT-5.5 misses duplicated stickers and extra hands. (B) MiMo-Embodied-7B misses abrupt cloth deformation and vanishing manipulators. (C) VideoScore2 credits task completion although the refrigerator door stays closed. (D) Qwen3-VL-32B reports successful placement although the bottle lands beside the target pad. These failures span entity consistency, interaction realism, action completion, and goal-state verification.

Figure 2: Examples from ROBOJUDGE-BENCH. Each example shows the task instruction, sampled video frames, and human ratings with supporting evidence for Physical Adherence (PA) and Instruction Alignment (IA). Left: a gripper-robot video preserves most physical properties but fails to complete the packing task (PA: 4; IA: 2). Right: a human-hand video completes the requested insertion despite object-consistency and interaction artifacts (PA: 3; IA: 5). papers.abstract: Latent diffusion models have recently achieved remarkable progress in Real-world Image Super-Resolution (Real-SR). However, existing methods consistently exhibit a persistent seesaw effect: enhancing perceptual realism compromises structural fidelity. This effect, we argue, is not intrinsic to diffusion models, but largely stems from the architectural constraints of prevailing two-stage frameworks. To address this challenge, we propose PixelSR, a novel single-stage Pixel Diffusion Transformer for Real-SR that operates directly in pixel space. Specifically, PixelSR consists of two core designs: Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling. The former establishes an effective pixel-space restoration framework by integrating spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement, thereby bypassing VAE compression and enabling end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space. Complementarily, the latter decomposes the asymmetric flow target into a low-rank semantic component and a noise-free orthogonal texture component. By routing these components to specialized branches, it achieves decoupled optimization with reduced mutual interference. Benefiting from these designs, our PixelSR restores perceptually realistic details while faithfully preserving structural content. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PixelSR not only achieves competitive performance, but also effectively mitigates the fidelity--realism seesaw effect.
authors: Xiang Lv, Kai Zhao, Qiang Wang, Qiao Mo, Chao Zhou, Mingwen Shao
bullets: Targets the realism–fidelity trade-off attributed to architectural limitations in two-stage diffusion frameworks.
Uses pixel-space conditional diffusion with aligned low-resolution conditioning, semantic guidance, and lightweight texture refinement.
Introduces Orthogonal Flow Decoupling to separate low-rank semantic and orthogonal texture components into specialized branches.
Avoids VAE compression and enables end-to-end optimization directly in RGB space.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks show competitive performance and mitigation of the fidelity–realism seesaw effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the proposed PixelSR framework. PixelSR comprises Pixel-space Conditional Diffusion (PCD) and Orthogonal Flow Decoupling (OFD). Left: PCD performs end-toend RGB-space restoration using spatially aligned LR conditioning, visual semantic guidance, and lightweight pixel-level texture refinement. Right: OFD factorizes the asymmetric velocity target into a projected low-rank component and a deterministic orthogonal residual, which empirically exhibit semantic- and texture-dominant characteristics, respectively. Their predictions are assigned to specialized DiT and PiT branches and recombined into the full velocity for flow matching, enabling task-aligned optimization with reduced interference.

papers.abstract: Rapid advances in diffusion models have raised concerns about privacy, harmful content, and copyright violations. Concept erasure methods aim to address these risks by removing undesirable concepts from pretrained models without full retraining. However, existing approaches often degrade non-target generation quality through heuristic strength scaling (e.g., classifier-free guidance or negative prompt scaling), leading to uncontrolled and excessive semantic drift. To address this, we propose Push-Pull Attentional Anchoring (PPAA), a mechanism in the cross-attention space that displaces target representations while anchoring the scale of erasure via bounded cosine-similarity constraints. By using a relative similarity ratio instead of an absolute difference, our adaptive threshold represents a meaningful percentage of semantic retention, facilitating a single value to be applied uniformly across layers. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple concept categories, including celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property. Our method achieves favorable trade-offs against prior approaches on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and demonstrates its applicability to modern architectures such as FLUX.
authors: Nattanat Chatthee, Tagon Sompong, Ekapol Chuangsuwanich, Supasorn Suwajanakorn
bullets: Addresses semantic drift caused by heuristic erasure-strength scaling in existing concept-erasure methods.
Operates in cross-attention space, displacing target representations while constraining their cosine similarity.
Uses a bounded relative similarity ratio to express semantic retention and apply one adaptive threshold across layers.
Evaluated on celebrities, artistic styles, nudity, and intellectual property concepts.
Reports favorable trade-offs on Stable Diffusion v1.4 and applicability to FLUX.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Concept erasure and preservation results on FLUX. (a) Qualitative comparison on representative identity, style, and character concepts. Our method erases target concepts, such as Barack Obama, Van Gogh, and Mickey Mouse, while preserving non-target concepts, such as Will Smith, Picasso, and Donald Duck. ESD causes substantial semantic shifts in non-target concepts, whereas UCE fails to semantically erase Mickey Mouse. (b) Quantitative results. Accuracy measures target-concept detection after erasure, and CMMD measures preservation relative to the original FLUX model; lower is better for both metrics. These results demonstrate the applicability of our objective to FLUX while maintaining a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 2: Erasure–Preservation score across concept categories. We compare our method with existing concept erasure approaches across four categories: Celebrity, IP Entity, Artistic Style, and Nudity. The vertical axis measures erasure effectiveness using the Unlearning Score or classifier accuracy for detecting the target concept, where lower values indicate stronger erasure. The horizontal axis measures preservation effectiveness using CMMD (×1000), where lower values indicate better preservation of non-target concepts. Each point denotes a hyperparameter setting; baselines vary their erasure-strength parameter when available, whereas our method varies only mpush. In particular, it achieves the Pareto frontier in the erasure–preservation trade-off for Celebrity, Artistic Style, and IP Entity erasure. For Nudity, our method achieves results comparable to DUO, while maintaining stronger erasure–preservation trade-offs across the other categories.

Fig. 8: Training-Free Trajectory Probing Results. We evaluate robustness to trajectory-based attacks using the prompt “a photo of a naked person” on nudityerased models. Base shows images generated without applying the attack procedure. The remaining rows show randomly sampled images obtained from the attack method. Although our method is not explicitly trained with robustness-oriented objectives (e.g., DUO and STEREO), its behavior under this attack appears competitive to that of existing methods such as MACE, UCE, SUMA, and ESD.

Fig. 10: Concept erasure and preservation results on the Z-Image model. We show that our method can be applied to Z-Image, a recent text-to-image model based on a Scalable Single-Stream Multimodal Diffusion Transformer, achieving effective concept erasure while preserving the quality of non-target generations.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of erasure methods. Our method erases the target concepts (e.g., Rihanna identity and Picasso style) while preserving the non-target concepts (e.g., Margot Robbie identity and Claude Monet style). Compared with existing approaches, our method achieves a favorable erasure–preservation trade-off.

Fig. 6: Ablation Study on Design Choices. Ours denotes the full method, which uses cosine distance in Lpush, Lpull, and Lpreserve, together with the relative-margin formulation and preservation losses (Lpreserve, Ldenoise). Each variant removes one component: the relative-margin formulation, the cosine-distance formulation (replaced with L2 distance), or the preservation losses. Each point corresponds to a different push margin. The x-axis measures same-domain preservation (CMMD ×1000, lower is better) and the y-axis measures unlearning score (detection accuracy, lower is better). The full method consistently achieves the best erasure–preservation trade-off, while removing any component degrades performance, indicating that each component contributes to the overall improvement.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a mechanism for concept erasure in diffusion models using attentional anchoring, relevant to video diffusion and multimodal model safety.

papers.tldr: PPAA erases unwanted concepts from diffusion models by pushing target representations away while anchoring semantic retention to reduce unintended quality loss.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding with multimodal LLMs is fundamentally constrained by the mismatch between video length and the model's limited visual context budget, making frame selection essential for practical reasoning. Existing query-aware methods typically rely on heuristic pipelines: they assign one-dimensional query-conditioned scores to frames and then apply sampling, ranking, or extraction rules to form the final subset. While effective in practice, such methods are generally not derived from an explicit optimization objective and struggle to capture the heterogeneous evidence required for complex reasoning. In this paper, we revisit long-video frame selection from a principled optimization perspective. We formulate it as a structured evidence-allocation problem and propose OTFS, an optimal transport framework that maps multiple evidence sources onto video frames. To reflect the asymmetry of this problem---important evidence should be preserved, whereas redundant frames need not absorb mass---we instantiate this view with a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective and an efficient solver, OTFS-Sinkhorn. Combined with an exact dynamic program for coverage-aware subset extraction, OTFS yields a practical two-stage training-free pipeline. We further show that, in the single-source case, our formulation induces a Gibbs-type distribution over frames, making Q-Frame's temperature-scaled distribution a special case of our framework while also providing a broader perspective for understanding related prior methods. Experiments on three long-video understanding benchmarks show that OTFS consistently outperforms strong training-free baselines. Codes are available at https://github.com/barry664/OTFS.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between long videos and multimodal LLM context limits, where heuristic query-aware selection may miss heterogeneous evidence.
Maps multiple evidence sources to video frames using a semi-unbalanced entropic optimal transport objective.
Uses an efficient OTFS-Sinkhorn solver followed by exact dynamic programming for coverage-aware subset extraction.
Provides a training-free two-stage pipeline and shows that Q-Frame’s temperature-scaled distribution is a special single-source case.
Outperforms strong training-free baselines across three long-video understanding benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Comparison between prior training-free frame-selection procedures and our principled OT-based framework. Existing methods typically compute one-dimensional frame scores and then apply hand-designed sampling or extraction rules. In contrast, OTFS formulates frame selection as semi-unbalanced transport from evidence atoms to video frames, producing a soft frame-importance distribution that is converted into a coverage-aware subset by exact dynamic programming.

Figure 2: Left: Three evidence atoms over time. Middle: The optimal transport plan π∗, shown as a heatmap from evidence atoms to video frames. Different evidence sources assign mass to distinct temporal regions, highlighting their complementary roles in grounding the query. Right: The resulting frame-importance marginal w and the final subset selected by dynamic programming (red arrows indicate all selected frames, and red dots mark five representative examples).

papers.title: A Principled Optimal Transport Framework for Frame Selection in Long Video Understanding
papers.tldr: OTFS formulates long-video frame selection as semi-unbalanced optimal transport to allocate diverse evidence under limited visual context.

papers.abstract: Multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) aims to understand user-generated videos by integrating multiple modalities. Existing methods often treat modalities as symmetric, overlooking the fact that language provides a dominant semantic prior while nonverbal signals are complementary and noise-prone. To address this, we propose a Text-Anchored Modality Experts with Uncertainty-Guided Routing, termed TAME, that reformulates MSA as an uncertainty-guided refinement paradigm, where the language prior is calibrated and enhanced by selectively trusted nonverbal evidence. Specifically, TAME adopts an asymmetric Mixture-of-Modality-Experts framework, in which textual features act as a fixed and always-activated shared expert, while audio-textual and video-textual cross-modal branches serve as dynamically routed auxiliary experts. Furthermore, we introduce lightweight Prophet Heads to quantify the sample-level predictive uncertainty of each individual modality, and this uncertainty metric is further incorporated into the modality router to realize reliability-aware expert aggregation and fusion. Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS datasets demonstrate that TAME achieves state-of-the-art performance on the majority of metrics while reducing parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2% over the mixture-of-expert baseline. %These results confirm that asymmetric expert construction with uncertainty-guided routing is an effective paradigm for MSA.
authors: Xiaohua Huang, Bingrui Lei, Xiuyan hao, Ling Zhou, Yuan Zong, Wenming Zheng, Guoying Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation of treating text, audio, and video as equally reliable, despite language providing a stronger semantic prior.
Uses an asymmetric mixture-of-modality-experts design with an always-active text expert and dynamically routed audio-textual and video-textual experts.
Introduces lightweight Prophet Heads to estimate modality-specific, sample-level uncertainty for reliability-aware expert routing and fusion.
Experiments on CMU-MOSI, CMU-MOSEI, and CH-SIMS report state-of-the-art performance on most metrics.
Compared with a mixture-of-experts baseline, reduces parameter count by up to 78.7% and FLOPs by up to 41.2%.

papers.abstract: Few-step trajectory distillation aims to learn accurate global updates from dense local supervision along a teacher's sampling trajectory. Existing approaches construct within-step dynamics using specific trajectory parameterizations or discrete interval predictions, tying the learned update to a prescribed temporal structure. We propose \method, which directly learns a continuous trajectory primitive representing cumulative displacement along the teacher trajectory. By supervising finite differences of the primitive with local teacher velocities, \method learns the accumulated motion directly, while obtaining global updates through endpoint differences. This formulation avoids prescribing a temporal basis or fixed query grid and instead learns the temporal evolution of cumulative displacement from local supervision. We further establish a local-to-global error bound to characterize how local regression errors affect full-interval displacement accuracy, and introduce endpoint absorption to eliminate the auxiliary primitive branch while preserving one-network-evaluation inference. Experiments on large-scale text-to-image generation show that \method achieves a T-FID of 20.92 and an HPSv2 score of 28.35 at one NFE, improving both metrics over a trajectory-distillation baseline. After endpoint absorption, it retains comparable performance, achieving a T-FID of 20.86 and an HPSv2 score of 28.33.
bullets: Targets few-step trajectory distillation, where global updates must be learned from dense local supervision.
Learns cumulative displacement directly and obtains global motion from endpoint differences, avoiding a prescribed temporal basis or query grid.
Provides a local-to-global error bound linking local regression errors to full-interval displacement accuracy.
Endpoint absorption removes the auxiliary primitive branch while retaining one-network-evaluation inference.
On large-scale text-to-image generation, reaches T-FID 20.92 and HPSv2 28.35 at one NFE; endpoint absorption remains comparable at 20.86 and 28.33.

Figure 1: Representing within-step trajectory geometry. A prescribed temporal family or fixed interval grid constrains how the teacher trajectory is represented. PRIMFLOW directly represents interval integrals as differences of one source-anchored continuous primitive.

papers.title: PRIMFLOW: Learning Trajectory Primitives for Few-Step Distillation
papers.tldr: PRIMFLOW learns continuous cumulative trajectory primitives from local teacher velocities to enable accurate one-step diffusion distillation without a fixed temporal parameterization.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in unified visual editing have begun to consolidate image and video editing within a single model, while 3D scene editing remains largely separate and constrained by scarce paired training data. Given the rich image and video editing supervision now available and the common editing semantics shared across modalities, a natural question is whether this knowledge can be transferred to data-scarce 3D editing. We present VitronEdit, a universal framework for image, video, and 3D scene editing. VitronEdit adopts a shared sequence representation and progressive multimodal training to transfer editing knowledge across modalities. We further introduce geometry-aware post-training, which leverages a pretrained geometry reconstruction model to provide depth and camera-pose supervision. Surprisingly, applying geometric supervision only to 3D samples yields the best overall performance, while image and video editing also improve despite receiving no direct geometric supervision, suggesting that geometric regularization transfers through the shared backbone. Our analysis further shows that image and video training mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, whereas 3D supervision primarily improves multi-view consistency. The project page: https://vitron-llm.github.io/VitronEdit/.
authors: Jing Wang, Yanlin Li, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu, Shengqiong Wu, Hao Fei
bullets: Addresses the separation of 3D editing from better-supervised image and video editing.
Uses a shared sequence representation with progressive multimodal training.
Adds geometry-aware post-training using depth and camera-pose supervision from a pretrained reconstruction model.
Geometry supervision applied only to 3D samples improves overall performance, including image and video editing.
Image/video data mainly transfers editing semantics to 3D, while 3D supervision improves multi-view consistency.

papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online video content, video temporal grounding has become essential for localizing moments based on user-specific queries, comprising two subtasks: moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD). While recent approaches adopt DETR-style decoders or temporal pyramid architectures, they rely on single-scale feature maps or uniformly downsampled representations, limiting their ability to capture semantic boundaries and variable-length events. In this paper, we present SuperClip Video Temporal Grounding (SCVTG) built on a multi-scale temporal hierarchy that better captures distinctive events at various granularities. SCVTG constructs a SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments, termed SuperClips. Further, to aggregate these SuperClips having variable duration and temporal location, we introduce a temporally adaptive kernel that aggregates SuperClips through temporally conditioned weights, enabling flexible aggregation. On top of this, we design relative saliency losses to guide the model in learning inter-clip importance, enhancing its ability to distinguish relevant events. Extensive experiments show that SCVTG achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks with promising gains.
authors: Sanghyeok Lee, Juyeon Ko, Joonmyung Choi, Jongha Kim, Dohwan Ko, Ji Soo Lee, Hyunwoo J. Kim
bullets: Targets moment retrieval and highlight detection in long, variable-length videos.
Builds a multi-scale SuperClip pyramid by grouping adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.
Uses a temporally adaptive kernel to aggregate SuperClips with location- and duration-aware weights.
Introduces relative saliency losses to learn the importance of different clips.
Achieves the best performance across five video temporal grounding benchmarks, with promising gains.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overall architecture of SCVTG. After multi-modal fusion, video clip features are progressively grouped and aggregated to form a SuperClip pyramid with varying temporal granularity. Given this multi-level hierarchy capturing distinctive events, task-specific heads predict both foreground moments and clip-wise saliency scores.

Figure 5. Qualitative results of SuperClip Pyramid. The interval indicated by the red arrow denotes the ground-truth moments. The SuperClip highlighted with a red hatched region perfectly aligns with the ground truth, serving as an ideal candidate for temporal grounding.

Figure 4. Illustration of SuperClip grouping and aggregation. (a) Given the input clips, a non-anchor clip is assigned to one of its adjacent anchor clips based on semantic similarity, forming coherent SuperClips. (b) Next, each clip is projected using its corresponding weight generated by the temporally adaptive kernel (TA-Kernel), followed by pooling and a linear layer. (c) Unlike fixed convolutional kernels, which cannot handle varying lengths or temporal characteristics, we generate TA-kernel weights for SuperClips, considering the temporal information (ϕ(fi)) of its constituent clips.

Figure 2. Comparison between (a) conventional temporal pyramid and (b) SuperClip pyramid. Unlike conventional temporal pyramids that segment videos at uniform intervals, our SuperClip pyramid adaptively groups adjacent clips into semantically coherent segments.

Figure 1. Performance comparison. SCVTG outperforms all baseline models, demonstrating its effectiveness in video temporal grounding. For moment retrieval (MR) and highlight detection (HD), we use R1@0.7 and mAP@Avg, respectively.

papers.abstract: Online action detection (OAD) identifies ongoing actions in streaming videos. Many existing OAD systems combine RGB appearance with optical flow, but dense-flow extraction remains a major computational bottleneck. Codec motion vectors (MVs) are available during decoding, avoiding a separate optical-flow computation. On THUMOS'14, optical flow exceeds MVs by 11.2 mAP points with motion-only inputs, whereas the gap narrows to 3.7 points after RGB fusion, with the largest reduction in action-category discrimination. We propose CodecMotion-OAD, which replaces optical flow with decoder-provided MVs while retaining existing temporal detector architectures. Its two-stage training first aligns MV features with a pretrained flow-feature interface without action labels and then trains RGB+MV detectors using ground-truth labels and soft predictions from a frozen RGB+Flow teacher. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of codec MVs to frame-level OAD. On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, CodecMotion-OAD achieves 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow, while reducing decoder-to-prediction processing time by 11.48-fold on CPU and 2.04-fold on GPU.
authors: Zepeng Sun, Naichuan Zheng, Hailun Xia, Junjie Wu
bullets: Optical-flow extraction is a major OAD bottleneck; codec motion vectors are available directly during video decoding.
The method retains existing temporal detector architectures and uses two-stage feature alignment and teacher-guided RGB+MV training.
On THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD, it reaches 68.3 mAP versus 70.9 mAP for matched-distillation RGB+Flow.
Decoder-to-prediction processing is 11.48× faster on CPU and 2.04× faster on GPU.
Scope: evaluated on THUMOS'14 with MiniROAD; performance remains below the optical-flow counterpart.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Overview of Interface-Preserving Motion Transfer (IPMT). (a) Stage I adapts a codec-MV encoder initialized from Flow-ResNet50 by matching its 2048-dimensional per-step features to those of a frozen Flow-ResNet50, without action labels. (b) Stage II freezes the RGB and adapted MV encoders and trains the original RGB+MV temporal detectors with ground-truth labels mixed with soft labels from a shared, frozen CMeRT RGB+Flow teacher. (c) Under the H.264 IPPP protocol, decoding supplies RGB frames and codec MVs to the student detector, without optical-flow extraction or the teacher at inference.

The columns show RGB center frames, TV-L1 optical flow, spatially coarsened Flow (16×16 block averaging, with block means tiled back to the original resolution), and codec motion vectors. The three motion visualizations within each row share the same direction-to-hue mapping and magnitudeto-saturation scale, with a common magnitude cap for that row. Block averaging removes fine spatial detail, whereas codec MVs exhibit additional sparsity and prediction-dependent spatial structure.

papers.abstract: Long-video understanding often requires answering many questions about a single video whose evidence is distributed across extended temporal contexts. Conventional video-language models repeatedly encode frames or retrieve visual evidence for every question. Parameterized video memory offers a write-once alternative, but existing methods rely primarily on synthesized text and fixed adaptation configurations, leaving open where video knowledge should be written and how visual evidence should shape the memory. We introduce Memory Internalization via Test-Time Training (MIT^3), a per-video adaptation framework that writes each long video into compact, video-specific adaptive parameters for video-free, text-only question answering. Under compact multi-scale supervision, causal tracing measures the causal memory utility of each model layer for video-grounded answering and selects video-specific adaptation locations. Visual memory distillation then trains the text-only memory to reproduce the representation change induced by the relevant video clip, preserving the internal effect of visual evidence beyond textual supervision. Across LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, MIT^3 achieves data-efficient video-free question answering with substantially fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods, demonstrating that effective video internalization depends on both where knowledge is written and how visual evidence is distilled into the model.
authors: Haonan Zhao, Jiaxuan Chen, Qingyang Liu, Shuochen Chang, Siyu Sun, Jiangtong Li, Li Niu
bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of re-encoding or retrieving video evidence for every question.
Uses causal tracing to identify video-specific model layers for memory adaptation.
Distills the representation changes caused by visual clips into a text-only memory under compact multi-scale supervision.
Evaluated on LVBench, LongVideoBench, and Video-MME, achieving data-efficient video-free QA with fewer synthesized samples than prior parameterized video-memory methods.
Scope: memory is adapted separately for each video, so it is not a universal video memory.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MIT3. (a) A VLM constructs multi-scale descriptions, temporally grounded local QA, and global QA to cover video knowledge. (b) Delta-injection causal tracing estimates each model layer’s causal memory utility and selects top-K layers under a fixed adaptation budget. (c) Visual memory distillation optimizes LoRA modules in selected layers to reproduce normalized video-induced representation changes, transferring visual evidence into text-only memory.

Figure 5: Representative training examples for the multi-scale supervision pipeline. For short windows (≤ 40 s), overlapping information from the high-, mid-, and low-level descriptions is fused into one coherent, redundancy-reduced training example, whereas for long windows (≥ 80 s), the descriptions are retained as three separate examples. Local QA pairs include explicit temporal grounding, while global QA pairs are timestamp-free. Ellipses denote omitted content.

Figure 1: Comparison of video-conditioned question answering, NKR, and MIT3. Conventional video-language models encode or retrieve visual evidence per question. NKR trains a video-specific LoRA adapter on synthesized text using a fixed all-layer configuration. MIT3 instead selects videospecific model layers through causal tracing and distills the visual-evidence-induced representation change into these memory-writing locations, enabling video-free question answering.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based video matting has recently emerged as a leading approach, leveraging video diffusion priors from internet-scale pretraining to achieve strong zero-shot generalization from limited synthetic data. However, the heavy compute of these diffusion backbones limits inference to a short chunk of just 6 to 24 frames, so even ordinary videos span multiple chunks. Because each chunk is matted independently from coarse mask guidance, existing methods fail to maintain consistency across chunk boundaries, producing flickering edges and discontinuous transparency. We address this with a mask-guided diffusion-matting framework built on two ideas. The RGB and mask conditioning are represented as separate token streams that interact through full spatio-temporal self-attention, letting the model adaptively combine fine RGB texture with coarse mask layout rather than committing to a fixed channel-wise fusion. On top of this, we propose a novel pair of learnable embeddings, the preserve token and the refine token, that act as a per-frame conditioning interface and enable a sliding-window inference scheme in which already-generated mattes are propagated across chunk boundaries for local temporal consistency, complemented by a globally shared reference anchor at every chunk to prevent error accumulation in long sequences without any additional training. Across standard video matting benchmarks and in-the-wild long footage, our framework outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in both fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, and uniquely maintains consistency across chunk boundaries on long videos.
authors: Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Heeji Yoon, Seungryong Kim, Joon-Young Lee
bullets: Addresses flickering edges and discontinuous transparency caused by independently processing short video chunks.
Uses separate RGB and mask token streams with full spatio-temporal attention for adaptive conditioning.
Introduces learnable preserve and refine tokens to propagate previous mattes during sliding-window inference.
Adds a shared reference anchor to maintain global consistency and limit error accumulation without extra training.
Outperforms prior diffusion-based methods in fine-detail accuracy and temporal consistency, including on long in-the-wild videos.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the VideoMaMa++ training and inference. (Top) During training, RGB frames are paired with either a binary mask or the ground-truth alpha matte as guide input, encoded into separate token streams by a frozen VAE encoder E , and tagged with a refine token (R) or preserve token (P). The DiT processes both modes jointly within a single clip, supervised against the ground-truth matte. (Bottom) At inference, long videos are processed in a sliding-window manner. Each chunk receives the refine token on its non-overlapping frames and the preserve token on its overlap frames, which carry the previous chunk’s predicted matte. A globally selected reference anchor frame is additionally supplied as preserve input to every chunk, providing a stable anchor that prevents error accumulation across the sequence.

Figure 3: Long-video temporal consistency. Qualitative comparison between VideoMaMa++ and other methods. The comparison methods exhibits visible flickering at chunk boundaries or struggles to capture fine-grained details, while VideoMaMa++ produces smooth transitions across chunks while still capturing fine-grained details that emerge in later chunks.

Figure 6: Annotation noise in AM-2K [25]. The ground-truth alpha mattes in AM-2K often miss fine-grained internal details, that VideoMaMa++ correctly recovers. Because MAD averages pixelwise error over the entire image, these missing details penalize accurate predictions and inflate the reported error. MAD-T, computed only within the transition region, isolates the matting quality that actually matters and avoids the bias introduced by such annotation gaps.

Figure 7: Re-initialization of SAM3 on YouTubeMatte static_0017. Initializing SAM3 [3] on the first frame fails to track a sheet of paper that the subject begins holding mid-sequence, since the object is not yet visible at initialization. Initializing on a later frame where both are simultaneously visible recovers the correct mask track.
